text: PC Gareth Browning, 33, was on foot in Whitley, Reading on 30 November when he was hit by a black Mazda Aerosport driven by Luke Haywood, 28. Haywood admitted causing death by dangerous driving and seven counts of causing serious injury by dangerous driving at Reading Crown Court today (12 January). Gareth died after being rushed to the Royal Berkshire Hospital with severe head injuries. He had been walking near his home in Upper Merton Road when he was struck. A postmortem examination found that Mr Browning suffered multiple fractures as well as other internal organ damage due to the force of collision. Luke Haywood's car Credit: Thames Valley PolicePA Wire The court heard that Haywood had "a long history" of offending but did not have any previous convictions for dangerous driving or drink-driving before this incident. However, police said they were unable to determine whether he was under the influence of alcohol at the time of the crash because there was no breath test available at the hospital. Mr Browning's family described him as "the adored" father of five children aged between 12 weeks and 26 years old who are all now without their dad. Speaking outside Reading Crown Court today, Detective Inspector Kate Collins, from the Serious Collision Investigation Unit based at Reading, thanked witnesses who came forward immediately following Mr Browning's accident about what happened. She also paid tribute to those men whose efforts helped save Mr Browning's life during CPR attempts. Det Insp Collins added: 'Both incidents involved two drivers travelling through residential areas at speed. They should never have been doing so - but sadly lives have been lost as a result."

I thought I was lucky when I ended up first in line to the new Hot Angels nightclub. Now I'm not so sure. I know you're supposed to arrive at a club casually late, but I couldn't help it. I had heard so much about the club since they announced the grand opening last week, and supposedly they were going to be giving out a new drink for free to until supplies ran out. Which could be soon, considering how many people could cram into the large refurbished factory. So I had shoved my friend Kara into a mini skirt and dragged her out into the brisk spring air two hours before the club opened. The odd thing was, the bouncer was a thin old woman. She looked like she could snap in the force of the next stiff breeze, but I had watched enough YouTube to know that you couldn't judge such aged books by their covers. In one video I had seen an old woman half her size and probably ten years older kick the shit out of a shoplifter twice her size. I even dragged one of my videography school buddies over to the computer to verify that it wasn't faked. After ages of avoiding eye contact with the bouncer, and walking in small circles with Kara to keep our bare legs warm while I endured her barrage of whining, the bouncer finally reached for the velvet rope that acted as the gate between the front of the line and the club. As she did so with her left hand, she reached up to my forehead with her right and said, in unison with the hundred people who stood in line behind us, "Before we enter, we pray." I froze, my eyes finding Kara to my left. She looked like she had just shoved a handful of chocolate in her mouth and discovered it was dog crap. I didn't know if I wanted to laugh, or cry. What the hell was this? Had we waited for two hours in front of the wrong club? I didn't want to interrupt as the old woman and the crowd muttered something in a language I couldn't quite make out. When they were done, the bouncer stepped back and said, "Go right in." I started to walk away from the door, a polite smile on my face as I said, "I think we're at the wrong place." The old woman grabbed my arm just above the elbow with an iron grip, returning my polite smile as she said, "Nonsense. You are exactly where you are meant to be, child." I looked to Kara for help, but she just shrugged and tried to back away. I always was the worst at picking friends. But before she could escape, a tall woman grabbed her by the shoulders and propelled her toward the club. Was it a club? Everyone was certainly dressed for the part, but no one was acting it. The old lady half-dragged me into the dark hallway, the sound of music already thumping from some distant speakers. It sounded like normal club music. The hall looked and smelled like a normal dance club hallway. I wanted to doubt what I had just seen, to chalk up the whole praying thing as a hallucination, but the bouncer's painful grip on my arm reminded me that I wasn't in Kansas anymore. The hall opened onto a large dance floor, new, yet thoroughly scuffed, with a large stage to the right, a man with a gaudy gold medallion hanging from his neck already bobbing his head as he played with the soundboard. The medallion looked religious, but it wasn't any symbol I recognized. To the left was a bar, with a cage on the wall behind it, a scantily dressed woman standing inside. At first, I thought she was a dancer. Then I realized she wasn't moving. Chains connected from her wrists to the ceiling of the cage, holding her upright. In the dim light, I couldn't tell if she was conscious or not, but I could make out a thin red cord extending from her thigh down to one of the taps. A row of glasses filled with a red beverage already lined the bar: tonight's limited edition new drink.

Despite this, the ethno-geographic caste hierarchy favored the Mongols and other ethnic groups, granting them greater status than the majority Han Chinese. While Han Chinese advisors often held more influence than high-ranking officials, their social standing was less clearly defined. Kublai Khan also discontinued China's traditional civil service exams, which were later restored under Ayurbarwada Buyantu Khan. Rossabi notes that Kublai acknowledged the need to employ Chinese advisors and officials for governance, but he could not completely depend on them due to the necessity of maintaining a balance between ruling the sedentary Chinese civilization and preserving Mongol culture and values. He was preoccupied with the interests of his Chinese subjects while also seeking to exploit the empire's resources for personal growth. According to Rossabi, his goals and priorities shifted throughout his reign. Van Praag states in The Status of Tibet that the Tibetans and Mongols maintained a dual system of governance and an interdependent relationship, which justified the succession of Mongol khans as universal Buddhist rulers, or chakravartins. Van Praag adds that Tibet remained an independent part of the empire and was never fully incorporated into it, citing examples like a licensed border market between China and Tibet during the Yuan Dynasty.

Some say it was Satan's way of tempting us or the gods way of judging us. Some claimed it to be aliens. Plenty more considered it evolution. Me? I'm going with the whole gist of'I don't know how it started, that doesn't matter, it's here now.' 15 Years ago, at the peak of the twenty first century, everyone gained the same ability - to'break' reality, to change themselves to'snap' their minds. You basically break a piece off, in return you unlock some form of power - be it near useless or something out of a comic book. People had varying amounts of control, but one thing remained common..... the larger the power, the greater the hole left behind - and that hole -always- filled itself with bad stuff. Once people learned how to'snap' their minds, there were thousands of vegetables worldwide who ignored the warnings everyone gave them, the powers of gods locked in a empty husk in a mind. So people began to try and find the'edge', where they keep their mind intact but still gained hefty powers. Chaos ensued shortly after. Major city's burnt and rioted as violent powers were soon given to those were now insane psychopaths. People who chose to do good or to heal any disease soon found themselves suicidal and depressed, never able to live long enough to use their powers the way they'd truly wanted. So the art of training ones mind to control exactly how much you snap and what powers you gain became the trend. I joined one of those once - they were very helpful in getting me where I am now. Of course plenty of people abused this and got subtle, weak powers while able to keep their mind more-or-less steady enough to use them correctly. There's the unending war of'super heroes' who took their powers to defend the innocent who refused to risk their minds from the'super-villains' who'd taken more power they can control and had gone mad. My father had been one of these super villains - he'd been away in middle east, fighting the latest conflict we'd decided to get involved with - and he wanted the power to end it without losing anymore lives. Word has it he's still rampaging through the desert, slaughtering indiscriminately. My mother is still a Senior Doctor, she wanted the ability to close flesh and wounds the like with the touch of a finger - able to perform conflicted operations in seconds and save countless lives. Sadly this gave her late-stage Alzheimer's and the next day she gets into work she's forgotten the name of all the patients she has saved, and quite often mine too. I however am the first in attempting a very particular type of snap - the reverse snap. Lose a power, regain a mental ability. I've suffered with both depression and autism my entire life until I tried this. I've lost the'power' to speak and move my legs. But personally, I think I've become the most powerful of them all - finally able to appreciate life for what it truly is.

Worries were expressed regarding the preparedness of the two nations to jointly host the competition, with concerns about potential incidents of fan violence and racism. However, during a BBC Sport interview, Pohorecki stated that Euro 2012 was a successful event. "We feel proud because many people doubted we could make it, but we did," he mentioned. The host nation was France, with 24 participating countries for the first time, increasing from 16 in 2012, and featuring 51 matches over a single month. Disputes occurred during a match between Russia and Poland in Warsaw on June 12, where rival fan groups clashed. While acknowledging improvements, Pohorecki downplayed these incidents and isolated instances of racial abuse. "From all the reported cases I've seen, there's always something we can improve upon for the next tournament," he said. "The next tournament is in France, so we'll share our insights with them." He also expressed surprise at a BBC Panorama program prior to the event, which questioned whether UEFA should have chosen Poland and Ukraine as hosts due to evidence of racist violence. "I was surprised by it because such programs can be made in any country," he asserted. "They can be made in England, the Netherlands, and even here in France. This type of message can be conveyed anywhere." Pohorecki noted that large-scale events inherently bring challenges, citing examples like riots in Warsaw followed by medical reports showing six injured individuals. He emphasized that such situations are common, comparing them to a typical wedding in Poland where six people might be hospitalized. Pohorecki supported UEFA President Michel Platini, who suggested that the 2020 European Championship could be held in multiple cities across Europe instead of a single location.

Several barriers protect organisms from infection, including mechanical, chemical, and biological barriers. The waxy cuticle of many leaves, the exoskeleton of insects, the shells and membranes of externally deposited eggs, and skin are examples of mechanical barriers that are the first line of defense against infection. However, as organisms cannot be completely sealed from their environments, other systems act to protect body openings such as the lungs, intestines, and the genitourinary tract. In the lungs, coughing and sneezing mechanically eject pathogens and other irritants from the respiratory tract. The flushing action of tears and urine also mechanically expels pathogens, while mucus secreted by the respiratory and gastrointestinal tract serves to trap and entangle microorganisms.

Approaches that use choreography for service composition usually assume that once a set of services is identified that appropriately fulfills the roles specified in the choreography, each service adheres to its assigned role. Honest services are not safeguarded from adversaries. We introduce a contract model grounded in an extended version of Petri nets, enabling services to defend themselves while still executing the choreography. This model is connected to Propositional Contract Logic through a translation of logical statements into our Petri nets, maintaining the concept of agreement and facilitating compositional validation.

Step 9: Marking Door Strike Location on Shaft If using two deadbolts like we have here, mark where they will be installed for easy reference when installing them. Remember the location where each strike should sit flush against the door frame so that we'll know which direction we need to install our long screws. We're going to use these marks as guides while putting together both lock mechanisms but also make sure there isn't any wood between the bolt headkeyway area and either the first or second holes drilled into our shafts. The easiest way I've found to do this was with masking tape wrapped around the bolts, then tracing out their exact path onto my piece of wood laying across the doorsill just below the top edge of the casing. I marked with pencil, since I'm not too confident about drilling through stainless steel...but if anyone has better advice please let me know!:) Once you've got everything lined up correctly, drill pilot holes into the bottom edges of the cleats near those marks, making certain to keep things even throughout the length of the hole. This may take some manipulation depending upon how close the faceplate sits to the outer edge, etc., but try to stay consistent otherwise the longer screw won't line back up properly after installation. Place the nuts over the ends of the threaded rods before tightening down each setscrew - remember what size nut goes on what sized rod? It's ok if you don't; most hardware stores sell kits specifically designed to solve such problems anyway. Once again, test fit the parts before fully assembling anything else because more often than not something might look right on paper only to require minor tweaks once tightened down completely. In other words, check stuff every step along the way rather than waiting till its almost time to put things away for winter. As a fan of Halloween-related events, I visited Universal Studios Halloween Horror Nights and Knott's Scary Farm, among others, and found this place to be one of the most impressive Halloween attractions outside the Las Vegas Strip. On a Sunday when we had free time, we decided to check out the Freakling Brothers Trilogy of Terror for some Halloween fun. The three houses look like carnival setups or places where people enter and never leave. I hadn't expected the buildings to be constructed from trailers connected together, but they felt just as authentic and well-made as many of my favorite haunts. All three were thoroughly executed. I won't reveal any details, but if you visit, make sure to purchase the VIP front-line pass. You also get a T-shirt as an extra, which isn't too bad. We began with the Circus of Terror. The ticket takers were dressed up, and before entering, a ringmaster asked if we wanted to go inside and provided the rules. Once inside, I was amazed at how detailed and eerie each location was. There were rooms with events and others where I had to figure out what to do. The conclusion was something I'll never forget. Next, we moved to Castle Vampyre. Igor handled our tickets, and the vampire woman explained the rules and ensured we wanted to go inside. It was dark and twisted again. This was my favorite of the three. There were rooms where I had to decide on actions and some effects that made me pause, thinking I needed to use a rope to cross. The ending left me in awe, watching more than just being scared. Our last stop was the Gates of Hell. You must sign a waiver since it's R-rated, and only those over 17 are allowed in. I admitted I was a bit nervous because I learned about one of the activities, but I was okay inside. This one was quite intense.

Cluster-wise linear regression (CLR), a clustering problem intertwined with regression, is to find clusters of entities such that the overall sum of squared errors from regressions performed over these clusters is minimized, where each cluster may have different variances. We generalize the CLR problem by allowing each entity to have more than one observation, and refer to it as generalized CLR. We propose an exact mathematical programming based approach relying on column generation, a column generation based heuristic algorithm that clusters predefined groups of entities, a metaheuristic genetic algorithm with adapted Lloyd's algorithm for K-means clustering, a two-stage approach, and a modified algorithm of Spath for solving generalized CLR. We examine the performance of our algorithms on a stock keeping unit (SKU) clustering problem employed in forecasting halo and cannibalization effects in promotions using real-world retail data from a large supermarket chain. In the SKU clustering problem, the retailer needs to cluster SKUs based on their seasonal effects in response to promotions. The seasonal effects are the results of regressions with predictors being promotion mechanisms and seasonal dummies performed over clusters generated. We compare the performance of all proposed algorithms for the SKU problem with real-world and synthetic data.

Massive MIMO base-stations utilizing TDDOFDM and depending on uplink training for both downlink and uplink transmissions are considered a promising option for 5G implementations due to their potential for high-area spectral and energy efficiency along with straightforward low-latency operations. Our study explores the application of non-orthogonal uplink pilot schemes to enhance the area spectral efficiency in the downlink of these advanced MIMO cellular systems. We propose a set of pilot design methods that ensure local orthogonality within each cell while maintaining minimal inner-product characteristics between codes from different cells. By leveraging channel estimates derived from these coded observations, each cell individually supports its active users through MU-MIMO transmission, which is also engineered to reduce interference to a group of "strongly interfered" users outside the cell. Simulation results demonstrate that this approach leads to improved user-rate cumulative distribution functions compared to traditional operations, offering opportunities to enhance both cell performance and throughput.

While significant improvements have been made in recent years in terms of end-to-end automatic speech recognition (ASR) performance, such improvements were obtained through the use of very large neural networks, unfit for embedded use on edge devices. That being said, in this paper, we work on simplifying and compressing Transformer-based encoder-decoder architectures for the end-to-end ASR task. We empirically introduce a more compact Speech-Transformer by investigating the impact of discarding particular modules on the performance of the model. Moreover, we evaluate reducing the numerical precision of our network's weights and activations while maintaining the performance of the full-precision model. Our experiments show that we can reduce the number of parameters of the full-precision model and then further compress the model 4x by fully quantizing to 8-bit fixed point precision.

In his book, The Greatest Show on Earth: The Evidence for Evolution, biologist Richard Dawkins grapples with the question of why pain has to be so very painful. He describes the alternative as a simple, mental raising of a "red flag." To argue why that red flag might be insufficient, Dawkins explains that drives must compete with each other within living beings. The most fit creature would be the one whose pains are well balanced. Those pains which mean certain death when ignored will become the most powerfully felt. The relative intensities of pain, then, may resemble the relative importance of that risk to our ancestors (lack of food, too much cold, or serious injuries are felt as agony, whereas minor damage is felt as mere discomfort). This resemblance will not be perfect, however, because natural selection can be a poor designer. The result is often glitches in animals, including supernormal stimuli. Such glitches help explain pains which are not, or at least no longer directly adaptive (e.g. perhaps some forms of toothache, or injury to fingernails).

Neon is not the correct term for these items; fluorescent colors are the right description because they emit light through fluorescence. Neon is simply a common misconception used for these colors. What does fluorescence mean? It refers to the process where materials absorb light that is not visible to the human eye and then emit visible light shortly after. This is what makes fluorescent colors appear brighter than white. For example, fluorescent materials like highlighters glow brightly under black light. The connection between fluorescent bulbs and this phenomenon lies in their composition: the inner part of the bulb contains a fluorescent coating, and when an electric arc passes through the gas inside (similar to neon signs), it produces ultraviolet (UV) light. This UV light interacts with the coating, causing it to emit visible light. Thus, fluorescent bulbs function similarly to the process described.

If you're referring to items like yellow safety vests or bright pink clothing, it’s because they are fluorescent. The UV light from the sun or an arc lamp causes them to glow. You might not notice the glow unless you use a UV light in a dimly lit room, but in sunlight, they appear much brighter. Laundry detergents contain fluorescent dyes that make white fabric glow faintly in UV light. You may observe this effect when wearing socks or T-shirts during a glow-bowling event. In sunlight, these items look whiter.

The primary objective of the European Central Bank, as mandated in Article 2 of the Statute of the ECB, is to maintain price stability within the Eurozone. The basic tasks, as defined in Article 3 of the Statute, are to define and implement the monetary policy for the Eurozone, to conduct foreign exchange operations, to take care of the foreign reserves of the European System of Central Banks and operation of the financial market infrastructure under the TARGET2 payments system and the technical platform (currently being developed) for settlement of securities in Europe (TARGET2 Securities). The idea that unifying all of the small countries in Europe into a single nation like the United States is a misguided one. Small countries often have their own distinct cultural identities and traditions, which would be lost if they were to be unified into one large nation. Furthermore, it would be difficult to adequately represent the needs and interests of all of these disparate cultures in a single government. Additionally, larger nations tend to have more centralized power, which could lead to a loss of local autonomy and increased inequality among citizens. Ultimately, there are better ways to ensure peace and stability in Europe without sacrificing the individual identities of its many small countries.

I think it's important for us as young scholars of literature at UBC to be reminded about what we learn from Fitzgerald. The importance of working on projects outside of our own fields is critical. Otherwise, we will never really recognize how valuable our work can be when compared with other disciplines or even literary works. We are all guilty of this; however, in the case of students like Fitzgerald who were interested in travelling abroad instead of pursuing their dreams, it may have affected his writing more than any potential employment. He probably would not have been able to take his studies abroad for several reasons: firstly (and most importantly), he did not want to leave his family behind, secondly because he knew that studying overseas would require him to sacrifice time away from them, and finally, because he felt pressure from an external perspective to pursue something outside of his field. However, by being exposed to new ideas, different perspectives and cultures he experienced through these experiences which "woke" within him, it opened up avenues for future exploration of himself. Through such experiences, the drive to write became stronger. This drives me towards the next topic: How do writers travel? How can the arts community encourage people to keep exploring themselves? Fitzgerald wrote about his travels in an autobiographical essay titled "Butterfly in the Garden" . In this piece, he discusses going to New York City to read a play during one of his trips, meeting others in New York for the first time who shared similar customs and lifestyles as he did, and trying to fit into their worlds. He also describes the sounds he hears at the theatre while performing; the way patrons whisper each other without knowing anyone else is eerie. He goes onto describe how everyone reacts differently depending upon whether they are wearing shoes or socks in public places. He went on to say that traveling inspired him to become a writer, but also called attention to the ways in which people can change over time: ..."you may begin your journey of self-discovery... then in a few years you must decide that art isn't for you anymore...." His last trip took place in Paris where he stayed with Soraya Jain, an English teacher who helped him realise scriving doesn't make life better in itself. She told him she had spent her days teaching children in Pakistan, only to see herself driven into the arms of a man twenty years older than her. He found out later that she was married to a neurosurgeon. And yet, despite these events, he continued to write, although the two ended up breaking off their relationship due to incompatibilities. What emerges from this experience is his determination to stay true to himself, and his drive to find a love and connection with someone who challenged him. And although there is no clear path to follow, Fitzgerald expressed genuine excitement about the possibility of being drawn into the human heart the ultimate romantic fantasy.[22] To be honest, I don't know if any of my friends have ever traveled internationally - I haven't either, to be honest! But we should always open ourselves up to new experiences and understand the power they hold in changing our lives.[23]

Often rules apply to all goods neutrally, but may have a greater practical effect on imports than domestic products. For such "indirect" discriminatory (or "indistinctly applicable measures the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) has developed the so-called "Mezza di Pasta doctrine." The Mezza di Pasta doctrine entails that in case an indirect discriminatory measure leads to an infringement of a fundamental freedom of the EU Treaty (e.g. free movement of goods, freedom of establishment, free movement of workers or capital), the EU-legislator may not apply the discriminatory measure. This has been confirmed by the CJEU in its recent judgement in the case "C-55016." In this case, the question arose whether the Mezza di Pasta doctrine would be applicable in the case of a restrictive measure for the import of products, in so far as the relevant regulation contained a derogation for the protection of public health. The case concerned the import of products, which had been tested in a laboratory outside the EU and, therefore, were not subject to the EU rules on the protection of laboratory animals. The EU-legislator considered that these products should be considered as not in conformity with the Directive on the protection of laboratory animals and prohibited the import thereof. However, the CJEU considered that the Directive on the protection of laboratory animals could not be applied to products imported from third countries, since this would lead to an infringement of the free movement of goods. According to the CJEU, the Directive could only apply to products that were manufactured in the EU, if the rules were applied in a non-discriminatory manner. The CJEU also considered the provision of the Directive, which provided for a derogation from the fundamental freedoms if they had to be limited for the protection of public health. However, the CJEU considered that this provision could not be applied in the present case, since the Directive was intended to protect laboratory animals and not to protect the health of humans. This judgement of the CJEU is important for companies importing products into the EU. The judgement shows that the EU-legislator cannot rely on a derogation for the protection of public health, if the EU-legislation in question does not aim to protect human health. Source: Judgement of 15 November 2018, case C-55016 International Trade, Customs WTO

Local Policy Search is a popular reinforcement learning approach for handling large state spaces. Formally, it searches locally in a parameterized policy space in order to maximize the associated value function averaged over some predefined distribution. It is probably commonly believed that the best one can hope in general from such an approach is to get a local optimum of this criterion. In this article, we show the following surprising result: any (approximate) local optimum enjoys a global performance guarantee . We compare this guarantee with the one that is satisfied by Direct Policy Iteration, an approximate dynamic programming algorithm that does some form of Policy Search: if the approximation error of Local Policy Search may generally be bigger (because local search requires to consider a space of stochastic policies), we argue that the concentrability coefficient that appears in the performance bound is much nicer. Finally, we discuss several practical and theoretical consequences of our analysis.

Since this is ELI5, I feel compelled to give some explanation instead of a simple "take this" answer. Also, IANAD (nor nurse nor other medical professional, but I do read labels). There are two types of common OTC painkillers in the US: acetaminophen (called paracetamol in most other countries, and best known as the ordinary Tylenol brand) and NSAIDs. Acetaminophen in the right dosage has fewer side effects, but (and it's a big but), it doesn't take a lot to take too much of it, causing serious liver damage. This is a problem because many multi-symptom cold medicines also contain it, and it can be bad if you take both acetaminophen for a headache and a cold medicine that also contains acetaminophen. NSAID stands for non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, which mean these not only reduce pain but also reduce inflammation (which acetaminophen doesn't). One of their side effects is stomach irritation, so you'd probably avoid them if you frequently have heartburn or upset stomach. But for most people, if you're only going to have one painkiller in the house, an NSAID is preferable for two reasons: One, it's better for joint and muscle pain than acetaminophen, and two, so many cold medicines are bundled with acetaminophen, that there's a risk of accidental overdose if you take both a cold medicine and a painkiller that has acetaminophen. After aspirin, the most commonly used OTC NSAID is ibuprofen, which is fine. For more chronic pain (say hand or wrist pain from too much typing), IMHO naproxen would be a better choice. But, they are always learning more about these drugs, so stay informed. They're safe to take as directed, which means for something like a sore joint, several days in a row is ok. But if you're getting headaches as frequently as once a week, it's time to see a doctor. Not because the medications are bad at that level (many people with arthritis will take such things daily), but because frequent headaches might be a symptom of something else that requires medical attention. Likewise for a very severe headache (which could be a migraine but could also be an indication of meningitis). The Home Affairs Committee noted that there were not enough officers initially deployed and that police training for handling public unrest was insufficient. The Metropolitan Police acknowledged its efforts to enhance these measures. A report on policing large-scale disorder, based on events in August 2011, indicated that deploying more police to the streets was essential in calming the situation. It stated, "Had more officers been deployed faster, some of the incidents might have been prevented." The report expressed regret at the outcome and viewed the operation in several towns and cities, especially London, as lacking in effectiveness. It mentioned that the mutual aid system, where officers are transferred between forces, could have functioned more efficiently; however, it may have left areas where officers were loaned to other forces vulnerable. The report cited anecdotal evidence suggesting that widespread disorder began when residents observed police "losing control" in Tottenham through TV and social media. This aligns with findings from the independent Riots Communities and Victims Panel. The report highlighted that there was a sense that valuable items could be obtained through theft, with an element of opportunistic crime and imitation behavior. It emphasized that the lack of police presence or the appearance of police officers remaining idle allowed criminal activities to occur, which was distressing for victims. Chairman Keith Vaz MP remarked that individual officers showed courage and were commended for their actions, but he noted that in London and other regions, compared to the effective responses in some towns, there was a failure in police coordination.

The thalidomide disaster revived Kefauver's legislation aimed at improving drug regulation, which had been blocked by Congress. The Kefauver-Harris Amendment was enacted on 10 October 1962. From then on, pharmaceutical companies had to demonstrate both efficacy and safety to the FDA before launching their medications in the U.S. The FDA gained the power to oversee prescription drug advertising and set standards for production quality. The law mandated that all drugs marketed between 1938 and 1962 must have proven effectiveness. A joint study by the FDA and the National Academy of Sciences found that about 40% of these products lacked effectiveness. A comparable thorough examination of over-the-counter products started ten years later.

Splits on canned beans appear in the process of preparation and canning. Researchers are studying how they are influenced by cooking environment and genotype. However, there is no existing method to automatically quantify or to characterize the severity of splits. To solve this, we propose two measures: the Bean Split Ratio (BSR) that quantifies the overall severity of splits, and the Bean Split Histogram (BSH) that characterizes the size distribution of splits. We create a pixel-wise segmentation method to automatically estimate these measures from images. We also present a bean dataset of recombinant inbred lines of two genotypes, use the BSR and BSH to assess canning quality, and explore heritability of these properties.

Independent Component Analysis (ICA) is a dimensionality reduction method that enhances the efficiency of machine learning models working with probability density functions, such as Bayesian neural networks. Adaptive ICA algorithms, although converging more slowly than their nonadaptive counterparts, can effectively track alterations in the underlying distribution of input features. The inherent slowness of adaptive methods, coupled with current hardware limitations that operate at extremely low clock speeds, requires significant advancements in both algorithmic and hardware design. This paper introduces an algorithm that facilitates efficient hardware implementation of ICA. Compared to prior research, our FPGA-based adaptive ICA achieves a minimum improvement of one order of magnitude in clock frequency and two orders of magnitude in data throughput. The proposed approach is not restricted to ICA and can be applied to diverse machine learning tasks involving stochastic gradient descent optimization.

We propose to combine the robustness merit of model-based approaches and the learning power of data-driven approaches for image restoration. Specifically, by integrating graph Laplacian regularization as a trainable module into a deep learning framework, we are less susceptible to overfitting than pure CNN-based approaches, achieving higher robustness to small dataset and cross-domain denoising. First, a sparse neighborhood graph is built from the output of a convolutional neural network (CNN). Then the image is restored by solving an unconstrained quadratic programming problem, using a corresponding graph Laplacian regularizer as a prior term. The proposed restoration pipeline is fully differentiable and hence can be end-to-end trained. Experimental results demonstrate that our work avoids overfitting given small training data. It is also endowed with strong cross-domain generalization power, outperforming the state-of-the-art approaches by remarkable margin.

Jolie's emotional speech was met with tears from the audience, as she spoke about her connection to the people and the history of Bosnia. "I will never forget the people I met and the stories I heard when I first came here years ago," Jolie said. Jolie is the latest recipient of the award, following in the footsteps of acclaimed directors such as Ken Loach, Mike Leigh, and Atom Egoyan. The Sarajevo Film Festival, which has been running since 1995, is one of the biggest cultural events in the Balkans. It aims to promote dialogue, understanding, and cultural exchange through the medium of film. On 18 September, Bismarck convened with Favre at the Chateau de Ferrieres and requested a French frontier free from retaliation, encompassing Strasbourg, Alsace, and much of the Moselle region in Lorraine, with Metz as its capital. In exchange for an armistice enabling the French to choose a National Assembly, Bismarck demanded the surrender of Strasbourg and Toul, a fortress city. To facilitate supplies to Paris, one of the outer fortifications had to be surrendered. Favre was unaware that Bismarck's demanding conditions were intended to secure a lasting peace along Germany's new western border, ideally through a treaty with a supportive government, under terms favorable to French public sentiment. An unbreakable military boundary was considered inferior by Bismarck, who preferred a more flexible arrangement favored by nationalist groups within Germany.

It was a normal day just like any other day. I had woken up early morning and headed to work while the sun was still rising. I had been feeling off for the last few weeks, but nothing had been out of the ordinary that would make me suspicious. I had been experiencing nausea, fatigue, and lack of appetite but these were symptoms, which were common to me whenever I had flu. But something didn't feel right, and I couldn't put my finger on it. As the days went by, I started to feel even more tired and weak than usual. I was signed off from work for two days, hoping that some rest would help me feel better. As I lay in bed, I couldn't shake off the feeling that something was different. I did a quick online search of my symptoms and was stunned when the search results showed that these could be early signs of pregnancy. I had never been pregnant before, and the thought of it was overwhelming. I didn't know how I would feel about it. I was scared, and my heart was racing faster than usual. I decided to take a test to confirm it. As I waited for the test results, my thoughts went crazy, thinking about all the responsibilities that come with being a mother. A few minutes went by, and I finally got the courage to check the results. I couldn't believe it! The test was positive. Tears rolled down my eyes as I looked at the test results. The thought of bringing another life in the world was overwhelming, but I knew I had to accept the responsibility. The day, which had started out to be normal, turned out to be an extraordinary day, and a new journey began. Although I was scared and didn't know what the future held, I knew I had to embrace it with an open mind and heart. Looking back now, I can't believe that it's been five years since the day I found out I was pregnant. My daughter, who is now five, is the joy of my life, and I wouldn't have it any other way. That was the day that changed my life forever.

European art music is largely distinguished from many other non-European and popular musical forms by its system of staff notation, in use since about the 16th century. Western staff notation is used by composers to prescribe to the performer the pitches (e.g., melodies, basslines andor chords), tempo, meter and rhythms for a piece of music. This leaves less room for practices such as improvisation and ad libitum ornamentation, which are frequently heard in non-European art music and in popular music styles such as jazz and blues. Another difference is that whereas most popular styles lend themselves to the song form, classical music has been noted for its development of highly sophisticated forms of instrumental music such as the concerto, symphony, sonata, and mixed vocal and instrumental styles such as opera which, since they are written down, can attain a high level of complexity.

Do you mean rugs made in Iran, or the general category of "Oriental" rugs? "Orientals" - which we'll describe generally as hand-tufted wool rugs - are, well, handmade. Since they're wool (or silk), typically on a cotton warp, with good care they'll last forever, and like other antiques, antique "Oriental" rugs appreciate with age (all other things like condition and workmanship being equal). The designs are original, and because they're handmade you get that made-by-hand quirkiness a lot of us like. Wool and silk also absorb dye (and reflect light) like no other fiber. They also "work" with virtually every decor style. We love them with Danish Modern furniture, for example, while my grandparents had them with the classic Jacobean repro furniture of the 1920s-30s. Persian rugs are particularly fine, with the best having more tufts of yarn per square inch than your average Central Asian tribal rug, for example. They're known for their pictorial (rather than geometric) motifs, which can be amazingly elaborate, looking more like fine embroidery than tufting. So basically: artistic quality, fine materials, and an incredible amount of labor.

However, these approaches are sensitive only to changes in pitch and can thus be defeated by short recordings with varying speeds or tempo - a technique called "sampling attack" that is frequently used for copyright infringement purposes on iTunes and Amazon Music. In order to overcome this limitation, alternative solutions based upon content analysis were proposed: Bayesian classification methods such as Support Vector Machines (SVM) classify spectrograms into classes according to their learned model; HMM techniques try to identify feature patterns common among tracks belonging to similar genres [3]; music fingerprinting algorithms attempt automatically extract musical features contained within each track's spectrum which allow them infer its genre type [4]; etc., as well other less advanced forms like clustering [5], dimensionality reduction [6] and morphological filtering [7-9]. In this context, a "drone" refers to an unmanned aircraft. It is a plane without a pilot. People are concerned about its use because it is often employed for surveillance, which is generally disliked. Compared to standard planes, drones can remain airborne for extended periods, operate quietly, and offer greater flexibility. Internationally, the United States frequently employs drones to target individuals in other nations, such as Pakistan and Yemen. This practice occurs without authorization from those countries, making it highly contentious.

The core idea behind unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) should not be controversial. The actual device itself is not the problem; rather, the specific use cases provoke concern. People aren't typically alarmed by planes that carry missiles, as long as they are used for legitimate purposes. UAVs are commonly linked to targeted assassinations, known as "drone strikes," and monitoring activities, but soon we'll witness their integration into various commercial sectors. For instance, institutions like MSU are utilizing drones for agricultural assessments, while emergency services in the Western U.S. employ them to monitor wildfires. These are only two examples, and numerous other applications are currently under development.

The lack of commercial adoption stems from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) not having established clear guidelines for UAV usage, and businesses aiming to create specialized drone technology must secure FAA approval. Once approved, these entities may develop and test their applications but cannot yet deploy drones commercially. As a result, we can expect to see commercial applications of drones within the next five to ten years. The use of drones beyond concerns related to privacy and foreign affairs will likely not be considered significant.

MIT announced that it is planning a 1 billion college called the MIT Stephen A. Schwarzman College of Computing, named after Blackstone CEO Steve Schwarzman who donated 350 million. The 300 million gift is the largest single donation in MIT's history. In the same announcement, MIT said that it will be using some of the gift to fund an ethics and AI study program, as well as a 5 million gift from the Omidyar Foundation for the same. "The MIT Schwarzman College of Computing will constitute both a global center for computing research and education, and an intellectual foundry for powerful new AI tools," MIT President L. Rafael Reif wrote in a letter to the university community. "In a world where machines will increasingly augment and even replace human capabilities, the college will equip students and researchers in any discipline to use computing to advance their fields; to think critically about the human impact of their work; and to hone both their skills and their responsibilities." The gift will help MIT create 50 new faculty positions within the college, as well as 100 new graduate fellowships. The college will also have new dedicated space within the university's main campus. "We are in an era of profound and unprecedented change, and MIT is uniquely situated to address the consequent opportunities and challenges," Reif said. "The MIT Schwarzman College of Computing will constitute both a global center for computing research and education, and an intellectual foundry for powerful new AI tools. In a world where machines will increasingly augment and even replace human capabilities, the college will equip students and researchers in any discipline to use computing to advance their fields; to think critically about the human impact of their work; and to hone both their skills and their responsibilities." The AI Ethics and Policy Initiative will be led by Harvard University's Berkman Klein Center for Internet and Society, the MIT Media Lab, and the MIT Institute for Data Systems and Society (IDSS). The initiative will look at both technical and ethical issues surrounding AI. "We have to think about the societal and ethical implications of artificial intelligence," MIT Provost Martin Schmidt said in a statement. "We need to understand how we control these systems, how they are going to behave, how they are going to affect society, how we can get the most out of them, how we can make sure they are safe." The effort will include a "five-day residency for 25 U.S. mayors focused on the policy and governance issues arising from advances in AI and related technologies." It will also support "research that addresses policy and ethics questions in artificial intelligence and related technologies, as well as the development of curricula for students to study these issues." "As the impact of AI and other technologies on society becomes more significant, it is important to ensure that these technologies are designed with ethical considerations in mind," Omidyar Network managing partner Matt Bannick said in a statement. "We are proud to partner with MIT to support the Ethics and Governance of Artificial Intelligence Initiative, which will convene global experts to develop frameworks to guide and govern the development and application of these powerful technologies."

A team of scientists launched a box containing four types of bacteria and fungus into the stratosphere to expose them to several hours of Mars-like conditions. The experiment found that the bacteria, not the fungi, were better able to survive in such difficult environmental conditions.[2] The researchers had previously tested bacterial survival under simulated Martian gravity on Earth with mixed results. This time, they used a small rocket to carry sterilized vials, packed inside an insulating "biobox" made from polymers including styrene sulfonate. Four chambers held each type of microorganism: Bacillus subtilis (two) and Penicillium chrysogenum (one), both common soil microbes; and Aspergilli spp., also known as moulds or mildews.[34] The box was ejected at around 100 kilometreshour, after which its temperature rose rapidly. On Earth, temperatures reached almost 45 C,[5] causing condensation within minutes, which meant water vapour and carbon dioxide formed ice crystals instead of gas bubbles.[6] Researchers expected to see similar results during this flight but did not expect how quickly it would happen as a result of the insulated biobox and expedited ejection.[7] A press release by NASA stated that "after just 6 minutes... The personal copying exemption in the copyright law of EU member states stems from the EU Copyright Directive of 2001, which is generally devised to allow EU members to enact laws sanctioning making copies without authorization, as long as they are for personal, noncommerical use. The Copyright Directive was not intended to legitimize file-sharing, but rather the common practice of space shifting copyright-protected content from a legally purchased CD (for example) to certain kinds of devices and media, provided rights holders are compensated and no copy protection measures are circumvented. Rights-holder compensation takes various forms, depending on the country, but is generally either a levy on "recording" devices and media, or a tax on the content itself. In some countries, such as Canada, the applicability of such laws to copying onto general-purpose storage devices like computer hard drives, portable media players, and phones, for which no levies are collected, has been the subject of debate and further efforts to reform copyright law.

Dr Henry McLaughlin believes that physical and mental wellbeing can be improved by a daily mountain climb. The idea is that people climb to the top of Slievemartin outside Rostrevor - known locally as the Cairn - take a selfie and then post the picture on the'Cairnuary' Facebook page. The mountain is 485m high, so Dr McLaughlin said if you climb it 31 times in a month, you've climbed higher than Everest. He said he could see how his patients have benefitted. "January's a time when I see a lot of depression and this challenge is pretty good for mental health and physical health," Dr McLaughlin said. "A lot of people buy exercise bikes and then they gather dust. So this is something that's free, they get to climb up the mountain every day for a month. "It's a good hard exercise, it takes them about an hour. "They don't need exercise bikes and they don't need to join gyms and pay money for stuff, it's out there and they can discover the mountains." Those climbing the mountain can chose their own route - which could involve anything up to a 10km hike - or they can use a bike if they want. Dr McLaughlin said between 30 to 50 people were now climbing the mountain daily and all sorts of people are taking part. "There's one lady who's a patient of mine who's been very ill in the past and has had surgeries to her feet and really shouldn't be able to do it, but she's going from the car park half way up the mountain and she's doing it every day," he said. "There's people with depression doing it - I know it's good for them - people who are overweight doing it, there are people who are very healthy doing it as well. "People are all very encouraging of each other." Dr McLaughlin said he climbed the mountain at about 06:00 GMT on Thursday and had eight other people for company. "Normally you'd climb the mountain at six o'clock in the morning and you wouldn't see a soul," he said. The final climb will be a communal one on Sunday, but Dr McLaughlin said he hoped to come up with something else to keep his patients exercising. "I'm hoping to follow it on with some sort of challenge for the rest of the year that will keep them doing stuff," he said. "As far as I'm concerned, it's probably doing my work good in that maybe some people are going to get fit that I won't see. "I'd recommend it to anybody. There could be a cairn near you, it doesn't have to be my cairn, it could be a hill or a mountain near you."

Early diagnosis and accurate segmentation of brain tumors are imperative for successful treatment. Unfortunately, manual segmentation is time consuming, costly and despite extensive human expertise often inaccurate. Here, we present an MRI-based tumor segmentation framework using an autoencoder-regularized 3D-convolutional neural network. We trained the model on manually segmented structural T1, T1ce, T2, and Flair MRI images of 335 patients with tumors of variable severity, size and location. We then tested the model using independent data of 125 patients and successfully segmented brain tumors into three subregions: the tumor core (TC), the enhancing tumor (ET) and the whole tumor (WT). We also explored several data augmentations and preprocessing steps to improve segmentation performance. Importantly, our model was implemented on a single NVIDIA GTX1060 graphics unit and hence optimizes tumor segmentation for widely affordable hardware. In sum, we present a memory-efficient and affordable solution to tumor segmentation to support the accurate diagnostics of oncological brain pathologies.

Fractals are objects that do not appear smooth even when examined closely. A simple example is the Sierpinski triangle. Begin with an equilateral triangle and remove the central smaller triangle, leaving three. Repeat this process on each of the three remaining triangles, creating nine, then twenty-seven, and so on, indefinitely. The Sierpinski triangle emerges as the result of this infinite iteration. When you zoom into it, you observe increasingly smaller voids and triangles filled with even smaller voids and triangles. In contrast, zooming into a standard triangle reveals that its sides eventually look like straight lines, after which they remain straight. Fractals aim to describe natural phenomena where perfect geometric forms are absent, replaced instead by progressively smaller irregularities. One of the earliest known examples is the coastline of Britain. Estimating the length of Britain's coast involves observing patterns in its outline. However, as you zoom in, the coastline becomes longer than initially thought, and the estimated length continues to grow with each magnification. This suggests that a coastline is not a straight line but a complex curve. Representing it as a line is therefore misleading, leading to the term "fractal." In summary, fractals are objects that never fully resemble geometric shapes, regardless of how close you examine them. Many natural entities exhibit this property. Self-similar fractals can be generated by applying simple iterative rules, such as the Sierpinski casket. Alternatively, one might simply recreate such structures.

It depends on the state. In some states, closed primaries are held, wherein voters must belong to a party to vote in that party's primaries. This means, for instance, only registered Democrats can vote in the Democratic primary for a particular office. Other states may have open primaries, where the voters can select a ballot from either party and select candidates from that party for a particular office. And then some states have jungle primaries - where all candidates, regardless of party, run in an initial primary or election and, if no candidate has more than 50 of the vote, a runoff between the top two vote getters occurs a short time thereafter. But belonging to a party is really meaningful if you are seeking to participate in the political system. At the statelocal level, being a party member means you may be eligible to participate in party conventions, which can help shape party policies. Additionally, for some offices or across the board in some states, parties may choose to select political candidates through a convention or caucus process, which may be limited to party members. Being a party member, however, gets you on callemail lists for candidates seeking to raise funds. Prior to the Hellenistic era, Greek cities were established along the coasts of the Crimean and Taman peninsulas. The Bosporan Kingdom was a diverse kingdom encompassing Greek city-states and local tribes like the Maeotians, Thracians, Crimean Scythians, and Cimmerians, ruled by the Spartocid dynasty (438–110 BCE). The Spartocids were a Hellenized Thracian family originating from Panticapaeum. The Bosporans maintained extensive trade relations with the Scythian people of the Pontic-Caspian steppe, and Hellenistic influences are evident in Scythian settlements in the Crimea, such as the Scythian Neapolis. Under King Paerisades V, Scythian pressure forced the Bosporan kingdom to adopt vassalage under the Pontic ruler Mithradates VI for protection, around 107 BCE. Later, it became a Roman client state. Scythian groups in Central Asia encountered Hellenistic culture through the Greeks of Bactria. Many Scythian elites bought Greek goods, and some Scythian artworks show Greek influences. Some Scythians appear to have adopted Hellenistic practices, as evidenced by conflicts among their elite classes regarding the adoption of Greek customs. These Hellenized Scythians were called the "young Scythians." The populations near Pontic Olbia, known as the Callipidae, were mixed and Hellenized, becoming Greco-Scythians.

From 2017 to 2019 the Text REtrieval Conference (TREC) held a challenge task on precision medicine using documents from medical publications (PubMed) and clinical trials. Despite lots of performance measurements carried out in these evaluation campaigns, the scientific community is still pretty unsure about the impact individual system features and their weights have on the overall system performance. In order to overcome this explanatory gap, we first determined optimal feature configurations using the Sequential Model-based Algorithm Configuration (SMAC) program and applied its output to a BM25-based search engine. We then ran an ablation study to systematically assess the individual contributions of relevant system features: BM25 parameters, query type and weighting schema, query expansion, stop word filtering, and keyword boosting. For evaluation, we employed the gold standard data from the three installments to evaluate the effectiveness of different features using the commonly shared infNDCG metric.

Other carriers joined in and eventually the ITU-R said, "That 3G is pretty advanced. I guess you guys can call it 4G." Depending on your carrier, 4G can mean different technologies and different levels of battery drainage (although battery drainage also depends on a number of other factors). If you're with Verizon, AT T, or Sprint, you're probably on LTE. LTE stands for "Long Term Evolution" and is the most widely used 4G technology. It's really fast, and an upcoming update will make it much faster. T-Mobile is eventually going to launch 4G as well. If you're with Sprint, you could also be on WiMax; WiMax is basically Wi-Fi on steroids. It's very fast, but it's not very popular outside of the USA. If you're on T-Mobile or AT T, you could also be on HSPA, which stands for "High Speed Packet Access." It's basically 3G but with a better internet connection. This is the network T-Mobile started calling "4G." I suspect it will eventually be demoted to 3.75G. HSPA can download 84 [Mbps] (URL2) at its very maximum. Wi-Fi can go up to 150 Mbps, depending on the kind of Wi-Fi you're using. LTE and WiMax are capable of going faster than that, up to about 1 Gbps. Of course, these are theoretical maximum speeds, so you're definitely not going to see speeds like this on your phone. And, to any Canadians out there, if your phone is "4G" it's probably using HSPA. Where I reside (America), it is illegal to have sex with someone who does not consent to it. This makes sense to me; it is easy to say "heshe did not consent to sex, you are not allowed to have sex with them." However, there is another rule involved. Someone is "not capable of consenting" if they are under 18, or under the influence of drugsalcohol. The idea as I understand it is that you cannot have sex with someone even if they say yes, if they are under 18 or if you know they are drunk. Even if you simply "should have known" (perhaps they never outright said it) they were drunk, their consent does not count. To me, this is unreasonable, because there are many people who are not smart enough to tell someone is drunk, or perhaps they have not been around alcohol enough to understand how drunk someone is. I know people who slur their words all the time; I can easily see someone who is socially awkward not picking up on the cues that someone is drunk, and thinking that they were sober enough to consent. However, they "should have known" they were drunk, generally the argument is that they were "obviously drunk." I don't think it is fair to charge someone with rape when they were unable to detect the (sometimes subtle) cues that someone was too inebriated to consent. What you need to realize is that clock speed isn't the whole story. What matters is also how many clock cycles an instruction takes. For example, lets say a multiplication takes 1 cycle on an intel processor and 2 cycles on an AMD processor. If they are both the same clock speed, the Intel CPU will be twice as fast when multiplying. Other things that would impact cost would be stuff like power-efficiency (I think Intel has AMD on this one), overclocking, cache size, etc. If you really want to compare CPUs, go to a benchmarking website. They run real tests of the CPU performance and are pretty accurate. This allows you to compare performance between different CPUs in a real-world way. To answer your question, AMD processors are cheap because they perform worse than a comparable speed Intel processor. However, the price-to-performance ratio is comparable (if not a bit better) than Intel. If you don't have any budget constraints then you would probably choose Intel over AMD, whereas if you had very little money to spend you would probably go with AMD over Intel.

In much the same way as drugs, prostitution, gambling, or other "victimless" crimes, dog fighting is going to happen irrespective of the law. The only thing that makes dog fighting wrong is the law. No one gets hurt, and the animals are happy. This debate does not have anything to do with dog fighting, it has to do with the legality of dog fighting. This is a simple question: should dog fighting be legal or not? The question is not how do we make dog fighting more humane, or how do we stop dog fighting. The question is solely whether dog fighting should be legal or illegal. Please do not bring up other arguments such as "it's inhumane" or "it's barbaric," because they are irrelevant. Quantum teleportation isn't quite accurate for describing the process. Typically, people associate teleportation with moving an object from one place to another without it being physically present. However, quantum teleportation is completely different. Why is the name used? We’ll explore that later. To understand quantum teleportation, we must first grasp entanglement, the key concept behind quantum mechanics. Entanglement occurs when two quantum particles become connected such that altering one affects the other instantly, regardless of distance. A quantum particle differs from a regular one because it can exist in multiple states simultaneously—like a coin that’s both heads and tails at once. This phenomenon seems strange, but it’s real. To perform quantum teleportation, you start by creating entangled particles and separating them. Then, you apply a small force to one particle; the other responds immediately, even though there’s no physical connection. This instantaneous reaction is what gives the process its name. While it might seem simple, this is a remarkable feat. The core idea is that the second particle reacts instantly, defying the known speed limit of light. This raises questions about the nature of reality. No one fully understands how this works, making it one of the greatest mysteries in science. Let’s imagine a scenario: suppose you have two playing cards, one a king and one a queen. You randomly pick one and put it in a box, leaving the other in another. You can then separate the cards and open your box to find out what’s in the other. You instantly know the contents.

We consider a multi-agent resource allocation setting that models the assignment of papers to reviewers. A recurring issue in allocation problems is the compatibility of welfareefficiency and fairness. Given an oracle to find a welfare-achieving allocation, we embed such an oracle into a flexible algorithm called the Constrained Round Robin (CRR) algorithm, that achieves the required welfare level. Our algorithm also allows the system designer to lower the welfare requirements in order to achieve a higher degree of fairness. If the welfare requirement is lowered enough, a strengthening of envy-freeness up to one item is guaranteed. Hence, our algorithm can be viewed as a computationally efficient way to interpolate between welfare and approximate envy-freeness in allocation problems.

Dwarf Fortress, the iconic ASCII-based computer game, has been in development for over two decades, and is still going strong. In a world where game developers often rush to release their latest titles, Dwarf Fortress stands out as a testament to one man's dedication, vision, and skill. The game, which has a massive following, is built entirely by Tarn Adams, who started working on it in 2002. Dwarf Fortress simulates a complex and intricate world, complete with complex social interactions and elaborate systems. With over 700,000 lines of code, the game is more complex than most modern computer programs. According to Adams, the game's staggering complexity is a result of his desire to create a truly unique experience for players. Dwarf Fortress features a procedurally generated world, with players tasked with building a thriving fortress while also dealing with the dangers and challenges that come with it. The game's development process has been long and arduous, with Adams frequently having to work through issues and bugs that would have simply been patched out in a modern game. Despite this, Adams has continued to push forward and improve his creation, adding new features over the years and building a dedicated community. For many players, Dwarf Fortress has been a beloved part of their gaming lives for years, with some even playing the game for over a decade. The game's dedicated following has even inspired numerous projects, from mods to countless YouTube tutorials. While Dwarf Fortress may not be a household name like mainstream titles such as Fortnite or Call of Duty, its impact on gaming culture cannot be overstated. The game is a reminder of the potential that lies in passion and dedication, and a testament to what one person can create through sheer force of will. As Adams continues to work on Dwarf Fortress, it's clear that his dedication to the game is unwavering. For players, this is surely a source of comfort, knowing that their favorite game will continue to improve and evolve for years to come.

Scene text recognition (STR) has attracted significant research interest in recent years. Several emerging techniques focus on adapting to the flexible shapes, arrangements, and orientations of scene texts, yet they often overlook the impact of diverse font styles, which can greatly hinder STR performance. These approaches typically combine font-specific and content-related features of individual characters, leading to suboptimal results when applied to scenes containing text in unfamiliar font types. To tackle this issue, we propose using font-agnostic features by generating glyphs across multiple font styles through an attention-based framework. We introduce learnable font embeddings to control the font characteristics of generated glyphs, while retaining only the core structural information of the scene text. The generation process employs a spatial attention mechanism, enabling the model to handle irregular text layouts and produce high-quality glyphs. Experimental evaluations on standard STR datasets confirm the effectiveness of our approach compared to current state-of-the-art methods.

In the past, all systems relied on ASCII, which employed seven bits per character, allowing for 128 distinct characters. It was created by English-speaking individuals, providing sufficient characters for English along with numbers and symbols. As other groups, such as European users with accents and special characters, sought to use computers, they found that these non-English characters were less common. To address this, they developed ISO-8859, an extension of ASCII that used eight bits, expanding the character set to 256. This allowed them to include additional symbols required for various languages. However, since not all characters fit into 256, each language often required its own variant. For instance, ISO-8859-1 catered to most Western European languages, while ISO-8859-5 handled Russian. Microsoft also introduced several proprietary character sets, aiming to accommodate specific needs like varying quotation mark shapes. The limitations of this approach included the need to identify the correct character set for a document and the inability to switch between multiple sets simultaneously. Over time, it became clear that this method was inefficient, leading to the development of Unicode and UTF-8, widely adopted on the internet. Unicode supports virtually every character, enabling the coexistence of characters like the sharp-s and Cyrillic letters. Nevertheless, issues persist; even if software supports a format, misinterpretation can occur. On a modern Unix system, executing `echo Rene xxd: 5265 6ec3 a90a` reveals UTF-8 encoding. The first three hex values, 52 65 6e, correspond to "Ren," backward-compatible with ASCII. The subsequent bytes, C3 A9 0A, represent a "e" in UTF-8. If interpreted differently, such as in ISO-8859-1, these bytes might yield different results.

Local Policy Search is a widely adopted reinforcement learning method for managing extensive state spaces. Mathematically, it examines policies within a parametrized space to optimize a value function, averaged across a specific distribution. It is typically assumed that such methods offer only local optima as their best possible outcome. This paper demonstrates a striking finding: any (approximate) local optimum satisfies a global performance guarantee. We contrast this guarantee with that of Direct Policy Iteration, an approximate dynamic programming technique that involves policy search. If the local search process necessitates considering a set of stochastic policies, the concentrability coefficient in the performance bound becomes significantly more favorable. Ultimately, we explore various practical and theoretical implications of our findings.

The continuous interpolation of real-valued data is defined by piecewise monotonic functions over a compact metric space. The topological total variation of a piecewise monotonic function $ f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} $ is a homeomorphism-invariant extension of the one-dimensional total variation. A varilet basis consists of an orthonormal set of piecewise monotonic functions $ \{g_i\}_{i=1}^n $, referred to as varilets, such that any linear combination $ \sum a_i g_i $ has a topological total variation equal to $ \sum a_i $. A varilet transform of $ f $ is a varilet basis where $ f = \sum a_i g_i $. Modifications to the coefficients $ a_i $ yield filtered versions of $ f $.

Evolution has adapted to allow pain receptors to function effectively even in cold environments, enabling individuals to sense pain despite the chill.

The introduction of LTE over unlicensed bands (LTE-U) will enable LTE base stations (BSs) to boost their capacity and offload their traffic by exploiting the underused unlicensed bands. However, to ensure fair coexistence with other wireless technologies sharing these bands, the LTE-U system needs to implement listen-before-talk (LBT) protocols to avoid interfering with other systems. This is a significant challenge for LTE-U, since the timing and duration of LTE-U transmissions must be carefully coordinated to avoid collisions with other systems sharing the same band. To address this challenge, LTE-U systems use a carrier sensing mechanism to detect the presence of other wireless signals before transmitting. If the channel is occupied, the LTE-U BS waits until the channel becomes available before transmitting. This approach ensures that transmissions over unlicensed bands do not interfere with other systems sharing the same channel. Overall, LTE-U can significantly boost the capacity of wireless networks by exploiting underutilized unlicensed bands. However, it must implement intelligent protocols like LBT to ensure fair coexistence with other wireless systems in the same band.

My shadow began to move independently of me - darting around corners and scurrying away from me down the street. I stopped and stared at it, dumbfounded. I tried chasing after my shadow, but it was too quick for me. It seemed to be toying with me, like a cat playing with a mouse. Everywhere I went, my shadow would be just out of reach, mocking me and my helplessness. Each night, the game continued. I'd try to corner it, but it was always one step ahead of me. Before long, I started to believe that my shadow was out to get me. It seemed to have a mind of its own - almost as if it had become my enemy. I started to dread the nights. I was scared to go outside, worried that my shadow would be waiting for me. I tried to stay inside as much as possible, but eventually I ran out of places to hide. That's when things got even worse... My shadow began to take on a life of its own. It started appearing in the strangest places - in my bedroom, in the hallways of my school, even at my workplace. I've learned to stay away from dark places and to keep a safe distance from my own shadow. For now, I'll just have to live with the fact that my shadow is no longer my friend.

The nonprofit landscape is highly varied, although many people have come to associate NPOs with charitable organizations. Although charities do comprise an often high profile or visible aspect of the sector, there are many other types of nonprofits. Overall, they tend to be either member-serving or community-serving. Member-serving organizations include mutual societies, cooperatives, trade unions, credit unions, industry associations, sports clubs, retired serviceman's clubs and peak bodies - organizations that benefit a particular group of people i.e. the members of the organization. Typically, community-serving organizations are focused on providing services to the community in general, either globally or locally: organizations delivering human services programs or projects, aid and development programs, medical research, education and health services, and so on. It could be argued many nonprofits sit across both camps, at least in terms of the impact they make. For example, the grassroots support group that provides a lifeline to those with a particular condition or disease could be deemed to be serving both its members (by directly supporting them) and the broader community (through the provision of a helping service for fellow citizens).
