An independent report commissioned by the Department of Health estimated these groups cost the NHS PS2bn a year. Ministers said some of that spending was unavoidable, but said it would be realistic to save a quarter. Savings would come from deterring so-called health tourism, recovering money owed by other countries and a levy on non-European temporary residents. One senior doctor questioned the government's figures and said doctors should not have to spend time "vetting eligibility" of patients. Health Secretary Jeremy Hunt said he did not want to "turn GPs into border guards" and no-one would be denied emergency treatment, but foreign visitors must make a "fair contribution." Mr Hunt said he recognised the NHS's duty of care must "transcend" financial concerns, but collecting an extra PS500m a year could pay for 4,000 extra doctors. "We have one of the most generous systems in the world when it comes to healthcare for foreign visitors, but it's time for action to ensure the NHS is a national health service - not an international one," he added. By Nick TriggleHealth correspondent The issue of which foreigners are entitled to treatment and which are not is complex. The first thing to say is if someone needs emergency care - for example if they have an accident - the NHS will treat them no matter where they come from. Another exemption is if someone has an infectious disease as treatment helps protect the wider public. Beyond that the UK has reciprocal agreements with most European countries and 28 other nations, including countries such as Canada and Australia. It means if their residents need care while here temporarily - either on holiday or working - they will be seen and the NHS will then reclaim the cost of that care from the other country. The research released by the Department of Health shows the NHS is not very good at clawing that money back. This is because of a perverse incentive in the system which ministers now want to rectify. Meanwhile, travelling to the UK deliberately for health treatment - so-called health tourism - is not allowed. The rules are less clear in other cases, such as expats and asylum seekers. The latest research is published in two separate reports by firms Prederi and Creative Research. The government has been criticised for using financial estimates from the Prederi report, but Mr Hunt said it was the "most thorough research there has ever been" in this area. The report itself notes that it is based on "incomplete data, sometimes of varying quality, and a large number of assumptions," but it says the estimates are the "best that can be made at present," and Mr Hunt said researchers had been "completely honest about what they do know and what they don't know." The government is currently consulting on the measures it will take to tackle this issue. It has already announced a PS200-a-year levy on migrants from outside the European Economic Area (EEA) staying for between six months and five years, and Mr Hunt said this could raise PS200m a year. A cost-recovery unit will also be set up to help hospitals claw back money they are owed by other governments for treating foreign nationals visiting the UK. Meanwhile, "deliberate health tourism" - whereby people travel to the UK to get NHS care - is estimated by Prederi to cost between PS60m and PS80m a year. The report's authors concede this figure is "uncertain" and the "plausible range" of the cost is PS20m-PS100m. Frequent visitors "taking advantage" by registering with GPs and getting access to prescriptions and some hospital referrals cost the NHS a further PS50m-PS200m a year, the report adds. The government accepts it cannot recoup all of this money and entirely stop health tourism and so it has put forward the "conservative" PS500m figure. To achieve this, it said a better system of identifying when visitors and migrants got treatment was needed. More details on what this will involve will be revealed in the coming weeks. Free NHS care is offered to anyone with living in the UK who has temporary or permanent permission to do so. Asylum seekers, non-EEA nationals who do not have permission to live in the UK, British ex-pats and visitors usually have to pay for treatment. The UK has reciprocal agreements with most European nations and 28 other countries, and under these visitors are given free NHS care. The NHS should claim these costs back from the relevant governments - but the research suggests just PS73m a year is recouped out of more than PS460m at present. This is because there is a perverse incentive in the system whereby if they declare the fact they have treated a foreign national it is up to the individual hospital to chase up the home nation for the money whereas if they do not declare it they get money from the NHS system for seeing a patient entitled to care. Shadow health secretary Andy Burnham said: "We are not against improving the recovery of costs from people with no entitlement to NHS treatment." But he added the figures were based on a "large number of assumptions" and was more about "spin than substance." Dr Chaand Nagpaul, chairman of the British Medical Association's GPs committee, said the government's PS500m savings figure was "exaggerated," partly because it did not take account of the costs of implementing its plans. He said migrants paying the proposed PS200-a-year levy could be more likely to use the NHS to "get their money's worth," and he said the cost of a single hospital outpatient appointment would be more than PS200. Dr Nagpaul said doctors should not be distracted from their work in order to check the eligibility of patients for treatments. Dr Clare Gerada, chairwoman of the Royal College of GPs, said it was imperative GPs were not tasked with being a "new border agency" in policing the NHS. "The risks to public health that will arise from these proposals are also very real. They will deter people from seeking medical help in the early stages of illness when they can be dealt with cost-effectively and efficiently in primary care, rather than requiring expensive specialist care and increasing admissions to emergency departments," she said. Jonathan Portes, of the Institute of Economic and Social Research think tank, said the research revealed the extent of deliberate health tourism had been "hugely overstated" and was in fact a "very small part of NHS expenditure."

This paper introduces an optimization-driven method for path planning of a mobile robot under time-bounded temporal constraints in a dynamic setting. Temporal logic (TL) effectively handles intricate task requirements like safety, coverage, and motion sequences. We employ metric temporal logic (MTL) to represent these task specifications along with timing restrictions. The MTL formulas are converted into mixed integer linear constraints, and the corresponding optimization problem is solved via a mixed integer linear programming solver. This methodology contrasts with automaton-based approaches, which create a finite representation of the environment and dynamics, and utilize automata theory to construct a path adhering to the TL. Our approach has been tested on multiple case studies within complex dynamical environments governed by timed temporal specifications.

With the advent of self-driving vehicles, the unavoidable will become clear: people are terrible drivers, and operating your own car is unacceptably reckless if a better alternative exists. I see no reason to stop at this point, since such things should be obvious by now. In fact, you can't even blame autonomous cars any more than you could blame the fact that women drive poorly or underweight compared with men. Yes, it's true that some people are bad drivers for reasons we don't understand (and probably never will understand), but humans are also human beings, not robots. That doesn't mean they're all perfect, however you feel about them; don't try to paint us in an artificial light. We're just as fallible as everyone else. But what about those who have their lives ruined? How do you react when someone who has lost everything because he was driving drunk gets a free ride from the police? Shouldn't the punishment match the crime? You certainly shouldn't encourage two groups - one being less responsible than another - to share responsibility for making decisions which put others at risk. And yet, too many laws exist aimed at keeping two sets of rules on the road so common sense would tell you that's exactly what is happening. The problem is that we make ourselves into societies where most decisions are made without regard to individual legal consequences. It may seem like the right thing to do, and it's important to recognize the benefits of increasing economic mobility for our society above anything else. But it also means we treat rights much like the weight of a feather; anyone can throw it up in the air, but it won't go far unless they have the necessary force. So naturally, we tend to give privileges to those who deserve them, often until they've earned enough to keep doing it, and once those privileges are gone they'll drop out pretty fast. All around the world today there seems to be a growing consensus that there needs to be a reset button pressed. The state needs to step aside; individuals need freedom to decide how they want to live, work and play. In order to achieve these goals, first of all there needs to be a complete change in the way courts deal with personal injury cases rather than relying on lawyers who only care about money. Lawyers might think they're helping their clients get justice, but actually they're just putting themselves ahead of other parties involved in the case. They're basically acting as the very opposite of heroes shining lights on the dark and ruining lives across a huge range of industries. I'm not advocating forcibly taking people away from their homes and forcing them onto welfare programs, nor am I suggesting cutting funding for law enforcement agencies to the tune of billions of dollars. Instead, I believe the best solution is to invest resources into education, training and access to health services especially mental health treatment and gender equality advocates. Governments should be working actively in tandem with social movements for equal pay and higher standards for working conditions, etc., instead of wasting time worrying about frivolous lawsuits and inability to enforce existing ones. We've already seen the devastating effects of automation. Is it really going to take a technological disaster before we realize that allowing machines to run our lives isn't the smartest idea anymore?

We present Nopol an approach for automatically repairing buggy if conditions and missing preconditions. As input, it takes a program and a test suite which contains passing test cases modeling the expected behavior of the program, as well as failing test cases that reveal the existing bugs in the program. Nopol then analyzes the failing tests and generates candidate patches that incorporate new if conditions or preconditions to fix the bugs. To evaluate the effectiveness of Nopol, it is applied to a set of real-world Java programs with known bugs. In the experimental evaluation, Nopol shows promising results, improving the correctness of the programs by fixing a significant number of bugs. Overall, Nopol is a useful tool for developers who wish to automate the process of bug fixing in their programs. It can save time and effort by automating the tedious process of trial-and-error patching, making it more efficient and reliable to improve the correctness of the code.

Throughout the Middle Ages, Newcastle was England's northern fortress. Incorporated first by Henry II, the city had a new charter granted by Elizabeth in 1589. A 25-foot (7.6 m) high stone wall, built to a length of three miles (4.8 km) in 1265 by the orders of Charles I, was the city's main protection against Scottish invaders during its time. The Scots did attack and captured the city in 1644, and the city had a number of other close calls. After the 15th century, Newcastle was England's chief coal port. Shown above is the Castle Keep, which is all that remains of the medieval castle that gave Newcastle its name. The rest of the castle was demolished in 1685. The Tyne Bridge was designed by Mott, Hay and Anderson, and built by Dorman Long and Co. of Middlesbrough. The bridge was officially opened on October 10, 1928, by King George V and has since become one of the most familiar symbols of Newcastle. In the late 18th century, the city became a center of the Industrial Revolution. Coal mining was at its height, and the city was the most productive coal port in the world. The population increased tenfold in the 19th century - from 40,000 in 1801 to 400,000 by 1901. Tyneside suffered severely in the world wars of the 20th century, particularly during the Second World War, when its strategic importance with regard to the nation's coal supply and armament industries made it a target for Nazi Germany. Heavy bombing during the war caused some areas of the city center and east end to become blighted. The period from 1939 to 1978 saw the replacement of most of the city's slum housing with more modern, suburban estates and tower blocks. Shown above is the Tyne Bridge at night. In recent years, Newcastle has been redeveloped as a center for culture and the arts, with the BALTIC Centre for Contemporary Art, the Sage Gateshead, a new performing arts and conference center on the south bank of the River Tyne, and the MetroCentre, the largest shopping and leisure center in the UK built in 1986. The city has also been a venue for sporting events, such as the 2012 Olympics. The Newcastle Falcons are the city's rugby union team, playing in the Guinness Premiership. Newcastle United Football Club have played at St James' Park since the club was established in 1892. The stadium was used as a venue in the 2012 Olympic Games. Today, Newcastle is known throughout the world as a tourist destination, in no small part because of its many pubs, nightclubs, and music venues.

We introduce a bandit algorithm called SAO (Stochastic and Adversarial Optimal), which achieves optimality in terms of regret for both adversarial and stochastic reward environments. SAO integrates the O(n) worst-case regret of Exp3 [ , ] for adversarial rewards with the (poly-logarithmic) regret of UCB1 [ , ] for stochastic rewards. Adversarial and stochastic reward settings are the primary frameworks studied in non-Bayesian multi-armed bandit research. Previous studies have treated these cases separately and have not sought to simultaneously optimize for both. Our findings align with a broader trend of enhancing worst-case performance while leveraging favorable problem structures, which is critical in designing algorithms with partially known input scenarios.

The Chalukya Empire (Kannada: [taukj was an Indian royal dynasty that ruled large parts of southern and central India between the 6th and the 12th centuries. During this period, they ruled as three related yet individual dynasties. The earliest dynasty, known as the "Badami Chalukyas," ruled from Vatapi (modern Badami) from the middle of the 6th century. The Badami Chalukyas began to assert their independence at the decline of the Kadamba kingdom of Banavasi and rapidly rose to prominence during the reign of Pulakeshin II. The rule of the Chalukyas marks an important milestone in the history of South India and a golden age in the history of Karnataka. The political atmosphere in South India shifted from smaller kingdoms to large empires with the ascendancy of Badami Chalukyas. A Southern India-based kingdom took control and consolidated the entire region between the Kaveri and the Narmada rivers. The rise of this empire saw the birth of efficient administration, overseas trade and commerce and the development of new style of architecture called "Chalukyan architecture." The Chalukya dynasty ruled parts of southern and central India from Badami in Karnataka between 550 and 750, and then again from Kalyani between 970 and 1190.

The five stages of grief are; denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance. It took me a while to get to the first one; I've always been optimistic and we've always been able to get out of any situation that's been thrown at us. But it's not us right now; it's just me, and I was never the tactician. Denial was probably the hardest part, oddly. There had to be a way to save them, while not sacrificing the victory we'd worked so hard to achieve. I spent a countless amount of time staring at the machine, trying to understand the failsafes, trying to work out the correct sequence of inputs to halt the wormhole. I can't affect anything while I'm using my power, but I can prepare for the instant when I let go of the moment. But the longer I stared and the more I understood, the more I realised that the process was too far gone; I could shut down the machine but they were too close to the centre of it. There was no way to save them. That was when anger started to set in. I was a fucking superhero; there had to be something that I could do! I paced around and around, trapped in a silent world with nothing but my own increasing desperation. I don't know when I started roaring at the world; screaming at the sheer injustice of it all, but eventually my voice died out and I found myself on my knees, stuck in the middle of this tableau of misery. Bargaining was next. Maybe if I sacrificed myself somehow, maybe that would save them? What if I just wasn't trying hard enough? Maybe if I concentrated for long enough, maybe I could make time creep back, second by second. I just had to try harder; just had to do this one thing to save them all. When that didn't work, I thought that maybe I just needed to think, to be smart about this. Every puzzle has a solution, it's just a matter of time. I have all the time in the world. Quite literally. I don't know how much time has passed. It's difficult to track it when I use my power like this; everything stops except me. The Engineer was going to try and make me a watch that would withstand my power, but now he was frozen in time before me, his expression a grimace of agony as he was pulled back towards the event horizon of the wormhole. Did he still feel pain like this? God, I hope not. I guess I'm in depression now. I have no ideas left; I don't know what to do. The General was always the one in charge; if he was here right now, he would know what to do. God, if any of them were here right now, they would know what to do. Any of them except me. I've never been as strong as them, and though they never intentionally put me down, I've always felt out of place. The Engineer can put together ridiculous machines out of nothing; The General is so strong and so fast and so smart that it's embarrassing to the rest of us. And then there's the Siren. I look up at her; I don't know when I ended up on the floor. God, I'm so sorry. She was always so nice to me, always so accepting, so happy to see me, even when I messed everything up. I think I love her. Or loved her. How do you describe something trapped in the flux between existence and annihilation? I don't know what to do. They're all going to die and there's nothing I can do. As long as I hold them here, they're still alive; there's still a chance that I can do something; anything. I don't know how long I've been here; how much time should have passed if I hadn't grabbed hold of this moment and held it tight. It's like being trapped in a photograph, surrounded by inescapable horror on all sides, and completely unable to do anything about it. I know what I should do; I need to let time continue, but I can't. I'm not ready to let them go. I don't know when I'll be ready; maybe in a moment, maybe in a thousand moments, maybe never at all. Will I ever get to acceptance? Some people never do. Mike, Pete, Sarah. I'm so sorry. I won't let you go. I won't ever let you go.

In 2012, Abigail Fisher, an undergraduate student at Louisiana State University, and Rachel Multer Michalewicz, a law student at Southern Methodist University, initiated a lawsuit against the University of Texas to challenge its admissions policy. They claimed the university's "race-conscious" policy violated their civil and constitutional rights. The University of Texas uses the "Top Ten Percent Law," ensuring admission to public universities in Texas is guaranteed for students who rank in the top ten percent of their high school classes. Fisher argued that she was denied entry to the University of Texas due to her race, asserting that this violated her right to equal protection under the Fourteenth Amendment. The Supreme Court heard oral arguments on October 10, 2012, and issued an unclear ruling in 2013, directing the case back to the lower court with only the requirement that the university prove it could achieve diversity without relying on race. In July 2014, the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that the University of Texas employed a "holistic" approach to affirmative action and could continue the practice. On February 10, 2015, Fisher's legal team filed a new appeal to the Supreme Court. This was a reassertion of the same claim, arguing that the Fifth Circuit made an error in its initial decision. The Supreme Court agreed to review the case again in June 2015, with a potential decision by June 2016.

Surprise frontrunner Francois Fillon said his project was "more radical," and vowed to implement sweeping changes in the first three months of his term. Alain Juppe insisted his proposals were more realistic. "I want France to return to the family of nations where she belongs," Fillon said, referring to the "Anglo-Saxon" world of Britain and the United States. "We need to go faster and faster, further and further," the former Prime Minister told the 16,000-strong audience in Paris' Bercy Arena. Fillon and Juppe are widely considered the frontrunners in the primary, which will be held in two rounds on Sunday and Nov. 27. The victor will face the winner of the Socialist primary, expected to be held in January. "I want a new French independence," he added, referring to the "dependency" on Germany, the European Union's powerhouse economy, that had "lost its radiance." "You're my family," Fillon told the crowd in the Bercy Arena, at the end of a sometimes-raucous debate. "It's a radical project, but it's not radicalism. It's deep-rooted in the founding values of our country," he told supporters, many of whom wore the blue scarves of the party, and waved French tricolors. Fillon, who clashed repeatedly with Juppe during the debate, said his proposals were "realistic" and "in line with the French people's aspirations." "This is no longer a primary of the right," Fillon said. "This is a primary of France." Alain Juppe, a former French Prime Minister, came in second, according to the same poll. The 62-year-old Juppe, who is considered more centrist than Fillon, proposed "a French renaissance" based on moderation, and reiterated his commitment to the EU. He vowed to slash unemployment, which currently stands at 10 percent, but said that he would not scrap the 35-hour work week, as Fillon has suggested. "I will be a reformer, but in a calm and balanced way," he said. "The French don't want us to be a country at war with itself." "I want to build a France that is modern, creative, and competitive," he said, adding that he would use his executive experience to "get France moving." The two leading candidates also clashed on immigration and security. Fillon proposed closing the border to all but a "limited" number of refugees and asylum seekers, while Juppe insisted that France was a "nation of welcome." Fillon repeated his pledge to restore military service, which was abolished in 1997, insisting that it would "toughen up" young people. Juppe rejected the plan as anachronistic. Fillon has surged in opinion polls since the start of the campaign, as the conservatives struggle to recover from the presidential election defeat of former President Nicolas Sarkozy in 2012. Sarkozy failed to make it to the second round of the primary, and announced he was retiring from politics on Sunday night. "I will be your first defender and your first loyal servant," Fillon said.

At 6 AM, a powerful sound disrupted my peaceful sleep, interrupting the pleasant dream I was having where a higher-order being controlled the temperature. I fell to the floor and hid under my bed, but I soon realized it wasn't an earthquake—it was far worse. Damn, how had they found me again? From outside, the speakers started playing their usual message: "Every thirty seconds, a polar bear dies from heatstroke." For whatever it was worth, the climate change activists were among the least annoying groups that often visited me. I looked out my front window and saw them setting up their projector screen and showing the familiar slide show of dying baby polar bears I had seen countless times. They could have created a new one—I had witnessed Perry, Popo, and Patrick's deaths so many times that they lost their emotional impact. "Hey, missy!" A man in a suit spotted me through my curtains and rushed to my window. "You must lower the temperature immediately, or you'll regret when your heating fails!" The radiator sales industry operated on the opposite end of annoyance; they used fear-based tactics to influence my emotions. Recently, they threatened to launch a nationwide boycott on selling to me if I didn't reduce the temperature by winter. In my mind, it was a risky approach: first, I didn't need a radiator if I kept the warmth outside, and second, their clumsy attempts to frighten me made me more angry than scared, keeping the temperature high. Their schemes weren't the worst of the group: North Face had vowed to make all my clothing choices outdated if I didn't meet their cooling requirements. "Go blow hot air somewhere else," I yelled back at him. "Yeah, if you need someone to vent to, we're here for you." Another man approached him from across my front yard.

Nobles were born into a noble family, adopted by a noble family (this was abolished in 1633) or ennobled by a king or Sejm for various reasons (bravery in combat, service to the state, etc. - yet this was the rarest means of gaining noble status). Many nobles were, in actuality, really usurpers, being commoners, who moved into another part of the country and falsely pretended to noble status. Hundreds of such false nobles were denounced by Hieronim Nekanda Trepka in his Liber generationis plebeanorium (or Liber chamorum) in the first half of the 16th century. The law forbade non-nobles from owning nobility-estates and promised the estate to the denouncer. Trepka was an impoverished nobleman who lived a townsman life and collected hundreds of such stories hoping to take over any of such estates. It does not seem he ever succeeded in proving one at the court. Many sejms issued decrees over the centuries in an attempt to resolve this issue, but with little success. It is unknown what percentage of the Polish nobility came from the 'lower' orders of society, but most historians agree that nobles of such base origins formed a 'significant' element of the szlachta.

The United States and Cuba were once close allies. Cuba was once a U.S. territory and considered for entry into the Union. In 1953, Fidel Castro initiated a communist revolution against the Cuban Batista government. The U.S. supported Batista due to its friendship with him and its hostility toward communism, during the Cold War. The U.S. sought to act cautiously and avoid confrontation, but Castro and his supporters were adept and determined, leading to his victory and the establishment of a communist Cuban state. In 1962, Cuba permitted the Soviet Union to deploy nuclear weapons on its soil, creating a significant threat to the U.S. This event, known as the Cuban Missile Crisis, brought humanity dangerously close to nuclear destruction. Older generations still harbor distrust towards Cuba. The U.S. has consistently refused to acknowledge Castro's government as legitimate and insists that U.S.-Cuban ties can only resume through fair, free multi-party elections. This has rendered travel and trade between the two countries illegal, although recent easing of tensions has enabled some travel. As with many aspects of life, the issue ultimately hinges on corporate interests. The Batista regime was notoriously corrupt, allowing American corporations to exploit Cuba's resources and use Cuban laborers as servants, while brutally suppressing any dissenting voices advocating for fair wages. This fueled a strong socialist movement in Cuba, akin to that in 19th-century America, and led to Castro's ousting of Batista and removal of American firms. However, as with many "socialist paradise" scenarios, the new populist leaders soon found themselves favoring luxury goods and high-end amenities. This, coupled with the U.S.'s longstanding resentment toward Castro, manifested in embargoes and diplomatic isolation.

Has it ended? My heart raced wildly. I closed my eyes and listened. The bombs had fallen, and the shouts of battle were silent. The wind was soft, and no one could know that war had just concluded. It was too quiet. I peered through the cracks of the wall separating me from the rest of the world. Everything was in ruin, and no one was visible. Was it really possible? I felt another tightening. It wasn’t my first, but I knew my child would arrive soon. I became anxious. Cold sweat spread down my back. I needed to leave! I had to escape! After struggling, I finally managed to pass through the narrow space in the wall. Once upon a time, this place was a thriving city, but now it's filled with debris and the scent of death. “I’m not the only one,” I told myself, trying to move past the broken structures blocking the way. For a moment, I wandered into the streets, hoping to find someone else like me, but I grew impatient. The sun was scorching, and my load was heavy. My legs ached, and I couldn’t walk easily. I stumbled as I felt another contraction. I couldn’t give birth here—this place was too dangerous. I took deep breaths, but they didn’t ease the pain. I searched for a shelter, but I was surprised to see a strange figure nearby. I tried to ask for help, but my mouth couldn’t form the words. Another contraction. Please, don’t. I tried to calm myself, but the baby was already crowning. The pain intensified, and the figure approached faster with every breath. I pushed harder, and with each push, the pain multiplied. It wasn’t until I felt something break that the baby emerged. She was wet and bleeding, yet she was beautiful. “My baby girl,” I whispered, reaching for her. She wriggled and for a moment, I experienced a happiness I hadn’t felt before. At that moment, the mysterious figure had already stood before me.

Before the Hellenistic period, Greek colonies had been established on the coast of the Crimean and Taman peninsulas. The Bosporan Kingdom was a multi-ethnic kingdom of Greek city states and local tribal peoples such as the Maeotians, Thracians, Crimean Scythians and Cimmerians under the Spartocid dynasty (438-110 BCE). The Spartocids were a hellenized Thracian family from Panticapaeum. The Bosporans had long lasting trade contacts with the Scythian peoples of the Pontic-Caspian steppe, and Hellenistic influence can be seen in the Scythian settlements of the Crimea, such as in the Scythian Neapolis. Scythian pressure on the Bosporan kingdom under Paerisades V led to its eventual vassalage under the Pontic king Mithradates VI for protection, circa 107 BCE. It later became a Roman client state. Other Scythians on the steppes of Central Asia came into contact with Hellenistic culture through the Greeks of Bactria. Many Scythian elites purchased Greek products and some Scythian art shows Greek influences. At least some Scythians seem to have become Hellenized, because we know of conflicts between the elites of the Scythian kingdom over the adoption of Greek ways. These Hellenized Scythians were known as the "young Scythians." The peoples around Pontic Olbia, known as the Callipidae, were intermixed and Hellenized Greco-Scythians.

England's Chester Zoo and a tissue bank called Nature's SAFE have partnered up to cryogenically freeze genetic material from animals that pass away at the zoo. The preserved material could be used by researchers in future disease outbreaks, such as bird flu or SARS-CoV2 (the virus responsible for COVID-19). The first step is to identify an animal with no known medical history and make sure it has not been vaccinated against the specific pathogens targeted by the study. This requires capturing an unvaccinated individual, sedating them, collecting blood samples via needle biopsy, isolating their RNA using molecular techniques, freezing the sample on dry ice until shipment of the frozen specimens takes place, then storing the specimens long term in liquid nitrogen tanks until needed. While this might sound like it would take months, these steps are time consuming: they require large numbers of personnel, several days worth of quarantine period in which the captured individuals can't mix with other humans before researchers start working; and the logistics involved mean shipping costs add another 1k-4K per specimen. But given how much money there is spent globally every year trying to treat coronavirus patients - around US8 billion - the cost seems relatively small when compared to potential outcomes, especially if any new treatments are found elsewhere and may never reach those regions anyway. There's also a chance the existing drugs we know about will stop doing anything once all of our high risk population dies out naturally, so preserving strains now should help researchers create better drug cocktails in the event of another pandemic. [Related Reading: 'Coronavirus' Could Kill Us All - Here's How We Can Stop It] And while most people think of politicians saying "we need more tests" after each new outbreak, this isn't always true: sometimes countries already have way too many tests because they were testing everything (and everyone) without knowing what they're looking for, leading to lots of false positives. The issue here is that the whole purpose of having preprints is to spread knowledge faster than traditional publishing allows. If you submit scientific results online before your peers even had a chance to read them, someone else just grabbed your credit and put themselves on top of the research roadmap. If only one person did this, science would move forward quickly enough, but since thousands of scientists do it at the same time, things slow down even further. And we still haven't figured out how to scale up the number of labs being able to produce sequencing data within hours rather than weeks. So taking preprinting off the table means that researchers who don't care for sharing information about their work right now will keep getting left behind. But ultimately, storing samples in freezers with liquid nitrogen seems fairly safe. They've got higher survival rates than living human beings over periods of years, and shortening the exposure times will certainly improve the chances of keeping live specimens alive during transport. As soon as a treatment comes into play, the zoos will send theirs back to normal conditions. In fact, some species - such as chimpanzees - will likely die out altogether due to extinction if nothing improves their odds of surviving beyond this point. By preserving genetic material, hopefully researchers will eventually find ways to tweak viruses to fit wild life habitats in order to protect endangered species from infectious diseases like COVID-19.

Michael Luciw, 27, from Nottingham, was a passenger in a van that was hit by a Mazda Premacy, being driven the wrong way on the motorway by Albert Kenneth Newman, who also died. Mr Luciw's family said retired people should undergo regular driving tests. Age UK said it was "vital" older people could drive for as long as possible. The family described Mr Luciw, the father of a baby girl, as generous, kind-hearted and a lover of practical jokes. "He had only just turned 27 and he had his whole life ahead of him," said his mum Andrea Shelton. "He was looking forward to his baby's first crawl. Now he will miss all of her life through no fault of his own." "It doesn't feel as if we have lost him - it feels as if he has been taken away from us," said Mr Luciw's brother Simon. "There are so many things that should be put in place so things like this could be avoided. People are driving that shouldn't be on the road. "The older you get, the more your reactions slow down. "There needs to be some sort of test introduced, in a car with a driving instructor, so you get a true reflection of how good a driver you are. "You get a free bus pass once you are in your 60s so people can't say they are going to lose their freedom if they have their licence removed." Mrs Shelton said Mr Luciw, a delivery driver, was on a long-distance journey with a colleague Andy Harrington when the crash happened at 02:00 GMT on 12 October near Kegworth, Leicestershire. Mr Newman's car was heading north on the southbound carriageway. Mr Harrington, who was driving the Ford Transit, said he had not seen Mr Newman's car until the last second. "I managed to swerve slightly towards the crash barrier but there was nothing I could do," he said. "You couldn't even blink that fast. "It lives with me. I still get sleepless nights. It's not something I will ever forget." Mr Harrington, who sustained serious injuries in the crash, said retired drivers should have to undergo medical examinations. "It's up to the government whether they listen to us," he said. "But if that driver hadn't been on the road that morning, Michael would still be here with his daughter." Currently drivers over 70 in the UK must fill in a self-assessment form every three years to renew their licences. The form does not include a medical or driving test. The Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA) which maintains the database of registered drivers said it had no plans to restrict licensing on the basis of age. "Evidence does not show that older drivers are more likely to cause a serious accident than others," it said. "The rules are clear that all drivers over 70 have to renew their licence every three years and have to tell DVLA about any medical conditions which might affect their driving. "If we find evidence a driver does not meet the appropriate medical standard we immediately remove their entitlement to drive." Caroline Abrahams, charity director of Age UK, said: "We know driving often allows older people to have the independence to get out and about, go shopping and attend appointments so it's vital that older people are supported to continue driving safely for as long as possible." For more on this subject watch Inside Out on BBC One East Midlands at 19:30 GMT on Monday 25 January and nationwide for 30 days thereafter on the iPlayer.

Having a child involves taking a significant risk. The child might be born with physical defects, lack intelligence, struggle socially, lack talent, suffer from chronic illnesses, develop mental health issues, or perish in a tragic accident or violent crime—just the beginning. Once a child is born, they must attend school, which many find stressful, worry about forming friendships, perform well academically, and eventually secure a job to support themselves. In the first world, this often means working hard to survive. Is this truly worth the occasional joy they may experience? And what about the third world? The contrast between pain and pleasure is stark. Imagine experiencing the purest pleasure (like consuming KFC and engaging in sexual activity simultaneously) and then enduring the most severe pain (such as being burned alive or losing limbs). Would you choose such a combination? Likely not. For any conscious being, existing is inherently harmful, making it worse than non-existence. Non-existence signifies the absence of both pain and pleasure. While the absence of pain is positive, the absence of pleasure is not necessarily negative. According to Benatar, a person is not deprived of anything by not being born. Many parents knowingly bring children into the world despite knowing life may not be worth living. They pass on their suffering to their children. When parents say, “life isn’t fair,” they inadvertently expose themselves to the truth.

The short and simple answer is that, if well-constructed, designed, and solid, it does not. It can destroy the environment if: - It is punctured, creating an oil spill - It is designed badly, creating an oil spill at some point without puncturing, OR it creates a barrier to important local species. - It is built badly, same as designed.', "What others said, plus there's still an impact to the environment since you need to haul piping out and install it. You might need to cut down trees, fill in some wetlands, or make other modifications to the environment in order to actually get the pipes and equipment out to remote areas and then securely install it.," "It does not destroy the environment unless it leaks. Then it can be a gigantic mess. Also, people opposed to fossil fuel consumption point out that the more pipelines we build, maybe the more fuel we'll end up using per year.,Because a pipeline doesn't just come out of nowhere, it has to be built and maintained. That means lots of big machinery, lots of manpower, and lots of big pieces of pipe that need to get moved into an area. The most obvious effect from all this construction is the emissions from the machinery, but let's ignore that because it's the smallest possible direct impact. The much bigger impact is going to be moving all that equipment, material, and people through an area for several months while the pipeline is built. A crane can't drive through a forest, much less the truck that's going to be delivering the giant piece of pipe. That means trees are going to have to be removed (if it goes through a wooded area) and an otherwise pristine ecosystem is going to get turned into a packed dirt parking lot. Ok, whatever, the grass will grow back and the mice will dig new holes once construction's done, right? Well, sorta, but you've irreversibly changed the lay of the land. There's a plot of land way out in the middle of nowhere that I hunt deer, it hasn't been driven on for at least a decade (and probably longer), but you can still pretty clearly see where the former owners drove through because them driving over and over the same area changed the way that area was going to erode, and it's continued down that path. Those old roads are covered in grass, but you can still very clearly see the effect of human intervention. Furthermore, an oil pipeline isn't a "set it and forget it" kind of thing. Some of these dirt roads the construction crew is going to make are going to have to be maintained so that repair crews can get out to the pipeline to fix and replace parts. Which brings me to the last of the big ways that an oil pipeline can damage an ecosystem: They're going to have to replace parts. Any engineer will tell you that every part that goes into a machine or factory has a shelf life. The fluorescent bulbs in your house have a specific number of times that they can be turned on and off before they'll break, and the engineers that designed them know that number. Similarly, the seals, valves, and every other part of an oil pipeline (and even the pipe itself) have a finite number of days that they'll continue to work correctly. This could be managable if everything went exactly to plan, but those shelf lives are based on statistics. Individual parts aren't always going to conform to that statistical value. You already know that though, do all the lights in your house break at the same time? No, and even if you took two bulbs from the same package they'd still break at different times. And just like that, some seal on the pipe is inevitably going to start leaking before anyone expects and now that ecosystem has a bunch more oil on it that it used to. (Sidenote: do you know how you detect a leak in a pipeline? It's this thing called downstream pressure loss; basically you measure the pressure at the end of the pipeline and compare it to the pressure you expect if everything was going fine. That means you can only ever detect a leak after it's already leaked. The damage is done by the time you even know to start fixing the problem.) That's how a pipeline can destroy an ecosystem.', "Depends on the pipeline, but for the most part they don't really. Obviously to install it they are cutting a straight line 100 feet wide through whatever forest or whatever is in the way. That's the real immediate damage. So the map says pipeline goes through a bear den, backhoe is going to remove the bear den, they don't go around whatever small animals they find. Depending on where it's installed migrating animals may not want to cross it, so it impacts them (some are installed up in the air and such, and many animals simply never go under small things, they always go around but can't go around a pipeline). The risk isn't that bad though, they usually install spots the animals don't mind crossing at when it's an issue. The final risk is leaks, many of these are underground, it's not like your car that you notice one day it's leaking oil because you spot a few drops of oil on the ground. No, either the leak is very small in which case it can leak for decades and nobody notices or it's a big leak, like so big that it forms a pond of oil or they notice that the oil in is way different than the oil out. You need a big leak to detect these because many are underground, and they are in rural wilderness, they don't have people walking the pipeline looking for drops, they have people flying over it looking for ponds. Like your car, they do get a warning when there is a leak, but by that time they've leaked a lot, just like your car. They have tools that detect various types of leaks from inside the pipe, but it doesn't really catch the tiny ones. Now when there is a big leak, how do you think they stop it? Turn off the pipe? It's hundreds of miles of large pipe, there is still thousands of gallons to come out even when the pipe is off. So someone hates your pipeline and drives a truck into it? Hundreds of thousands of gallons of oil leaking out is likely. And even smaller ones are likely. People like to shoot the pipelines, how long do you think it takes them to find a bullet sized hole? That will get you the pond size leak, they might spot it in a few hours to a day...but that's easily hundreds of gallons. And finally, location, these leaks are not happening in Manhattan where there are no animals and trees, no, these are happening in pristine wilderness hundreds of miles from civilization. All these potential leaks are basically in the worse spot for leaks. Yes, pipelines leak a whole lot less than trucks, so everyone says it's safer and better, but trucks don't drive through the woods, they stay on the highways, they are more likely to leak, but also more likely to do so in a spot like NYC where it's spotted instantly and there are no bears or Elk or whatever. And they all leak, and they all have spills, so talking like it won't happen is just lies. The only argument is that you reduce leaks and spills with a pipeline, so hopefully that reduces environmental impact.

Same concept.', "To master a language requires practice. Growing up, my grandmother helped raise me, she spoke a dialect of Chinese that due to her speaking it to me from early on, I was able to understand, but she took care of me less as I was growing up so I did not develop the ability to speak her dialect, but I can still listen to it. As an adult learning a new language, mandarin, right now, I can tell you for most people learning to read comes first because you naturally will spend a lot of time translating words between languages, meaning more practice. Listening is next as your classroom will be based in that language, and you will have lots of time to listen to lectures in another language, or more practice. Writing is the third part that comes, due to your classroom learning, you will have homework, and writing assignments, but with computers, you may spend more time typing than writing nowadays. Finally speaking comes last because, you will have the least practice in it. You may answer some of teachers questions every now and then, but most likely you won't have much time to practice speaking to anyone outside of class. So experience wise, you get the least experience with speaking than you do with the other aspects of language, making it more likely for you to be able to understand a language but not speak it.,Speaking and understanding are completely different things. Look at a small child. A small child can't speak, but they understand you. You can ask them to fetch a particular toy and they can do it easily. They clearly understand that "ball" refers to something different than "rattle" and they know that when you say, "Get your ball" you want them to retrieve an object. Yet, the same child can't speak. They may be able to call the object in their hands a "baw," but obviously that's not a proper term and they certainly can't speak in complete sentences even though they can understand them. They have the physical ability to speak in the complete sentences, but can't even though they understand them. In short, it's kind of two different parts of the brain. I know some Spanish. Because Spanish is so similar to say, Portuguese I can read some Portuguese signs and if people are speaking Portuguese I can sometimes pick up some words here and there and get the gist of what they're saying. I can't speak Portuguese to save my life. I don't know how to conjugate the verbs. I don't know how to construct a sentence properly. I don't know the words for all the various things we come in contact with on a daily basis. Understanding and speaking are two different things.', "When speaking a language you can understand but don't speak often, you have to consciously assemble the grammar correctly. This is the hard part. Hearing it, the grammar part is already done for you, all you have to do is recognize it (which the brain can do almost subconsciously). If you overthink the grammar or aren't confident in your knowledge of pronouns and tenses, chances are you will get it wrong, which discourages the person from attempting to speak it. Also, when they say that they understand a language, if it requires certain sounds not in their primary language, they may not have the proper mouth memory of how to articulate the sounds correctly, hindering the comprehension of others if they try to speak and mess up the phonemes. Source: personal experience with English, Spanish and Greek. I am most fluent in English, though Spanish is my first. Greek is pretty much like this for me. I can understand it but my speech is iffy.," "You might not know a particular word in a language, but a lot of languages share root words. We'get' a word because we understand the root. Eddie Izzard was in a [documentary] (URL0) where he converses in Old English with a man in Holland who speaks Frisian. The languages at one point were evolving together. Frisian survived in a pocket of the country, whereas English kept intermingling and changing. Red, green, and blue (RGB) are the primary colors for light (i.e., additive color). In this case, "black" is the absence of any light, and "white" is 100 of all possible RGB frequencies in terms of luminance over the range 0100. Current methods have several limitations: 1.) Due to a limitation on spatial resolution andor sampling rate of cameras, camera image quality does not always satisfy all practical needs for visual perception in real-world environments. For example, current video standards such as MPEG-2 or H.264 achieve high compression ratios by exploiting temporal redundancy within frames. High frame rates used with these video coding schemes can reduce artifacts related to motion but they do so at the expense of increasing computational complexity. Although the latter issue may be addressed using hardware accelerators, the former cannot easily be dealt with without complex modifications to existing encoding algorithms; 2.) Current techniques typically rely upon an assumption that motion compensation artifact filtering is done at full precision before accumulation since there are no known means of properly interleaving intra (I) and predicted (P) frames. Accumulation implies floating point operations which take considerable processing time and power. Thus, conventional techniques require more storage bandwidth than necessary while also contributing additional latency when compared to standard pixel buffers; 3.) There exists insufficient information about how human eyes process images. Typically, such knowledge has been acquired from psychophysics studies rather than direct observation under controlled laboratory conditions. These approaches tend to focus exclusively on physical details such as contrast response due to the lack of other confounding factors such as illumination variation, depth cues, etc.; and 4.) Workflows based on brute force corner detection, histogram analysis, tracking, segmentation, edge extraction, dilation, erosion, template matching, feature identification, clustering, etc. usually consume considerable processing resources, memory capacity, and often introduce undesirable delays where the accuracy of each step depends heavily upon user input parameters.

I previously asked this question to a CS major friend. I hope I got it right: Typically, when a program becomes unresponsive, it’s trapped in a loop. However, being stuck in that loop doesn’t stop other programs from functioning normally. Your operating system—whether Windows, macOS, Linux, or others—will monitor which programs are active and continue performing their tasks. If it detects that Spotify is repeatedly looping through the same set of code without progress, it’ll display the "This program is unresponsive" message. Additionally, attempting to close the program may result in an error because the program can’t complete its usual shutdown process due to being stuck in the loop. You’ll need to manually allow the computer to terminate the program.

Computers can’t perform multiple tasks simultaneously, though this isn’t entirely accurate today. Older computers were limited to executing one task at a time; the user would start a program, let it run until completion, and then switch to another task, like a deck of cards or a paper strip with holes. This process was cumbersome, so later innovations introduced programs that could sequentially pass data to the computer. The computer wasn’t fully aware of this change, and each program had a small piece of code that loaded the next program after it finished. In many ways, your computer is similar. The operating system divides tasks into segments and runs itself between these segments. The computer alternates between running user applications and OS code. In any given moment, your computer executes a small part of a word processing program, and so on.

When discussions focus on major topics such as climate change, gun rights, or healthcare policies, people often don't prioritize the importance of evidence. Their shifting opinions tend to stem from emotional factors rather than factual reasoning. Even those who are aware of current events may rely on selectively chosen facts to justify their positions. However, new evidence typically doesn't sway individuals' convictions. If people formed their beliefs based on evidence, there would likely be more variety in the perspectives held. Currently, if someone shows interest in climate change, they might lean towards opposing gun rights and supporting abortion. Similarly, a strong stance on border security could correlate with advocating for limited government and supporting gun rights. These seemingly disconnected issues often coexist within individuals' belief systems, with over 80% of people holding these clusters of views. People rarely alter their major beliefs due to lack of evidential basis; instead, they often shift due to broader societal changes. The only instances where individuals change their minds are either through a shift in societal norms or through personal experiences. For instance, my son coming out has influenced my stance on same-sex marriage. While I recognize that persuasion through rational arguments and concrete evidence is possible, I emphasize that this should be grounded in objective facts rather than emotional appeals. I acknowledge that there may be nuances, but the core idea remains consistent.

We present a deep neural network model designed to calculate the prices and sensitivities (deltas) of American options in high-dimensional settings. The system employs a series of neural networks, each tasked with capturing the disparity between price functions at consecutive time steps. We define the loss function as the least squares residual from the corresponding backward stochastic differential equation. This method enables accurate pricing and sensitivity calculations across the full spacetime domain, not just at specific points. The computational complexity scales quadratically with the dimension, effectively mitigating the challenges posed by the curse of dimensionality. Numerical experiments validate our findings, demonstrating superior performance compared to existing methods in high-dimensional scenarios.

The development of autonomous robotic systems that can learn from human demonstrations to imitate a desired behavior - rather than being manually programmed - has huge technological potential. One major challenge in imitation learning is the correspondence problem: how to establish corresponding states and actions between the expert and learner, when the embodiments of the agents are different (morphology, dynamics, degrees of freedom, etc.). Many existing approaches in imitation learning circumvent the correspondence problem, for example, kinesthetic teaching or teleoperation, which are performed on the robot. In this work we explicitly address the correspondence problem by introducing a distance measure between dissimilar embodiments. This measure is then used as a loss function for static pose imitation and as a feedback signal within a model-free deep reinforcement learning framework for dynamic movement imitation between two anthropomorphic robotic arms in simulation. We find that the measure is well suited for describing the similarity between embodiments and for learning imitation policies by distance minimization.

The Tendai monastic complex at Mount Hiei became closely tied to the imperial court's new capital located nearby. This connection led Tendai to emphasize deep respect for the emperor and the nation. Kammu, a notable patron of the mystical Tendai sect, contributed to its rise to power over many years. A scenario involving a statistician in a dual-node system receiving limited-rate data from a transmitter regarding marginal observations of a memoryless process drawn from two potential distributions is considered. This receiver must initially verify the validity of its sender by determining the joint distribution of the process, followed by generating a suitable reconstruction of the observations that meets an average per-letter distortion criterion. The efficacy of this configuration is analyzed via the corresponding rate-error-distortion region, which outlines the balance between communication rate, the error introduced by detection, and the distortion caused by source reconstruction. In the specific case of testing against independence, where the alternative hypothesis suggests independence between the sources, the optimal rate-error-distortion region is identified. An illustrative example with binary symmetric sources is presented, along with the explicit formula for the rate-error-distortion region. The case of "general hypotheses" is also examined. A novel rate-error-distortion region is derived using non-asymptotic binning, enhancing the quality of transmitted descriptions. Further optimization of performance in the general case is demonstrated by relaxing the requirement for source reconstruction, differing from the scenario under general hypotheses.

This paper focuses on reduced-order models (ROMs) built for the efficient treatment of PDEs having solutions that bifurcate as the values of multiple input parameters change. First, we consider a method called local ROM that uses k-means algorithm to cluster snapshots and construct local POD bases, one for each cluster. We investigate one key ingredient of this approach: the local basis selection criterion. Several criteria are compared and it is found that a criterion based on a regression artificial neural network (ANN) provides the most accurate results for a channel flow problem exhibiting a supercritical pitchfork bifurcation. The same benchmark test is then used to compare the local ROM approach with the regression ANN selection criterion to an established global projection-based ROM and a recently proposed ANN based method called POD-NN. We show that our local ROM approach gains more than an order of magnitude in accuracy over the global projection-based ROM. However, the POD-NN provides consistently more accurate approximations than the local projection-based ROM.

The core idea of the information processing model revolves around understanding brain functions by analyzing how information flows and algorithms are implemented. An influential early work was a 1959 paper titled "What the frog's eye tells the frog's brain," which investigated the visual responses of neurons in the frog's retina and optic tectum, concluding that certain neurons in the tectum combine basic responses to function as "bug perceivers." Later, David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel identified cells in the primary visual cortex of monkeys that activate when sharp edges move across specific points in the visual field—this discovery earned them a Nobel Prize. Subsequent research in higher-order visual regions uncovered cells capable of detecting binocular disparity, color, motion, and shape, with responses becoming more intricate as these areas became farther from the primary visual cortex. Additional studies on brain regions beyond vision revealed cells with diverse response patterns, including those related to memory and abstract cognitive processes like spatial reasoning.

As there is no universally accepted definition of "life," we determine whether something is alive by examining how many of the seven key characteristics of life it possesses. These characteristics must be flexible enough to classify computers as living entities, especially if we ever want to categorize unknown alien lifeforms as alive. I believe computers display these properties in the following manner.  

- **1. Composed of cells**: Computers have a foundational unit—transistors—that underpins their operation.  
- **2. Emergent properties and levels of organization**: There are multiple layers of complexity, from hardware to software, with specialized components akin to "organs."  
- **3. Uses energy**: While some argue they consume excessive power, they still utilize energy for functioning.  
- **4. Responds to environment**: Computers react to inputs, such as users, robots, or environmental data.  
- **5. Grows**: Through updates, computers enhance their capabilities and physical form, if relevant to the definition.  
- **6. Reproduces**: Bots create other bots, and parts of systems can build objects like cars and toys, indicating reproduction-like behavior.  
- **7. Adapts to environment**: While complex, computers adjust to tasks and environments, such as shutting down during storms. Upgrades allow for continuous adaptation.  

Computers demonstrate life's characteristics in various forms, making them a compelling candidate for redefining what it means to be alive.

Wireless Network-on-Chip (WNoC) appears as a promising alternative to conventional interconnect fabrics for chip-scale communications. The WNoC paradigm has been extensively analyzed from the physical, network and architecture perspectives assuming mmWave band operation. However, there has not been a comprehensive study at this band for realistic chip packages and, thus, the characteristics of such wireless channel remain not fully understood. This work addresses this issue by accurately modeling a flip-chip package and investigating the wave propagation inside it. Through parametric studies, a locally optimal configuration for 60 GHz WNoC is obtained, showing that chip-wide attenuation below 32.6 dB could be achieved with standard processes. Finally, the applicability of the methodology is discussed for higher bands and other integrated environments such as a Software-Defined Metamaterial (SDM).

Since 1718, transportation to the American colonies had been a penalty for various criminal offences in Britain, with approximately one thousand convicts transported per year across the Atlantic. Forced to find an alternative location after the loss of the 13 Colonies in 1783, the British government turned to the newly discovered lands of Australia. The western coast of Australia had been discovered for Europeans by the Dutch explorer Willem Jansz in 1606 and was later named New Holland by the Dutch East India Company, but there was no attempt to colonise it. In 1770 James Cook discovered the eastern coast of Australia while on a scientific voyage to the South Pacific Ocean, claimed the continent for Britain, and named it New South Wales. In 1778, Joseph Banks, Cook's botanist on the voyage, presented evidence to the government on the suitability of Botany Bay for the establishment of a penal settlement, and in 1787 the first shipment of convicts set sail, arriving in 1788. Britain continued to transport convicts to New South Wales until 1840. The Australian colonies became profitable exporters of wool and gold, mainly because of gold rushes in the colony of Victoria, making its capital Melbourne the richest city in the world and the largest city after London in the British Empire.

Face analysis plays a critical role in computer vision. Research indicates that facial movements can offer significant insights for face analysis. The movement of a specific facial region during an expression is linked to the movements of other facial regions. This paper introduces a new deep learning method called the facial dynamics interpreter network, aimed at identifying key relationships among local dynamics to estimate facial characteristics from expression sequences. The network is structured to capture relational significance, enabling it to explain how facial local dynamics relate to the estimation of facial features. Comparative experiments validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach. The facial dynamics interpreter network investigates the relationships between facial local dynamics in gender classification and age estimation. Experimental results demonstrate that the method surpasses existing techniques in these tasks.

Microorganisms frequently adhere to surfaces and develop dense clusters known as biofilms or bacterial mats. These layers can vary in thickness from a few micrometers to up to half a meter and may include various types of bacteria, protists, and archaea. Cells within biofilms organize into intricate arrangements with extracellular substances, creating secondary structures like microcolonies that facilitate nutrient transport via internal channels. In natural settings, most bacteria reside in biofilms on surfaces such as soil or plant surfaces. Biofilms play a significant role in medicine, as they are commonly found in persistent bacterial infections or in infections associated with implanted medical devices. Bacteria enclosed within biofilms are generally more resistant to elimination compared to free-living bacteria.

Consider the problem where a statistician in a two-node system receives rate-limited information from a transmitter about marginal observations of a memoryless process generated from two possible distributions. Using its own observations, this receiver is required to first identify the legitimacy of its sender by declaring the joint distribution of the process, and then depending on such authentication it generates the adequate reconstruction of the observations satisfying an average per-letter distortion. The performance of this setup is investigated through the corresponding rate-error-distortion region describing the trade-off between: the communication rate, the error exponent induced by the detection and the distortion incurred by the source reconstruction. In the special case of testing against independence , where the alternative hypothesis implies that the sources are independent, the optimal rate-error-distortion region is characterized. An application example to binary symmetric sources is given subsequently and the explicit expression for the rate-error-distortion region is provided as well. The case of "general hypotheses" is also investigated. A new achievable rate-error-distortion region is derived based on the use of non-asymptotic binning , improving the quality of communicated descriptions. Further improvement of performance in the general case is shown to be possible when the requirement of source reconstruction is relaxed, which stands in contrast to the case of general hypotheses.

Price differentiation describes a marketing strategy to determine the price of goods on the basis of a potential customer's attributes like location, financial status, possessions, or behavior. Several cases of online price differentiation have been revealed in recent years. For example, different pricing based on a user's location was discovered for online office supply chain stores and there were indications that offers for hotel rooms are priced higher for Apple users compared to Windows users at certain online booking websites. One potential source for relevant distinctive features are system fingerprints , i.e., a technique to recognize users' systems by identifying unique attributes such as the source IP address or system configuration. In this paper, we shed light on the ecosystem of pricing at online platforms and aim to detect if and how such platform providers make use of price differentiation based on digital system fingerprints. We designed and implemented an automated price scanner capable of disguising itself as an arbitrary system, leveraging real-world system fingerprints, and searched for price differences related to different features (e.g., user location, language setting, or operating system). This system allows us to explore price differentiation cases and expose those characteristic features of a system that may influence a product's price.

Now imagine the road itself is expanding at all points, not just at the edges. If you drive at a constant speed 10 km according to your odometer the road behind you has expanded a little in the time it's taken you to drive those 10 km, so it's possible that your starting point is now, say, 11 km away. If you drive another 10 km you've now got 20 km of expanding road behind you and it's been expanding for twice as long, so maybe now the distance to your starting point is more like 24 km. Your odometer still reads 20 km and at no point were you travelling faster than your initial constant speed, but you've covered an extra 4 km in distance relative to your starting point. If you stop here for a week the road continues to expand and you might find yourself hundreds of km away from your starting point, even though your odometer still reads 20 km. Space is expanding in the same way. As you move further away from your reference point the amount of expanding space between you and it increases. At some point there's so much expanding space between that the distance to your reference point is actually growing faster than the speed of light. At that point your reference is unreachable, you can never get back to it assuming the expansion rate of the universe remains the same. So to say "space is expanding faster than the speed of light" isn't quite right. Space expands [very slowly] (URL0) relative to the distances involved, but at huge distances (we're talking billions of light years) there's just so much space separating the two points that the distance between them grows faster than light could cross it.

Most deraining works focus on rain streaks removal but they cannot deal adequately with heavy rain images. In heavy rain, streaks are strongly visible, dense rain accumulation or rain veiling effect significantly washes out the image, further scenes are relatively more blurry, etc. In this paper, we propose a novel method to address these problems. We put forth a 2-stage network: a physics-based backbone followed by a depth-guided GAN refinement. The first stage estimates the rain streaks, the transmission, and the atmospheric light governed by the underlying physics. To tease out these components more reliably, a guided filtering framework is used to decompose the image into its low- and high-frequency components. This filtering is guided by a rain-free residue image - its content is used to set the passbands for the two channels in a spatially-variant manner so that the background details do not get mixed up with the rain-streaks. For the second stage, the refinement stage, we put forth a depth-guided GAN to recover the background details failed to be retrieved by the first stage, as well as correcting artefacts introduced by that stage. We have evaluated our method against the state of the art methods. Extensive experiments show that our method outperforms them on real rain image data, recovering visually clean images with good details.

The achievements of Notre Dame's football team brought the university into the public eye. This success mirrored the growing influence of Irish Americans and Catholic communities in the 1920s. Catholics supported the team and listened to games on the radio, particularly during matches against institutions representing Protestant dominance—Harvard, Yale, Princeton, and Army. However, Notre Dame's prominence as a Catholic symbol also made it vulnerable to anti-Catholic prejudice. One of the most notable incidents was the confrontation between Notre Dame students and the Ku Klux Klan in 1924. Nativism and anti-Catholic sentiment, often tied to the KKK's messaging, viewed Notre Dame as a representation of the Catholic Church's threat. The KKK organized a week-long Klavern in South Bend, leading to violent clashes with students on March 17, when they blocked Klansmen from entering the station and destroyed their clothing. On May 19, thousands of students gathered downtown to protest, preventing further conflict, though the presence of college president Fr. Matthew Walsh halted the situation. That same day, football coach Knute Rockne addressed a campus rally, urging students to respect the president and avoid further violence. Days later, the Klavern dissolved, but the students' hostility marked a turning point in the KKK's decline in Indiana.

Jean Say killed his son and daughter two years ago. The Independent Police Complaints Commission (IPCC) said Southwark Sapphire unit in south London "encouraged" victims to withdraw allegations to boost detection rates. The Metropolitan Police said substantial changes had been made. The rape allegation against Say was dismissed by a detective sergeant based at Southwark, who said the circumstances did not constitute rape because the woman "consented." The report by the IPCC said: "There is no doubt from the evidence that the woman made an allegation of rape at Walworth police station which should have been believed and thoroughly investigated." The IPCC said the Southwark Sapphire squad's approach of "failing to believe victims" was "wholly inappropriate." It also said it was "under-performing and over-stretched." Deputy chairwoman of the IPCC Deborah Glass said: "There's no doubt this was an incredibly serious, shocking incident. "We know with all the cases that we've dealt with that the consequences of not dealing with allegations of rape can be extremely serious. "This is yet another tragic illustration of that." Say, 62, a retired concierge, attacked his daughter Regina, eight, and son Rolls, 10, in their beds at his home in Southwark in 2011, while they were on a weekend access visit. The Old Bailey heard he killed them to spite his wife who had left him. He was given a 30-year minimum term. The case sparked a wider investigation into the work of the unit between July 2008 and September 2009, the results of which have now been published. The IPCC has carried out five previous inquiries into Southwark Sapphire command and it is the police watchdog's ninth investigation into the Met's response to victims of sexual violence. By Danny ShawHome affairs correspondent, BBC News No one will ever know if Jean Say's children would be alive today if he'd been arrested and investigated for rape three years before he stabbed them to death. But if police hadn't "no-crimed" the rape allegation, the chances are Say's threatening and violent behaviour would have been uncovered. The Say case is the most egregious example of the dysfunctional approach to rape investigations at the Southwark Sapphire unit; what we don't know is how many other sexual assault victims were wrongly disbelieved and the impact that's had on them and on others. Although Scotland Yard says the Sapphire units have changed for the better, the practice of no-crimeing is still a problem across other forces: in England and Wales reported rapes are three times as likely to be written off as other incidents are. Home affairs correspondent Danny Shaw said three Metropolitan officers who had been facing possible dismissal over a previous bungled investigation into the serial sex offender Kirk Reid, were still with the force. Two of them, a superintendent and a detective inspector, have been promoted. A detective sergeant is facing disciplinary proceedings for alleged gross misconduct in connection with the allegations. In another case, Det Con Ryan Coleman-Farrow, who was based in Southwark, was jailed for 16 months in October last year for failing to investigate rape and sexual assault claims. A second officer, based in Islington, north London, is still under criminal investigation. In total 19 officers from across London have been disciplined, including three who have been sacked. A Met Police spokesman said: "We have for some time acknowledged that previous investigation of rape and serious sexual assault in the MPS was below standard. "The activities identified in this report came during that era and highlight specific issues within Southwark which resulted in unacceptable actions by local officers. "It is as a result of such failings that we have made substantial changes to the investigation of rape and serious sexual assault, both in terms of structure and revised working practices."
