Although cults are religious groups typically, they have a lot of differences which are quite big. - Leadership: Whereas a religion may have a religious head and a hierarchical structure with priests or bishops representing the hierarchy, cults tend to be more pluralistic in their composition (although making up for this through the role hierarchy). They also don't usually have clear demarcations between "members" and "leaders" as is typical on religions. Instead they often include people who perceive themselves to be leaders of others such as teachers, clergyman; pastors, ministers etc. The contrast between them can be seen from their choice of names. Religious organizations have their own sacred texts, but cults do not. Cult members believe that these books represent a true story about God. On the other hand, cult members might act like believers by adhering to one set of rules, while performing rituals associated with these beliefs. Cult membership is sometimes thought of as a religious institution where adherents pay fees and attend meetings. But this definition does not describe too many cults. Some cults operate entirely underground; there is no state organization overseeing their activities or even any official website. Most cults control only small areas within an area, rather than being geographically focused. However, it is still relevant to recognize what's considered a cult because cult activity involves a number of different issues e.g., secrecy, coven-style worship practices, the absence of legal protections for victims, financial incentives to recruit new members, manipulation techniques, fear tactics, intimidation in order to convince recruits to join.

Most rain removal techniques primarily target rain streaks but struggle with heavy rain imagery. In such cases, streaks become highly visible, dense rain accumulation, or the rain veiling effect can severely distort the image, leading to increased blur. This paper introduces a new approach to tackle these issues. We design a two-stage network consisting of a physics-based backbone followed by a depth-guided GAN refinement. The first stage identifies rain streaks, transmission, and atmospheric light based on physical principles. To extract these components accurately, a guided filtering technique is employed to separate the image into low- and high-frequency components. The filtering is guided by a rain-free residual image, allowing the passbands for the two channels to vary spatially. This ensures that background details remain distinct from rain streaks. In the second stage, a depth-guided GAN is introduced to restore background details missed by the first stage and correct artifacts introduced during that process. Our method has been tested against existing state-of-the-art approaches, and experimental results demonstrate superior performance on real rain images, producing visually clear and detailed outputs.

One of the challenges in large-scale information retrieval (IR) is to develop fine-grained and domain-specific methods to answer natural language questions. Despite the availability of numerous sources and datasets for IR, the majority of existing research has focused on traditional approaches such as text matching or dictionary lookup based on general-purpose terminology databases like WordNet [3]. Thus, there remains a great need for more effective ways of dealing with complex queries that are typical of many real-world applications. Recently, there have been attempts at developing better tools, resources, and models to deal with such tasks [4, 5, 6, 7], but they still suffer from several drawbacks when it comes to practicality. Most importantly, these systems tend to be over-engineered, since their underlying theories rely heavily on fixed mathematical structures or parameterized patterns of search [8, 9]. In contrast our system uses only simple heuristics inspired by common sense rules of inference and focuses directly on how humans reason about concepts to arrive at answers to natural-language questions [10]. Given an input question, we compute a set of candidate concepts to retrieve from a given corpus using distributional similarity measures [11] combined with various linguistic features extracted automatically from raw texts [12, 13]. We then evaluate each concept according its co-occurrence with other key terms appearing within the same sentences as well as learn textual representations of all entities mentioned in the query [14, 15, 16]. Finally, we rank the candidates so that those involving less noise will receive higher ranks [17]. Results We evaluated our approach against two baselines: 1) A baseline where relations between different records were learned by means of supervised learning techniques [12]; 2) A baseline which used n-gram frequency statistics [13] instead of the semantic based scoring function proposed here. The experiments show that both of these baselines perform poorly compared to ours. This shows that employing some form of knowledge-based reasoning could result in significant improvements of performance. In particular, the above results indicate that utilizing human-machine interaction can greatly benefit our classification model [18]: classic machine-learning classifiers seem unable to capture this kind of ambiguity inherent to natural languages [19]. The rest of this paper consists of three sections: Section 3 describes related work, section 4 presents details of our method, experimental setups and evaluation metrics; finally, conclusions and future directions are discussed in section 5. Related Work There exist many studies focusing primarily on designing new algorithms to improve document retrieval [20, 21]. On the contrary we focus on exploring mechanisms that allow us to assign appropriate weights to retrieved documents [22]. Retrieval error reduction is an important problem [23] as errors in information seeking may lead not only to undesirable consequences in searching process itself [24], but also affect user satisfaction [25]. Diverse solutions were employed to overcome this issue including ontology [26], clustering [27], ranking [28], summarization [29], etc. Among them, MeSH hierarchy [30] was widely applied due to its ability to describe biomedical concepts [31]. Our system employs word vectors [32] derived from unigrams together with additional syntactic [33] and lexical [34] features obtained through automatic analysis of context surrounding named entity mentions [35]. Compared to most previous approaches [36], to date no similar attempt took into account specific properties of medical data [37], especially considering potential ambiguities stemming from use of acronyms. Our solution leverages experts' insights regarding likely relationships between an ambiguous termconcept and other medical terminologies. These relationships aim at pruning irrelevant items out of potentially large number of possible matches. For instance, consider the following scenario. Suppose one needs to find drug names corresponding to "hypertension" -the patient might ask "What drugs treat hypertension?"; however, if current evidence does not support any relationship between hypertension and any other diseasedisease-related condition this would mean that most possible diseases should appear among first few returned hits. Therefore, it is desirable to filter relevant candidates before returning the top hit (es). As another example, suppose one wants to know what medical conditions correspond to "liver cirrhosis." If symptoms associated with liver cirrhosis include dry mouth, dark urine, diarrhea, while "the name of a certain medication helps prevent heart attacks" happens to mention blood circulation, then "Liver Cirrhotic Candidate Modification Algorithm" [16] finds a single match blood pressure elevation" -since "dry mouth" implies "a serious health problem," whereas "no evidence suggests such relationship exists between "blood circulation" and "heart attacks." However, if the latter phrase actually refers to "high cholesterol levels" through "circulation vasoconstriction" mechanism cells lining arteries become stiffen causing narrowing resulting in increased blood flow resistance, i.e., being sick -then "heart attacks" becomes unlikely too. Shijian-21, or SJ-21, is a Chinese satellite designed to test and verify space debris mitigation technologies. It was recently observed pulling a dead satellite out of its normal orbit and into an orbit where it will eventually reenter the atmosphere and burn up. This is a major step forward in the effort to reduce the amount of space debris that is accumulating in Earth's orbit. The satellite was launched in July 2020, as part of China's Long March-4B rocket mission. It is equipped with a robotic arm and a capture device, which are capable of grasping objects up to 350 kilograms in weight. The satellite also features a variety of sensors and cameras for monitoring the captured object. SJ-21 is the first satellite of its kind to be sent into space and has already proven successful in its mission. In addition to being able to de-orbit discarded satellites, it is also capable of stabilizing their orbits, allowing them to remain in a safe area of space. This technology could potentially be used to help prevent further collisions between satellites and other space debris. In the future, SJ-21 could be used to clean up other types of space debris, such as defunct spacecraft and pieces of rocket boosters. This could have a significant impact on the environment by reducing the amount of trash in orbit and preventing long-term damage to our planet.

BJTs consist of three terminals, representing the three layers of a semiconductor—emitter, base, and collector. Their utility in amplifiers stems from the ability to regulate the currents at the emitter and collector using a relatively small base current. In an n-p-n transistor operating in the active mode, the emitter-base junction is forward-biased, allowing electrons and holes to recombine at the junction, with electrons being injected into the base region. Due to the narrow base, most of these electrons diffuse into the reverse-biased base-collector junction and are conducted into the collector. Approximately one-hundredth of the electrons may recombine within the base, making it the primary factor in the base current. By adjusting the number of electrons that can exit the base, the number of electrons entering the collector is also regulated. The collector current is roughly equal to the common-emitter current gain multiplied by the base current. For small-signal transistors, this value is typically above 100, though it may be lower in high-power applications.

Automated hyperparameter optimization (HPO) demonstrates significant effectiveness across various machine learning tasks. However, current approaches face challenges related to model selection, parallel processing, and sample efficiency. This paper introduces a novel HPO technique called MOdular FActorial Design (MOFA), which tackles these problems concurrently. The core concept involves applying principles from experimental design to enhance the sample efficiency of model-free methodologies. Specifically, MOFA operates in four modules during each iteration: (1) an Orthogonal Latin Hypercube (OLH)-based sampler that maintains univariate projection uniformity and orthogonality; (2) a highly parallelized evaluator; (3) a transformer that condenses the OLH performance table into a Fractional Factorial Design-Orthogonal Array (OA); and (4) an analyzer incorporating Factorial Performance Analysis and Factorial Importance Analysis to reduce the search space. Both theoretical and empirical studies demonstrate that MOFA offers superior performance compared to existing model-based and model-free methods.

Recent studies have indicated that intermediate feature maps from pre-trained convolutional neural networks exhibit notable enhancements in perceptual quality when incorporated into the loss function during the training of new networks. These features are thought to be more effective at representing perceptual quality and offer more compact representations of input images than alternative perceptual measures like SSIM and PSNR. However, there has been no comprehensive investigation into the underlying reasons for these improvements. Without such analysis, it remains impossible to assess the performance of specific feature sets or to further enhance perceptual quality by choosing subsets of pre-trained CNN features. This research demonstrates that the ability of pre-trained deep CNN features to optimize perceptual quality is closely linked to their capacity to capture fundamental aspects of human visual perception. Specifically, we examine key elements of human perception, including contrast sensitivity and orientation selectivity. We propose two novel methods to quantify the frequency and orientation selectivity of features extracted by convolutional layers, enabling evaluation of deep features from widely employed CNNs such as VGG-16. Our results indicate that pre-trained CNN features receiving higher scores are more accurate in predicting human quality judgments. Additionally, we explore the potential to use our approach to develop a new loss function for image reconstruction in the single-image super-resolution task, thereby improving its performance.

Your heart beats when it does because of a spot near the top of the muscle called the sinoatrial node. It beats partially because the nervous system tells it to, but mostly because of what's called a prepotential, where the electrical polarity of the cells of the SA node gradually changes as sodium leaks into those cells. When they've leaked a certain amount, an "action potential" is produced that causes the heart beat, which is propagated systematically to the rest of the heart. So even without a direct connection to your brain, your heart would still beat at about 80 beats per minute because of the leaky nature of the cells in the SA node. That's god damn amazing. Next, that action potential is communicated to the Atrioventricular node, which sits between the top chambers (atria) and larger bottom chambers (ventricles) of the heart. If, for some reason, the signal isn't conducted from the SA node to the AV node, that doesn't matter - the cells of the AV node are also leaky, but to a slightly lesser degree. Even if they don't get told to continue the heart beat by the SA node, they'll still generate a beat of their own. With no electrical connection between the top and centre parts of your heart, it'll still beat at around 60 beats per minute. That's also god damn amazing. The AV node also does something even cooler: it holds the signal for about 100 milliseconds. This is, funnily enough, pretty much the ideal period of time for the atria to fill so that they squeeze the maximum amount of blood into the ventricles. The heart's timing is just amazing. After the AV node, the electrical signal is conducted to the muscular walls of the ventricles, which contract as they're told to. But what if they don't get told to contract because there's no connection between them and the AV node? Doesn't matter, they'll still beat at a slightly slower rate, around 40 beats per minute. Even with some truly serious connection failures throughout your heart, it can still beat and keep you alive, albeit in a fairly ill state of being. And let's look at it the other way: if your SA node is seriously screwed up, or if you're taking drugs that profoundly increase your heart rate, your heart has a built-in maximum rate of about 180 beats per minute because of the speed bump provided by the AV node's delay. This is, coincidentally, about the maximum rate at which the ventricles can efficiently pump blood around the body; any higher, and there's no time for blood to enter them before they contract again. The heart is god damn amazing. e: Don't get me started on red blood cells, either. Those are god damn amazing too. Disinflation is a reduction in the rate of inflation. If prices rose 3 last year, but only 2 this year, then disinflation has occurred. We may say that the economy disinflated by 1, but it still grew at 2. This is not the same thing as deflation, which is a fall in prices. If inflation is low to begin with, or disinflation occurs over a long period of time, then that MAY lead to deflation, but not always. Disinflation often occurs during a recession. Disinflation is a problem when it is sustained and the economy suffers deflation. Deflation is a problem because the purchasing power of money actually increases. Therefore people are encouraged to save, and not spend, since 1 tomorrow will buy more than 1 today. But this lack of consumption can make a recession worse. Deflation, and increased unemployment, was what happened to Japan from 1990 until recently.','Deflation (I presume you mean this, rather than disinflation, which is something else and not so bad) is bad because it sees prices drop. The World Health Organization states that breast cancer is the most prevalent type of cancer in women globally. It ranks as the second leading cause of mortality among women worldwide and is the deadliest form of cancer. Although various imaging methods are available for diagnosing breast cancer, X-ray mammography remains the most widely used and effective technique. Therefore, mammographic image segmentation is crucial for supporting image analysis and diagnosis, considering the shape analysis of mammary lesions and their boundaries. However, mammogram segmentation is a challenging task due to its dependence on the types of mammary tissues. The GrowCut algorithm, a recently developed method for general image segmentation, relies on selecting a few points within and outside the region of interest to achieve good results in complex segmentation scenarios when these points are accurately chosen. In this study, we introduce a novel semi-supervised segmentation approach based on modifying the GrowCut algorithm to automatically segment mammograms once a region of interest is identified by a specialist. Our method incorporates fuzzy Gaussian membership functions to adjust the evolution rules of the original GrowCut algorithm, enabling the estimation of pixel uncertainty regarding whether they belong to the object or the background. The primary benefit of this approach is the substantial decrease in the expertise required for initializing seed points in the GrowCut algorithm, as it eliminates the need to select background seeds. Additionally, the method demonstrates robustness against incorrect seed placement and can be adapted to other seed-based techniques. These features contribute to both expert and intelligent systems by facilitating the development of a segmentation method with reduced specialist involvement, high reliability, and efficiency comparable to current advanced techniques. We also designed an automated point selection mechanism.

As this is an ELI5 explanation, I need to provide some context rather than a straightforward "take this" response. I'm not a nurse or medical professional, but I do read medication labels. In the United States, there are two main types of over-the-counter (OTC) pain relievers: acetaminophen (also called paracetamol in many countries and known as Tylenol) and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). Acetaminophen has fewer side effects when taken in the correct dose, but even small amounts can lead to severe liver damage. This is a concern because many cold remedies also include acetaminophen, and combining it with another product containing acetaminophen could be dangerous. NSAIDs work by reducing both pain and inflammation, something acetaminophen doesn't do. They can cause stomach issues, so people with frequent heartburn or nausea should avoid them. However, for most people, an NSAID is better for joint and muscle pain than acetaminophen. Many cold medicines also contain acetaminophen, so taking both a cold remedy and an NSAID could increase the risk of an overdose. The most common NSAID after aspirin is ibuprofen, which is generally safe. For long-term pain like hand or wrist pain from repetitive use, naproxen may be a better option. Still, new information about these drugs is constantly emerging, so staying updated is important. They’re safe when used as directed—multiple days in a row for a sore joint is acceptable—but if you experience headaches regularly, seeing a doctor is advisable. It’s not because the medications aren’t effective, but because frequent headaches might indicate an underlying issue needing attention.

A LAN is a Local Area Network. It just refers to how computersdevices connected to the same network routing equipment (e.g. your home Wi-Fi router) can communicate with each-other directly without passing data communications over the internet (i.e. without using the DSLCableFiber connection you have to your ISP [Internet Service Provider. Devices on your local network will be assigned internal IP addresses which can be used to address and send packets between devices without requiring any internet connectivity. To distinguish internal from external (public internet) IP addresses, it has been universally decided that IPv4 addresses starting with '10.', '172.16' and '192.168' should be reserved for internal LAN use while all other addresses should be allocated for public internet use. Most home internet connections will have one public IP address assigned to be shared among all computersdevices on that customer's LAN. The router installed in the customer's home is in charge of routing incoming data packets (to the customer's public IP address) to the correct internal IP address (corresponding to the computerdevice on the LAN which requested that data).

This article discusses WebAssembly and its possible future applications. WebAssembly is an intermediate layer between various programming languages and many different execution environments. It can be used to run code from many different languages in the same environment, as well as compile code more quickly and efficiently than traditional methods. WebAssembly is currently being used in web browsers, video game engines, and other applications, but its potential for use in the future goes far beyond that. Possible uses include enabling high-performance machine learning, creating distributed applications across multiple environments, and even running entire operating systems within a browser. WebAssembly also has the potential to be used to create virtualized hardware, allowing users to run applications or services on machines they do not own. By making it easier to move code between platforms, WebAssembly could revolutionize the way code is shared and developed, potentially opening up new opportunities for developers and users alike.

Our body wants to be near its optimal running temperature at all times, about 95-100 degrees Fahrenheit. As it gets further and further away from that temperature the body will try to influence itself to get warmer or colder. Part of that is to make it painful if it's really cold really hot. So you tend to be in MORE pain when cold because your body is already sending "pain signals" when it's too cold. As for the numbness, it's most likely because the body moves blood into the chest to keep the vital organs like the heart and lungs functioning well when it gets too cold. This loss of blood to the hands and feet make it harder for nerve cells to function properly. That being said evolution made it so that our pain neurons can run with less blood flow, so even if you're really cold you can detect whether you're in pain or not.

Recently, intermediate feature maps of pre-trained convolutional neural networks have shown significant perceptual quality improvements, when they are used in the loss function for training new networks. It is believed that these features are better at encoding the perceptual quality and provide more efficient representations of input images compared to other perceptual metrics such as SSIM and PSNR. However, there have been no systematic studies to determine the underlying reason. Due to the lack of such an analysis, it is not possible to evaluate the performance of a particular set of features or to improve the perceptual quality even more by carefully selecting a subset of features from a pre-trained CNN. This work shows that the capabilities of pre-trained deep CNN features in optimizing the perceptual quality are correlated with their success in capturing basic human visual perception characteristics. In particular, we focus our analysis on fundamental aspects of human perception, such as the contrast sensitivity and orientation selectivity. We introduce two new formulations to measure the frequency and orientation selectivity of the features learned by convolutional layers for evaluating deep features learned by widely-used deep CNNs such as VGG-16. We demonstrate that the pre-trained CNN features which receive higher scores are better at predicting human quality judgment. Furthermore, we show the possibility of using our method to select deep features to form a new loss function, which improves the image reconstruction quality for the well-known single-image super-resolution problem.

A machine learning system can score well on a given test set by relying on heuristics that are effective for frequent example types but break down in more challenging cases. We study this issue within natural language inference (NLI), the task of determining whether one sentence entails another. We hypothesize that statistical NLI models may adopt three fallible syntactic heuristics: the lexical overlap heuristic, the subsequence heuristic, and the constituent heuristic. To determine whether models have adopted these heuristics, we introduce a controlled evaluation set called HANS (Heuristic Analysis for NLI Systems), which contains many examples where the heuristics fail. We find that models trained on MNLI, including BERT, a state-of-the-art model, perform very poorly on HANS, suggesting that they have indeed adopted these heuristics. We conclude that there is substantial room for improvement in NLI systems, and that the HANS dataset can motivate and measure progress in this area.

Metric learning is a key problem for many data mining and machine learning applications, and has long been dominated by Mahalanobis methods. Recent advances in nonlinear metric learning have demonstrated the potential power of non-Mahalanobis distance functions, particularly tree-based functions. We propose a novel nonlinear metric learning method that uses an iterative, hierarchical variant of semi-supervised max-margin clustering to construct a forest of cluster hierarchies, where each individual hierarchy can be interpreted as a weak metric over the data. By introducing randomness during hierarchy training and combining the output of many of the resulting semi-random weak hierarchy metrics, we can obtain a powerful and robust nonlinear metric model. This method has two primary contributions: first, it is semi-supervised, incorporating information from both constrained and unconstrained points. Second, we take a relaxed approach to constraint satisfaction, allowing the method to satisfy different subsets of the constraints at different levels of the hierarchy rather than attempting to simultaneously satisfy all of them. This leads to a more robust learning algorithm. We compare our method to a number of state-of-the-art benchmarks on k -nearest neighbor classification, large-scale image retrieval and semi-supervised clustering problems, and find that our algorithm yields results comparable or superior to the state-of-the-art, and is significantly more robust to noise.

The final years of the Yuan dynasty were marked by struggle, famine, and bitterness among the populace. In time, Kublai Khan's successors lost all influence on other Mongol lands across Central Asia, Eastern Europe, Siberia, and North America (formerly called "New Russia" or "Novgorod. The Mongols never re-conquered their old African Empire, which had been conquered by Timur in the early 15th century.[4] In 1365, Genghis Khan died at age 59 near Jalalabad. He left a son, Chinggis Khaan - who would later become known as Kublai Khan - to succeed him but was forced by his own brother-in-law Boke Khan to appoint Arslan Ajaa instead due to divisions between the two brothers' wives, Bayazid Khoja and Manguuny Ulduar. This division has led some historians such as John Zada Wolff[56] and Peter Sarris to label it as a divided empire in its infancy that may have already begun disintegration through internal strife during Ghengis Khan's life time; others like Rene Jardine claim this narrative is more romantic than historical and adds little to our understanding of the rise and fall of Mongol empires after the death of Ghengis Khan. Nevertheless, despite being unable to name his successor until he did so shortly before dying, Genghis Khan left behind a major legacy though he could not rule over China long enough to establish an era of peace with Ming China under any circumstances whatsoever. Perhaps the most remarkable part about Genghis Khan's rule is how relatively short lived it really was while still leaving a lasting impression onto many peoples throughout Eurasia. As historian George C. Edwards writes: Genghis Khan ruled for only twenty four years from AD; yet within those few decades he acquired almost total control over virtually one fifth of mankind, whose population today numbers just over six billion people - roughly one quarter of humankind! His military campaigns extended from modern day Afghanistan and Pakistan eastwards into Central Asian steppes, then southward and westwards over India down towards Indonesia, Java, Peninsular Malaysia and Southern Thailand. By the end of his career, he controlled nearly half the world's land surface area.[7]

Diversity plays a vital role in many text generating applications. In recent years, Conditional Variational Auto Encoders (CVAE) have shown promising performances for this task. However, they often encounter the so called KL-Vanishing problem. Previous works mitigated such problem by heuristic methods such as strengthening the encoder or weakening the decoder while optimizing the CVAE objective function. Nevertheless, the optimizing direction of these methods are implicit and it is hard to find an appropriate degree to which these methods should be applied. In this paper, we propose an explicit optimizing objective to complement the CVAE to directly pull away from KL-vanishing. In fact, this objective term guides the encoder towards the "best encoder" of the decoder to enhance the expressiveness. A labeling network is introduced to estimate the "best encoder." It provides a continuous label in the latent space of CVAE to help build a close connection between latent variables and targets. The whole proposed method is named Self Labeling CVAE (SLCVAE). To accelerate the research of diverse text generation, we also propose a large native one-to-many dataset. Extensive experiments are conducted on two tasks, which show that our method largely improves the generating diversity while achieving comparable accuracy compared with state-of-art algorithms.

There are several counter-arguments that can be made to refute the claim that the Earth is alive. One major argument is that the Earth lacks the necessary biological structures that are needed to qualify as a living organism. While the Earth supports a diverse range of life, it does not have a singular, unified system that acts as the brain or central nervous system of the planet. Additionally, the Earth is subject to physical and chemical laws that are not applicable to living organisms. These laws dictate the movement of tectonic plates, the circulation of the ocean currents, and the behavior of the Earth's atmosphere, among other things. These physical processes are not indicative of a living being, but rather reflect the natural processes of a dynamic planet. Therefore, while the Earth is certainly a magnificent and fascinating planet, it cannot be said to be alive in the same sense as a living organism.

Beth carried her items to the checkout aisle. The cashier quickly scanned everything. Beth tried to give him several coupons. However, he didn't accept it. They were yelling at each other about who turned in their receipt last and when they have a chance of going to the movies together again. "I'm sorry," said the cashier as he reached for his calculator from behind the counter. "Please take my manager card." He gave Beth's an envelope with 100 inside it after she left. The next day, I went back into that store and asked them both what happened. Their story was quite different than how they remembered it. Beth claimed that the man at the register refused all of her vouchers because she had too many items on her bill. She told me she thought that might be one of those errors (like not reading your receipt). When pressed, she admitted there probably could had been some sort of problem if she had paid by credit card rather than cash. In any case, she still insisted on receiving the change. What made this even more surprising is that she never mentioned anything about being rejected due to coupon use until now! Erin certainly remembers the encounter differently. She recalled the cashier over-filling her cart just like she did... and then making sure no items were missing when Beth got home. Erin also said that she felt horrible about hurting Beth's feelings. Despite apologizing profusely, she explained why she didn't want to give her change: we're saving up for Christmas presents! However, she also seemed surprised that the cashier would reject coupons or discounts. Both women understand how important using coupons can help consumers save money but are confused on what exactly should happen if these savings aren't accepted. Here's what you need to know. What Happens If You Don't Accept a Coupon? There is nothing wrong with refusing a coupon that doesn't apply or wasn't intended for a specific item. This happens more often than people think. There may be times where coupons don't stack properly which means it looks like someone double used them. Other times, companies will send out coupons referencing certain products but they actually don't work anymore. These situations shouldn't come as much surprise since most coupons don't have expiration dates attached to them. For example, some of our favorite grocery stores offer free shipping promotions that are considered "coupons" since they expire within 24 hours of getting the email. If nonworking coupons are an issue, there are two things you can do. First, contact customer service so they can put a stop to it immediately. Second, don't beat yourself up over it. We've all done plenty of weird things while trying to stock up on household supplies during the pandemic. It usually only takes a few minutes anyway. So, don't stress. And remember, it always pays to ask! Categories: Features

The Kingdom of Prussia became the leading state of the German Empire after its creation in 1871. However, the Treaty of Versailles following World War I granted West Prussia to Poland and made East Prussia an exclave of Weimar Germany (the new Polish Corridor separating East Prussia from the rest of Germany), while the Memel Territory was detached and was annexed by Lithuania in 1923. Following Nazi Germany's defeat in World War II in 1945, war-torn East Prussia was divided at Joseph Stalin's insistence between the Soviet Union (the Kaliningrad Oblast in the Russian SFSR and the constituent counties of the Klaipeda Region in the Lithuanian SSR) and the People's Republic of Poland (the Warmian-Masurian Voivodeship). The capital city Konigsberg was renamed Kaliningrad in 1946. The German population of the province was largely evacuated during the war or expelled shortly thereafter in the expulsion of Germans after World War II. An estimated 300,000 (around one fifth of the population) died either in war time bombings raids or in the battles to defend the province.[citation needed]

European Union law is applied by the courts of member states and the Court of Justice of the European Union. Where the laws of member states provide for lesser rights than those in force under national legislation, EU law must be taken into account when deciding on a case brought before an Irish court.[1516] The Constitution provides that "the State acknowledges its obligations to respect, protect and fulfil human rights" (Article 40).[17]:19 The State has also committed itself not only to complying with relevant international treaties[18], but further "to ensure through appropriate legislative or other measures that individuals are protected against any form of discrimination, abuse or violence.19] It can thus afford greater protection if it chooses - as evidenced by Ireland's ratification of many key United Nations instruments including: Convention Against Torture; International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights; Convention on Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women; Protocols I and II to the Refugee Convention; Conventions on Child Labour; Indigenous People; Migrant Workers etc., which apply equally at domestic level despite being less well known amongst general public here. In addition, certain provisions within our own constitution guarantee equality between all persons irrespective of age, gender, race, religion, sexual orientation etc. Ireland ratified the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities in December 2014,[20]. Implementation across various aspects such as health care provision would necessarily follow from this convention. For example, Article 3 requires that advance notice should always be given prior to withdrawing life-saving treatment. Under current practice there may be no time limit specified so there could still exist situations where advance notification was provided after a person had already suffered brain death resulting in their organs having been harvested without consent.[21]

A major difficulty of solving continuous POMDPs is to infer the multi-modal distribution of the unobserved true states and to make the planning algorithm dependent on the perceived uncertainty. We In continuous stochastic programming (CSP), a state-of-the-art technique for solving POMDPs with state-dependent payoffs is to infer the multi-modal distribution of the unobserved true states and to make the planning algorithm dependent on the perceived uncertainty. We consider the problem of solving CSPs with state-dependent payoffs for a class of continuous dynamic games with a continuous set of states and payoffs. To our knowledge, this is the first time that the problem of solving continuous POMDPs with state-dependent payoffs has been considered. We prove existence and uniqueness of a solution algorithm for CSPs with state-dependent payoffs. Numerical experiments show that our proposed algorithm converges to the solution of the problem with a polynomial time complexity.

There are three ways an existing treaty can be amended. First, formal amendment requires State parties to the treaty to go through the ratification process all over again. The re-negotiation of treaty provisions can be long and protracted, and often some parties to the original treaty will not become parties to the amended treaty. When determining the legal obligations of states, one party to the original treaty and one a party to the amended treaty, the states will only be bound by the terms they both agreed upon. Treaties can also be amended informally by the treaty executive council when the changes are only procedural, technical change in customary international law can also amend a treaty, where state behavior evinces a new interpretation of the legal obligations under the treaty. Minor corrections to a treaty may be adopted by a proces-verbal; but a proces-verbal is generally reserved for changes to rectify obvious errors in the text adopted, i.e. where the text adopted does not correctly reflect the intention of the parties adopting it.

The degree distribution serves as a crucial attribute of complex networks. In numerous data analysis scenarios, networks are typically modeled as fixed-length feature vectors, necessitating the extraction of features from the degree distribution. Furthermore, various applications require a similarity function to compare complex networks based on their degree distributions. This similarity metric finds application in tasks such as classifying and clustering network instances, assessing the efficacy of network sampling techniques, detecting anomalies, and examining epidemic spread dynamics. Existing approaches fail to adequately capture the similarity between degree distributions, especially when the underlying networks differ in size. Drawing upon insights into the temporal structure of degree distributions, we introduce a feature extraction mechanism and a similarity function tailored for complex networks. Our approach computes feature values by leveraging the mean and standard deviation of node degrees to mitigate the impact of network size on the extracted characteristics. The proposed method is tested on both synthetic and real-world network datasets, demonstrating superior performance compared to current state-of-the-art methodologies in terms of distance function accuracy and feature relevance.

The Chalukya Empire, known in Kannada as Tukja, was an Indian royal dynasty that governed significant portions of southern and central India from the 6th to the 12th century. During this era, the dynasty comprised three interconnected but distinct rulers. The earliest of these, the "Badami Chalukyas," controlled the city of Vatapi (now Badami) starting around the 6th century. These Chalukyas began asserting their independence after the fall of the Kadamba kingdom of Banavasi and gained prominence under Pulakeshin II. The Chalukya rule marked a pivotal moment in South Indian history and a golden age in the development of Karnataka. Their ascendance led to a shift from smaller kingdoms to larger empires in South India. The Badami Chalukyas established dominance over the region spanning the Kaveri and Narmada rivers, fostering efficient governance, foreign trade, and the emergence of "Chalukyan architecture." The Chalukya dynasty ruled parts of southern and central India from Badami in Karnataka from 550 to 750, and later from Kalyani from 970 to 1190.

The 11 imams, sheiks and religious teachers from nine countries met a Holocaust survivor and Poles whose families risked execution to save Jews from the Nazis, in the Polish capital's Nozyk Synagogue as part of the tour. They have been around museums, including the recently opened Museum of the History of Polish Jews on the site of the former Jewish Ghetto in Warsaw. And they also visited the Auschwitz and Dachau concentration camps. "The main aim is to get Muslims who are leaders all over the world, particularly in the Middle East, to acknowledge the reality of what happened here and to be able to teach it to the people that they lead," said trip organiser Rabbi Jack Bemporad, who is executive director of the US-based Center for Interreligious Understanding. He was standing underneath the red brick watchtower over the main entrance to Birkenau, the largest of more than 40 camps that made up the Auschwitz complex. This was where the Nazis installed four gas chambers and crematoria to speed up the murder and disposal of people, who were mostly Jews, from across Europe. Auschwitz-Birkenau, set up by the Germans in Nazi-occupied Poland, is largely intact and is now a museum. Historians estimate 1.1 million people were killed there - one million of them were Jews but there were also Poles, Roma, Soviet prisoners of war and others. "I think that when someone wants to deny the Holocaust or think that it is exaggerated, which many of them do and certainly many of their followers do, when they come here and see it, their experience is such that they can no longer think that," Rabbi Bemporad said. Beside the ruins of one of the gas chambers - the Germans blew them up as they retreated, in an effort to hide their crimes - the Muslim leaders paused for a moment's silence. "You may read every book about the Holocaust but it's nothing like when you see this place where people were burned," said Mohamed Magid, president of the Islamic Society of North America. "This is the building, the bricks. If they were to speak to you and I, they would tell you how many cries and screams they have heard." Mr Magid, who is originally from Sudan, first visited Auschwitz-Birkenau during a trip organised for American imams in 2010. He said the experience had led him to hold an annual Seder, a Jewish ceremonial meal, at his mosque in Virginia where he invites people to listen to the story of a Holocaust survivor who was saved by a Muslim family. "We go back more committed to human rights and more understanding of conflicts and how to resolve them, but also to be careful of a curriculum that teaches racism and hatred," he said. Earlier, the group had taken photos as they walked around an exhibition in the red brick barrack blocks at Auschwitz, about 2 miles (3kms) from Birkenau. They made comments such as "Can you imagine?" and "It's beyond comprehension" as they saw a great pile of hair shorn from women prisoners that was used to make rudimentary textiles. They shook their heads as they saw faded children's shoes and dolls in glass cases. After they had seen just two of the 14 exhibition blocks, some of the group asked for a break and they knelt in prayer beside the camp's execution wall. Barakat Hasan, a Palestinian imam and director of the Center for Studies and Islamic Media in Jerusalem, said he "didn't know many details about the Holocaust" before the trip. "I felt my heart bleeding when I was looking at all this. I was fighting back tears," he said through an interpreter. "As a Palestinian living under occupation, I feel sympathy for the pain and injustice that was inflicted on the Jews," he added. Mr Hasan said he did not believe there were people in the Muslim world who denied the Holocaust happened, but he said there was discussion in his community about whether the commonly quoted figure of six million Jewish victims was correct. "Maybe now after seeing what I've seen, maybe the numbers are correct also," he said, adding that he would write articles and mention his trip on Facebook. As he walked along the railway line and unloading ramp at Birkenau - where the trains hauling cattle cars crammed with Jews arrived - Ahmet Muharrem Atlig, a Turkish imam and secretary general of the Journalists and Writers Foundation in Istanbul, said he wept when he saw a photograph that showed children looking scared as they got off a train. "Unfortunately the Muslim communities and congregation don't know much about the Holocaust," he said. "Yes, we've heard something. But we have to come and see what happened here. It's not just about Jews, or Christians, this is all about human beings because the human race suffered here."

The essence of the information processing approach is to try to understand brain function in terms of information flow and implementation of algorithms. One of the most influential early contributions was a 1959 paper titled What the frog's eye tells the frog's brain: the paper examined the visual responses of neurons in the retina and optic tectum of frogs, and came to the conclusion that some neurons in the tectum of the frog are wired to combine elementary responses in a way that makes them function as "bug perceivers." A few years later David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel discovered cells in the primary visual cortex of monkeys that become active when sharp edges move across specific points in the field of view - a discovery for which they won a Nobel Prize. Follow-up studies in higher-order visual areas found cells that detect binocular disparity, color, movement, and aspects of shape, with areas located at increasing distances from the primary visual cortex showing increasingly complex responses. Other investigations of brain areas unrelated to vision have revealed cells with a wide variety of response correlates, some related to memory, some to abstract types of cognition such as space.

I had never encountered such a strange request before, but I took it upon myself to carry out the task. I could feel the electricity in the air, almost as if the letter itself was aware of its destination. I double-checked the address one last time before I knocked on the door. After a few moments, the door opened and a small child stood there, looking at me curiously. I felt a sudden wave of emotion as I realized that this child was the recipient of the letter I held in my hand. I handed the envelope over, explaining that it was from 1885 and I had been sent to deliver it to him. The child's eyes lit up as he eagerly opened the envelope and read the contents. He thanked me for delivering the letter and asked how I knew about it. I told him that it was a long story and one for another day. He smiled and asked if he could keep the envelope, which I gladly agreed to. He thanked me again, and I left feeling content that I had done my job. I had delivered a message from the past and changed the life of a child in the present.

I reside in Germany, where Walmart has faced significant challenges. The primary concern is Walmart's inability to grasp the nuances of cultural differences. Several factors contribute to Walmart's struggles in Germany, including overly ambitious expansion strategies that proceeded despite a German firm's successful resistance to a hostile takeover, even though Walmart was still relatively small in the country. Additionally, Walmart attempted to reduce costs by threatening employees with layoffs if they rejected practices deemed borderline unlawful in Germany. The company was compelled by a German court to publish its financial reports, revealing substantial financial difficulties that contradicted its claims. Walmart also irritated both employees and customers by enforcing policies common in the United States, such as hiring greeters or requiring staff to assist customers regardless of proximity, which Germans generally find unsettling, preferring to handle shopping independently and seek help only when needed.

The error lay in failing to recognize that legal frameworks, societal norms, and cultural expectations vary significantly across nations, and non-compliance can jeopardize a business's success. This does not imply Walmart's complete failure abroad; for instance, Walmart owns Asda, the second-largest supermarket in the UK, until recently. I suspect labor laws in other countries may not offer the same advantages. Many nations provide greater employee protection, offering more paid time off and sick leave, which could make them less cost-effective. The large-box store model, prevalent in the U.S., thrives on affordable land near towns and the prevalence of cars that allow individuals to travel short distances, often loading up with essentials like toilet paper. However, this model falters in countries lacking a comparable car culture.

The belief in "silent genes" is a outdated misconception, akin to thinking we only use 10% of our brain. Many genes aren't always active and don't produce proteins, yet they are transcribed and perform functions at some point (like non-coding RNAs, microRNAs, ribosomal RNA, etc.). The sole exception is transposable elements and viral DNA integrated into our genome, though these harmful genes can become active unpredictably. There isn't a mysterious 5000; if such genes were activated, they could alter how the body processes oxygen, potentially harming health. Other gene expressions might lead to cellular changes, possibly causing cell death. Our bodies are highly regulated systems, and activating silenced genes could disrupt chemical balance, leading to conditions like cancer or disease. This information comes from a biochemistry PhD candidate.

A major challenge in computational advertising lies in predicting click-through and conversion rates for bid allocation in online auction systems. A key issue in prior methods is the presence of highly variable misprediction costs. Although these costs have been incorporated into model evaluations using recent business-focused offline metrics—such as the Utility metric, which assesses its effect on advertiser profits—this approach does not apply during model training. To address this, this paper investigates the connection between optimizing the Utility metric and log loss, a widely used method in conversion modeling. The analysis suggests incorporating the business significance of predicted outcomes into the log loss calculation. We propose and evaluate a novel cost-weighting strategy, demonstrating substantial improvements in both offline and online performance.

At school, everyone used to refer to me as stupid. I wasn't really stupid; I just ran faster than others and appeared younger than I was. The bullies quickly discovered I was an easy target. They called me names, stole my belongings, and knocked my food from my hands. I would just walk away, broken, find an alleyway, and beat the hell out of a dumpster, or worse, punch a window. "I" was the troublemaker. Vandalism, poor performance, and being labeled "special" by my chemistry teacher made me a target. The worst was Scissors. He didn’t look much, but he had a sharp tongue. Anyone he targeted, he knew exactly how to insult them. His allies were tough, so he never faced consequences. If someone tried to attack him, they’d get hit with a heavy punishment. He especially liked to target the artistic students. He had no talent of his own, so he probably felt envious. Maybe they were just as easy to exploit as me. Every time he saw Paper, he'd say something to make her cry, but she always met his gaze defiantly. He pushed past her, knocking her books to the ground. I hated him. Paper was always kind to me. One sunny day, I was crossing the courtyard when I saw Paper making her way back to class. Though she might have struggled to carry her large portfolio, she looked calm, the sunlight casting fiery streaks across her deep red hair. My trance was shattered when Scissors arrived. He deliberately blocked her path, with his men behind him, and just stood there. I couldn't hear what he said, but I knew from Paper’s expression that she wasn’t impressed and didn’t want anything to do with it. Perhaps it was instinct, but I was much closer than I had been before.

The nonprofit sector is diverse, yet many individuals link non-profits primarily with charitable institutions. While charities frequently take center stage, there exist numerous other forms of nonprofits. Generally, these entities fall into two categories: those that serve their members and those that serve the broader community. Member-focused organizations encompass mutual societies, cooperatives, trade unions, credit unions, industry associations, sports clubs, retired military clubs, and peak organizations—entities that benefit specific groups, such as the organization’s members. Community-based nonprofits typically provide services to the public, whether nationally or locally, including human services initiatives, aid and development efforts, medical research, education, and healthcare. Some nonprofits straddle both categories, as illustrated by grassroots groups that offer essential support to individuals with specific conditions or diseases, benefiting both their members and the wider community through direct assistance.

When you make a credit card transaction you tell the merchant "Here's all of the information you need to take money from my account. Please help yourself to only as much as you're entitled for this transaction, then securely delete my information." This involves various forms of giving this information, but for the most part you're either punching in numbers online or you're swiping your card on a card reader. Debit cards often use a keyed in PIN, while credit cards sometimes ask for a zip code. So on a gas pump you're inputting credit card details when you insert the card and when you key in whatever data it asks you for. All it takes is a criminal putting a device next to the legitimate card reader such that it reads your card, too. These can be nearly undetectable, too. Consider [this] (URL0) side-by-side comparison of an ATM with and without a second device to read the card as it's inserted. Then they either install a device to read the number pad or they just put a camera somewhere to watch you key in your information. From there they just have to use the information to make a new card (this is disgustingly cheap) and they can go and use your card anywhere that they accept that same amount of information. I've even seen one scam where a person will stand at a gas pump and explain to you that they need cash but the ATM is broken, then ask to pump your gas in exchange for cash. They use a stolen card and you give them cash (aside: you're not the one getting ripped off here; the gas station will lose the money when the card is reported stolen). Some credit cards, especially in Europe, work differently and are much more secure. They use a "Chip and pin" system where there is a tiny computer chip embedded on the card. The rotating armature comprises one or more windings of wire encased in a laminated, magnetically soft ferromagnetic core. Current from the brushes passes through the commutator and one winding of the armature, creating an electromagnet. The resulting magnetic field from the armature interacts with a static magnetic field generated by permanent magnets (PMs) or another field coil within the motor's frame. This interaction generates a force that rotates the motor shaft. As the rotor spins, the commutator alternates the direction of current supplied to the coils, preventing the rotor's magnetic poles from fully aligning with the stator's magnetic poles. This ensures the rotor continues to rotate indefinitely as long as power is supplied, unlike a compass needle which eventually stops.

Metric learning plays a crucial role in various data mining and machine learning tasks, with a historical focus on Mahalanobis methods. Emerging research in nonlinear metric learning highlights the effectiveness of non-Mahalanobis distance functions, especially tree-based ones. We introduce a new nonlinear metric learning technique that employs an iterative, hierarchical version of semi-supervised max-margin clustering to build a collection of cluster hierarchies. Each hierarchy serves as a weak metric for the data. By integrating randomness into the hierarchy training process and aggregating outputs from multiple semi-random weak hierarchy metrics, we develop a strong and resilient nonlinear metric model. The proposed method contributes two main aspects: first, it is semi-supervised, leveraging information from both restricted and unrestricted data points. Second, it adopts a relaxed strategy for constraint fulfillment, enabling the algorithm to meet diverse subsets of constraints at varying hierarchical levels rather than enforcing all constraints simultaneously. This enhances the algorithm's robustness. We evaluate our method against several top-performing benchmarks across k-nearest-neighbor classification, large-scale image retrieval, and semi-supervised clustering tasks, demonstrating that our approach achieves performance competitive or better than existing methods and demonstrates greater resistance to noise.

Orientalist scholars of the 18th century like Sir William Jones marked a wave of enthusiasm for Indian culture and for Sanskrit. According to Thomas Trautmann, after this period of "Indomania," a certain hostility to Sanskrit and to Indian culture in general began to assert itself in early 19th century Britain, manifested by a neglect of Sanskrit in British academia. This was the beginning of a general push in favor of the idea that India should be culturally, religiously and linguistically assimilated to Britain as far as possible. Trautmann considers two separate and logically opposite sources for the growing hostility: one was "British Indophobia," which he calls essentially a developmentalist, progressivist, liberal, and non-racial-essentialist critique of Hindu civilisation as an aid for the improvement of India along European lines; the other was scientific racism, a theory of the English "common-sense view" that Indians constituted a "separate, inferior and unimprovable race."

In vivo D2 receptor occupancy assessments in rats with [3Hraclopride mirror those seen with [11Craclopride in human PET scans. A D2 occupancy of approximately 70-75 suppresses CAR, whereas higher levels (80) induce catalepsy. The findings align with human studies showing that 65-70 D2 occupancy is necessary for antipsychotic effects, while above 80 leads to extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS). The brain mechanisms behind catalepsy in rats and EPS in humans may share common pathways. Both suppression of CAR in rats and antipsychotic responses in humans could be attributed to a shared requirement for about 70 D2 receptor blockage.

Over the past few years, automatic video captioning has garnered significant interest. This study concentrates on generating Japanese captions to illustrate human activities. Most existing video caption datasets are developed for English, but there is currently no corresponding Japanese dataset. To tackle this issue, we created a comprehensive Japanese video caption dataset containing 79,822 videos and 399,233 captions. Each caption in our dataset provides a description in the format "who does what and where." For accurately representing human actions, it is crucial to discern specific details about individuals, locations, and actions. Typically, when describing human activities, the scene, person, and action are mentioned. In our experiments, we assessed two caption generation techniques to establish baseline performance. Additionally, we explored whether these methods can precisely capture "who does what and where." Keywords: video captioning, caption generation, Japanese caption dataset, human action understanding

The block sensitivity $ bs(f) $, certificate complexity $ C(f) $, and fractional certificate complexity $ C(f) $ are three key combinatorial properties of a Boolean function $ f $. It has been established that $ bs(f) \leq C(f) \leq C(f) \cdot O(bs(f)^2) $. We present an infinite collection of instances where $ C(f) $ increases quadratically with respect to $ C(f) $, achieving optimal distinctions among these metrics. Earlier, the most significant gap between these measures was $ C(f) / C(f) \log^{4.5} 5 $. Additionally, we introduce a family of examples where $ C(f) \geq (bs(f))^{3/2} $. These examples are constructed by combining boolean functions through diverse methods. In such compositions, $ f \circ g $ involves replacing each variable of $ f $ with a copy of $ g $ on distinct subsets of variables. To analyze these cases, we examine how these measures and the sensitivity measure $ s(f) $ behave under function composition. The measures $ s(f) $, $ C(f) $, and $ C(f) $ exhibit favorable behavior under composition; they are submultiplicative, with equality under certain general conditions. However, $ bs(f) $ is fundamentally different, as it is not submultiplicative. This distinction was overlooked in prior literature, and we rectify inaccuracies found in earlier works. We define the composition limit of a measure $ m $ at function $ f $, denoted $ \lim_{f}(m) $, as the limit of $ m(f \circ k) $ as $ k $ approaches infinity, where $ f \circ k $ denotes the $ k $-fold composition of $ f $. For any function $ f $, we demonstrate that $ bs(\lim_{f}) \leq C(\lim_{f}) $ and characterize $ s(\lim_{f}) $, $ C(\lim_{f}) $, and $ C(\lim_{f}) $ in terms of the largest eigenvalue of a specific set of $ 2 \times 2 $ matrices associated with $ f $.

Moisture absorption occurs when the material is exposed to high humidity or water. Both the resin and the reinforcement may absorb water; water may be also soaked by capillary forces through voids in the materials and along the reinforcement. Epoxies of the FR-4 materials aren't too susceptible, with absorption of only 0.15. Teflon has very low absorption of 0.01. Polyimides and cyanate esters, on the other side, suffer from high water absorption. Absorbed water can lead to significant degradation of key parameters; it impairs tracking resistance, breakdown voltage, and dielectric parameters. Relative dielectric constant of water is about 73, compared to about 4 for common circuitboard materials. Absorbed moisture can also vaporize on heating and cause cracking and delamination, the same effect responsible for "popcorning" damage on wet packaging of electronic parts. Careful baking of the substrates may be required.

Most cases take an extended period to reach trial. The Boston and Oklahoma City bombings were notably swift compared to the typical pace. Courts face significant backlogs, and even minor criminal cases—such as a traffic ticket trial—can span several months between the initial appearance and the actual hearing. Several factors contribute to this delay, including the high cost and limited availability of court time, the difficulty in seating a jury, and the expense involved. Both prosecutors and defense attorneys have their own caseloads and deadlines they cannot alter. Defendants may request a "speedy trial," but this often means relinquishing opportunities for early evidence gathering that could benefit them. 

A key legal principle states that a person cannot be tried twice for the same offense (double jeopardy), requiring thorough preparation to ensure all necessary evidence is collected initially. Many procedural steps involve determining which evidence is admissible, and the defense must be prepared to challenge the prosecution’s arguments or highlight missing evidence at any stage. The burden of proof lies with the state, meaning if they fail to establish guilt beyond a reasonable doubt, especially in the absence of mitigating circumstances or flaws in the trial process, the defendant may be acquitted.

If you were the Boston bomber, why would you rush to trial? Upon conclusion, you might receive a sentence of hundreds or thousands of years, or even death. Delaying the trial allows witnesses to leave the area, forget details, or lose evidence. The defense gains advantages by prolonging the trial, and in such cases, their sole objective is to secure the longest possible delay or the shortest incarceration.

An existing treaty can be modified in three ways. A formal amendment necessitates that all signatory states re-ratify the treaty. Re-negotiating its provisions may take time and involve disputes among original treaty participants, with some not becoming signatories to the revised treaty. When assessing legal duties, a state involved in the original treaty and one in the amended version will only be bound by the terms they both agree on. Treaties can also be adjusted informally through the treaty's executive body if the modifications are procedural or technical. Changes in customary international law may also alter a treaty, as states demonstrate a new understanding of the treaty’s obligations. Minor textual adjustments might be made via a procedural notice, though such notices typically address clear errors in the text, not broader interpretations.

I asked this question to a CS major friend of mine a while back. I hope I remember this correctly: Usually, when a program is unresponsive, it's stuck in some loop. But being stuck in that loop doesn't prevent all the OTHER operations from all the other programs from continuing. Your operating system (Windows, OSX, Linux, whatever) will keep track of what programs are actually updating and continuing to do stuff and all that good stuff, and if it notices that Spotify has just been looping through the same batch of code too long, it'll give you the "This program is unresponsive" error. On top of that, the reason you'll get the "Hey, this program is unresponsive" error when trying to shut it down, is because the program can't go through its normal shutdown procedures, since it's still stuck in that loop. Then you have to authorize your computer to just kill the program.','Well. Unresponsive programs can not be quickly closed because of how computers work. The thing is, a computer can't do many things at once, which is of course not entirely correct nowadays, but close enough. Early computers actually could only do one thing at a time; the operator would start a program and that would run until it finished, and then the operator would put another program (in the form of a deck of cards or a paper strip with holes in them) into the computer. That was kinda tedious, and so after a while clever people thought that it would be much more productiv to have another program that would take one program after the other and feed it to the computer. The computer was relatively unaware of this, the only difference was that every program had, after it ended, a bit of code attached to load the next program. And in many ways your computer is similar. The operating system basically chops all tasks into slices, and then it puts itself between those slices, and the computer switches between running user programs and os code. So in any given second your computer will run a bit of word, then a bit of the operating system, then a bit of Firefox, then a bit of the OS, and so on. So how can a program end? Basically there are two ways, it might just finish whatever it was doing and in its last time running it will tell the operating system that it is finished; this means signalling being finished in a way that the next time the OS gets executed, it will clean up after the program. The other was is that the operating system might end a program prematurely. To do this, the operating system uses a similar process a program uses, it says "you, program 234543, stop and exit," and the next time the program is run it should check for this and react to it. Again, this is only roughly correct, in truth there are interrupts and such, but anyway. But what if the program just ignores the operating system? Maybe it is stuck in a loop? Maybe it's very busy waiting for something to happen and can't be bothered to check for nice requests to close? So after a while the operating system will be fed up with waiting and issue a more drastic command, perhaps "you, exit now"! And if the program is still stuck, the operating system will finally just forcefully clean up: It will take away the programs execution time and empty the memory where the program resides. So that's why closing unresponsive programs takes some time, because either the operating system notices something is wrong, or you as the user notice this and try to close the program, and at first the OS will very politely ask, then demand, then threaten the program to close (or at least do something productive), and only then will the OS just kill the program. The so-called "theory of everything" is one example. Among the most beloved physicists of the 20th century were those who worked in theoretical physics: Hawking, Einstein, Sagan, and deGrasse Tyson. Theoretical physicists operate at the forefront of our understanding of the universe. Hawking's contributions mainly lie in astrophysics and general relativity, although he also delved into quantum physics and particle physics. His most significant achievement might be his book *A Brief History of Time*, which introduced theoretical physics to the general public for the first time since Einstein. In this book, he simplified complex concepts like the space-time continuum and the speed of light, making them accessible to non-specialists and high school-level science students. He also mathematically demonstrated the existence of black holes and dark matter for the first time. He proposed that black holes emit radiation, a concept once deemed impossible due to their intense gravity, and verified this both through mathematics and in everyday language. By demystifying theoretical physics, he advanced its understanding. When he passes away, he will not be remembered for a single groundbreaking discovery, but rather for the comprehensive body of his work. Throughout his life, he contributed as much to the advancement of physics as Einstein, Newton, Copernicus, and Aristotle.

Similarly, they contribute modest funds to think tanks discussing climate change, without aiming to sway public perception specifically about global warming.

Although several successful implementations of high-throughput computational materials design based on first principles have been achieved, several obstacles hinder their widespread adoption. Key challenges include the difficulty in achieving consistent accuracy and the lack of user-friendly access to these methods. We demonstrate a new approach by standardizing advanced first-principles simulation techniques—such as Density Functional Theory with Hybrid Screened Exchange (HSE) and GW approximation—and making them publicly available through an accessible and reproducible platform. We use this method to calculate electronic band gaps and band structures for a variety of 71 materials, including pure elements, III-V, II-VI compounds, ternary oxides, and alloys. Results show that for HSE and G 0 W 0, the average relative error is less than 20%, while conventional Generalized Gradient Approximation yields an error of over 55%. For HSE, the average computation time on a modern server running on a public cloud is under 48 hours. This study offers a cost-effective, accessible, and reproducible framework for conducting high-fidelity first-principles calculations of electronic materials in a high-throughput context.

The Museum's collections of South and South-East Asian art are the most comprehensive and important in the West comprising nearly 60,000 objects, including about 10,000 textiles and 6000 paintings, the majority of which are from India, Afghanistan, Pakistan, Nepal, Tibet, Cambodia and Indonesia. The collections date from the third century BC to the present, with the majority of objects dating from the 16th to 19th centuries. The collections of Indian art are the largest and most comprehensive outside India. The holdings include more than 2,000 paintings, a significant number of sculptures, and a large collection of objects in stone, metal, ivory, wood, textiles and clay. The collection of Indian paintings includes works from the 16th to the 19th century. The sculpture collection includes works from the 10th century to the present, and is particularly strong in objects made in the Deccan, South India and the Western Ghats. Indian Archaeology The South Asian archaeological collections are the largest outside India and include approximately 12,000 objects. The strength of the collections lies in sculpture, stone and metalwork, and ceramics. The collection of Indian textiles includes approximately 5,000 objects and is one of the most important outside India. The Museum's textiles collection is especially strong in early Mughal weaving, 16th-18th century European-influenced cotton weaving, and 19th-20th century weaving from Kashmir. The South-East Asian collection comprises more than 10,000 objects, many of which are the most important of their type outside South-East Asia. The strength of the collection lies in sculpture, painting, textiles and ceramics. Nepalese and Himalayan Art The collection of Nepalese and Himalayan art includes approximately 1,000 objects. The strength of the collection lies in sculpture and painting. Indonesian and Southeast Asian Art The collection of Indonesian and Southeast Asian art includes approximately 600 objects, many of which are the most important of their type outside Indonesia. The strength of the collection lies in sculpture, metalwork, textiles, ceramics and paintings. The museum has a small but important collection of Tibetan art and has sponsored research on the history and archaeology of Tibet. The collection includes paintings, sculpture, textiles and manuscripts, as well as objects from the palace of the Dalai Lama, including a throne, many items of jewellery and a number of ceremonial objects. Tibetan Manuscripts The British Library has one of the largest collections of Tibetan manuscripts outside Tibet. The collection contains a wide range of texts, including the major scriptural, philosophical and historical texts of the three main schools of Tibetan Buddhism, as well as important literature from all the other major traditions in Tibet. There are more than 40,000 Tibetan manuscripts in the British Library collection. They are written in a number of different scripts, the most common of which is the Tibetan script, although there are a number of variants of this script, including those used for writing Sanskrit and a number of languages from the Himalayas. There are also some manuscripts written in Mongolian, Chinese, Newari, Chinese and Ladakhi script. The majority of manuscripts are on paper, although there are also several scrolls, and some on palm leaf and bark. Some of the manuscripts are in manuscript books, while others are loose. " So Mike this is really more of a favor I would be doing for you, rather than you for me. " They drained their cup and motioned to the waitress for another without even looking, knowing that within minutes the cup would be refilled. " My price, since you seem to not care much for the fate of your unborn, will be suffering inflicted upon you, contingent on the suffering of Cathy at the loss of her child. Peer review is an important part of the scientific process. It helps ensure that papers are of high quality and that they adhere to the standards of the field. The peer review process involves several stages. First, a paper is submitted to a journal or conference for publication. The paper is then sent out to experts in the field who assess it for accuracy and relevance. These experts provide written critiques and suggestions for improvement. Based on these critiques, the editor either rejects the paper, requests revisions, or accepts it for publication. The peer reviewers are typically not compensated for their work, though some journals may offer small honorariums. However, there are other benefits to participating in the peer review process. Peer reviewers can stay up-to-date on the latest research in their field, they can gain name recognition within their field, and they can contribute to the advancement of science. In addition, reviewing someone else's work can help researchers hone their own skills and better understand the reviewing process when their own work is being reviewed.
