The software giant shared the details with tech news sites Digital Foundry and Eurogamer. The console has reportedly been designed from the start to make newer games playable at ultra-high 4K resolutions and at high frame rates. The console's graphics chip uses 40 high-speed processing cores to produce the high-definition images. Detailed specifications shared with the websites reveal that the hardware inside the console will have a central processor with eight cores that run at 2.3GHz. By contrast, the eight cores in Sony's PS4 Pro run at 2.1Ghz and those in the Xbox One at 1.75GHz. The 40 cores in the graphics unit also run at a higher speed than those in the 36 cores in the Sony console and the 12 in the Xbox One. Microsoft said it set itself a target of making the whole device capable of handling six teraflops per second - one it claims to have hit. Eurogamer estimates that the graphical processing unit inside the Scorpio box is 4.6 times more powerful than the chips in the Xbox One. Just as important, it said, was the amount of memory available to games. "That means fast streaming of very high-quality art assets, which will really help at the 4K ultra HD resolutions that Microsoft is gunning for," said Eurogamer editor Oli Welsh. However, he added that the magazine's reporters had seen only one demo, that used a very well-refined game engine. Piers Harding-Rolls, a games industry analyst at IHS Technology, said the powerful hardware would help Microsoft distinguish the new devices from the Xbox One S and give it credibility with gamers keen to get the latest hardware. Scorpio's ability to handle 4K resolutions should also help align its Xbox and Windows PC gaming strategies. He added: "Third-party publishers that are developing games for both PC and console are progressively developing 4K level content, so the overhead to develop for this new platform is not as onerous as seems at first glance." Seth Barton from game news site MCV said Microsoft still had some key decisions to take with the console. "Price is the real key here," he wrote, adding that the hardware shown suggested the cost would be higher than PS400. "For most it simply remains a very powerful console, without a clear marketing plan or a price," he said. "And so we're no closer to seeing how Microsoft is going to turn the silicon into a saleable product." Microsoft first mentioned Project Scorpio in June last year and the console is due to go on sale in time for Christmas this year. The firm is expected to give further information, including the console's name, at the E3 games show in June.

Only if a and q are coprime can there be infinitely many primes, which means their greatest common divisor is one. When this condition holds, Dirichlet's theorem on arithmetic progressions guarantees that the sequence contains infinitely many primes. The diagram below shows this with q = 9: numbers wrap around as soon as a multiple of 9 is reached. Primes are shown in red. Rows starting with a = 3, 6, or 9 contain at most one prime. In all other rows (where a = 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, or 8), there are infinitely many primes. Furthermore, in the long run, the distribution of primes is equal across these rows; the density of primes congruent to a modulo 9 is 16.

Today promises to be a positive day. It's a flight from LaGuardia to LAX, much like any other journey. The weather is favorable, and it's my final flight before starting my vacation. My name is Captain Dustin Phillips, and I've been with United Airlines for 20 years. I fly to and from every airport, and I operate every aircraft. I can handle any bird I encounter and direct it as needed. In terms of personal challenges, I need to take my medication. I suffer from bipolar disorder and schizophrenia, which are my deepest secrets. I would not have a set of wings if anyone discovered my condition. I pay a high price for a doctor to manage my illness and ensure he keeps his mouth shut; my wife is a pharmacist, so my medical needs are well taken care of. I go to the bathroom, and then it strikes me—my medication is missing. I search every pocket... nothing. The thoughts racing through my mind are terrifying. Imagine committing a crime and waiting for the police to arrest you, the guilt overwhelming you as you realize how brief your actions truly were. I'm beginning to understand the brevity of my mistake and how irresponsible I was. I'm terrified of the thoughts that flood my mind when left alone. I'm more than Captain Dustin Phillips—I'm God. I'm a being beyond reproach, judgmental, and omniscient. I know everything, and I can justify almost any action because I convince myself it's the right thing. I have to stop thinking about it. It'll only take around 36 hours until I get back, leaving me with 60 hours without it. I'll be fine. I have to be. I put on my uniform, grab lunch and a cup of coffee. I go through my routines; routine is the foundation of sanity, right? I smile and hide my worries. It's impossible not to feel worried. I know what awaits me. "Hey man, how are you feeling?" I turn to see my co-pilot, Allen. "I'm good. Really good." I give a smirk and we board the plane. I know the moment I lost my sense of sanity. I look at the overweight baggage.

Police were targeted with fireworks, while motorists described "petrol bombs" being thrown at cars on Commercial Road, Pill, on 20 October. Three teenagers - aged 16 to 17 - were sentenced to five months' custody at Cwmbran Youth Court on Tuesday. Two 13-year-olds were handed non-custodial 12-month referral orders. All five of the teenagers - who cannot be named - had earlier admitted violent disorder, with one of the 16-year-olds also admitting a separate charge of breaching a dispersal order. District Judge David Parsons said no other sentences could be justified because of the "uninhibited, unlawful behaviour." Prosecutor Paul Hewitt told the court police received calls at 19:45 BST to say youths had set off fireworks. Officers arrived at the scene but a lit firework was thrown at them and, when about 20 youths began throwing stones and eggs, they retreated. "At about 20:35, police were called to another riot on Commercial Road, where there were fires being set in bins and fireworks thrown at buildings," Mr Hewitt said. "There was a large group in the street, throwing items at vehicles. The windscreen of a police van was smashed by a brick, causing significant damage." Mr Hewitt described wheelie bins being set alight and put into the road, "petrol bombs" being thrown at vehicles with "terrified" motorists making three-point turns to escape. He added: "Local people were terrified. Police feared their vehicles would be pelted with fireworks and the entire area was under siege. "A dispersal order was issued and a police helicopter was used to tell the crowd on loudspeaker." Locals and motorists described "missiles and bombs" being thrown at cars and thousands of pounds worth of damage caused. A video taken on a mobile phone was shown, with a youth heard shouting "there are Molotov cocktails out here, throw it" as cars were set alight. Judge Parsons handed each of the three older defendants - two were aged 16 and one 17 - a 10-month detention and training order, half of which will be served in custody with the rest under supervision in the community. He said the court had an "overwhelming obligation" to "protect the public in their homes or businesses or in the street." "Those that partake in disturbances of this magnitude, causing harm and fear to even the most steel-hearted of residents, must be punished accordingly," he added.

The Recommended Exposure Index (REI) technique, new in the 2006 version of the standard, allows the manufacturer to specify a camera model's EI choices arbitrarily. The choices are based solely on the manufacturer's opinion of what EI values produce well-exposed sRGB images at the various sensor sensitivity settings. This is the only technique available under the standard for output formats that are not in the sRGB color space. This is also the only technique available under the standard when multi-zone metering (also called pattern metering) is used.

Katiya remembered when the men of her tribe used to don their heavy furs and thick soled boots, seeking food for the mouths of the hungry. It seemed so long ago when they would come back, sleds laden with thick cuts of meat, luxurious furs and bright silks and sweets that would melt away in her mouth quicker than a snowflake. There was laughter and celebrations all the time, thanks to the hunters and the tradesmen. Katiya remembers. But the world became meaner, striping away the love it used to dole out. First, the men would come come back will less and less. The meat that used to taste so delicious became nothing more than fat and gristle. Furs and silks were few and far between and Katiya only had the memory of sweets. "Why is there no laughter, Papa?" she had asked, noticing his face was lined with worry. "Why are things changing?" Her father had placed a tired smile on his lips. "It will be okay soon, myshka," he assured her, patting her head and she had believed him. But it was never okay again. Finally then hunters and tradesmen would come back empty handed. The air around them would fill with the cries of the hungry. And with the hunger sometimes came sickness. Katiya saw too many of her tribe members fade away into nothing. She feared she would be the only one left. Every day, she would wake up with her father and watch him disappear into the darkness with the other tribesmen, desperate. And every evening, she would see the disappointment and despair etched onto their faces. Eventually, the world began to turn on them. Instead of being the hunters, they became the hunted. Beasts stalked them with new found confidence, waiting for the perfect time to pick them off finally high enough on the evolutionary ladder to take revenge. The first day they had come back one man short, the stares of the tribesmen were hollow and their clothes were painted in blood of their friend. After that, there would always be one or two less men with them when the returned. Instead of silently watch her father go into the unknown, Katiya began to cry and beg him not to leave. "Hush, myshka," he would say, wiping away her tears. "Papa will always return to you." And then, one day, he didn't. No one did. And then she was alone.

A filibuster is an obstructionist tactic used in the Senate where a senator in the minority abuses his right to unlimited debate, speaking for a length of time with the intention of stalling for time rather than making any persuasive gains. Some background: After the removal of a formal way to force a vote in the Senate, it became possible to filibuster a bill. The Senate rules allow any senator to speak for as long as he wants on any topic that he chooses. The original rule to "move the previous question" and so force a vote was removed because it was seen as unnecessary; it wasn't used in years. Over a century later, after filibusters started happening, a formal way to end debate, called "cloture," was introduced in Senate Rule 22. Instead of ending debate, however, cloture limits it to 30 hours, with each senator getting no more than one hour to speak. This means that even if cloture is successful, it could take another two days for the issue to move to a vote. Getting cloture isn't easy, either. Normal bills in the Senate require a simple majority (51 senators out of 100) to be passed. Cloture, on the other hand, needs 60 senators to agree on. This means that if 41 people don't want to move on to voting (for fear of losing), the issue will stay on the table indefinitely. The good: Since the Senate requires a simple majority, a group of 49 will lose the vote. 49 senators is significant. In a situation like that, a filibuster will allow more time for the minority to voice their concerns and maybe persuade one other senator to change his mind. This way, the filibuster serves as a balance to prevent 51 senators from steamrolling the opposition. Note that since cloture requires 60 votes, if it's not a very controversial issue, a filibuster won't be as effective. The bad: In the last 40 years, the amount of filibusters in the Senate has [skyrocketed] . Filibusters are being invoked as an easy way to raise the amount of votes required for a bill. Instead of the regular 51, a filibustered bill would need 60 votes to actually move forward. An example of this would be Senator Mitch McConnell filibustering [his own proposition] . He basically proposed an expensive reform to end the debt-ceiling gridlock thinking the Democratic majority would reject it. When they didn't, he filibustered it to raise the votes required. It's obvious that the filibuster is doing little else other than stalling the legislative process. The usefulness inherent in giving the minority an "extra chance" at debate has long been outlived due to repeated abuse. So why is stalling bad? The majority of bills the average American never hears or learns about, even if they manage to get passed. But what about something like the Civil Rights Act of 1957? This act was meant to overturn practices in voting that made it impossible for African Americans. The Act was filibustered by Senator Strom Thurmond for a total of 24 hours and 18 minutes. Imagine if the bill was filibustered even longer: what effect would it have if it was filibustered during voting time? The difference of having an entire group of people voting could mean the difference of whether a senator was voted in or not. If we still need a way to help out a significant minority in the Senate, there should be some reform to the filibuster or other avenues available. A common suggestion is to reduce the amount of votes needed for cloture to a simple majority. This would remove filibusters as a tactic to force more votes. Another possibility is to make it harder to start a filibuster. Right now, any one person can start speaking whenever they want. Instead, they should require a petition for filibuster which needs to be signed by a number of Senators. The petition would need to have the reasons for starting a filibuster clearly stated, and signed by 40 or so senators. This would make it so that there would need to be a good reason to stall the proceedings and that those reasons would be addressed in debate. (Credit for this idea goes to [Gerhardt and Painter] .) Alternatively, the rules of unlimited debate could just be taken out altogether. Australian Parliament works similarly to US Congress, but they have strictly enforced rules on use of time, so this type of filibuster is impossible. Any of these changes would be an improvement because, as it is now, filibusters are doing much more harm than good. CMV.

We demonstrate how to expand conventional intrinsic image decompositions to include additional layers beyond albedo and shading. Acquiring data for training a multi-layer decomposition is challenging, so instead, we train models to decompose an image into layers that resemble specific examples by creating generative models for each layer using proxy data that represent the Platonic ideal (such as Mondrian-style images for albedo, rendered 3D primitives for shading, and material swatches for shading details). This method produces image layers, one from each model, that collectively explain the original image. Our strategy relies on advancements in image-based generative models. We present a Convolutional Variational Autoencoder (conv-VAE), a new VAE architecture capable of accurately reconstructing high-quality images. The approach is versatile and does not necessitate that the layers have a physical interpretation.

Timely identification and precise division of brain tumors are crucial for effective therapy. However, manual segmentation is laborious, expensive, and frequently yields inaccurate results due to limited human expertise. In this study, we introduce an MRI-driven tumor segmentation system employing an autoencoder-regulated 3D-convolutional neural network. The model was trained on manually annotated T1, T1ce, T2, and Flair MRI scans from 335 patients with varying tumor characteristics. It was subsequently validated on an independent dataset of 125 patients, successfully dividing brain tumors into three regions: the tumor core (TC), the enhancing tumor (ET), and the entire tumor (WT). Additionally, we investigated various data augmentation and preprocessing techniques to enhance segmentation accuracy. Our approach runs efficiently on a single NVIDIA GTX1060 GPU, making it cost-effective and accessible for widespread use. Overall, we propose a memory-efficient and budget-friendly method for tumor segmentation, supporting reliable diagnosis of neurological diseases.

The officer said he found the black animal toy wearing an officer's shirt at a police station in central London. Scotland Yard promised to look into the matter but the detective was himself investigated for making the story up. He was later cleared at a misconduct hearing and received damages from the force after taking legal action. The details emerged after a separate case at Thames Valley Police in which an officer put a monkey on a black colleague's desk. A misconduct panel concluded last month that Det Sgt Andrew Mottau was not being racist but should have realised the toy animal could be offensive. The incident involving the Metropolitan Police began in September 2013 when the Indian-born detective constable claimed to have seen a large monkey toy in the office of the Case Progression Unit at Belgravia police station. He said the stuffed black toy had a police officer's shirt on and a label saying "night-duty ERO" - Evidential Review Officer. One of the EROs at the time was a black police officer. The detective was concerned the use of the toy was racist and had not been investigated properly. He raised the matter during a live internal website chat known as the "Commissioner's Forum," where staff are encouraged to discuss problems with the Met Commissioner, who at the time was Sir Bernard Hogan-Howe. The detective received an online reply saying: "What is described - if accurate - is unacceptable" and was told that it would be looked into "immediately." But a month later, the detective himself was put under investigation for allegedly posting "untrue and potentially inflammatory comments." He was told his actions had "breached the standards of professional behaviour.... relating to "honesty and integrity" and "discreditable conduct," claims which, if proved, could have led to his dismissal Eventually, in June 2015, after protracted internal disciplinary proceedings, the officer attended a gross misconduct hearing where it was ruled there was "no case to answer" and he was cleared. Paul Turpin, who was a representative for the Metropolitan Police Federation and supported the officer through the process, said: "I was surprised when the matter was referred to a gross misconduct hearing and was not surprised when that hearing found the officer had no case to answer." He suggested the allegation should never have got that far: "Matters should be dealt with at the lowest appropriate level at the earliest possible opportunity." Scotland Yard said there had been an "internal review" of the handling of the case after the hearing. It said the original allegation about the monkey had been "investigated locally and progressed as far as it could be," though the inquiry was unable to establish who had placed the black toy animal in the police station. The Asian detective, who has not been named by the BBC at his own request, began legal proceedings against the Met at an employment tribunal alleging he had been racially discriminated against and victimised. But before a full hearing took place the force reached a settlement and agreed to pay damages. The details of the agreement are confidential but the amount of compensation is thought to be in the region of PS35,000. The officer declined to comment and has not divulged any details of the agreement to the BBC. The Met confirmed a settlement had been reached "following judicial mediation" at the Tribunal Services in March 2016. Deputy Assistant Commissioner Richard Martin, who is in charge of professionalism at Scotland Yard, said the force had made "significant investment" in improving the way it handled staff complaints linked to discrimination, bullying or harassment and had introduced a new "whistle-blowing" policy. "We have long recognised that people.... fear being victimised if they raise a complaint, regardless of whether that fear is justified," he said. "That has never been acceptable and we continue to make it very clear to our staff that victimisation will never be tolerated, that it will be investigated, and will have serious repercussions if it occurs." But Janet Hills, chairwoman of the Metropolitan Black Police Association, said the use of a black monkey toy and the treatment of the Asian police detective indicated there was still a long way to go. "We're still trying to get rid of the dinosaurs in policing who are still protecting that culture," she said, describing the "monkey" incident as "unbelievable" and "unacceptable." "It's not just a toy, it's a toy to be used to say'this is what I think of you'," she said. Over the weekend, the Ikea at Harajuku in Tokyo hosted an installation starring Imma, a virtual influencer. People who passed by the first floor of the store were able to interact with her and take pictures using their phone screens; she even made herself jump around on cue as people took selfies next to her while wearing 3D glasses. It was all part of what the company called "The Unseen 2021," which explored new forms of interaction between humans and technology through augmented reality (AR) - something that is set to become increasingly important for some brands during this current global crisis. "We are living in such challenging times right now due to COVID-19, which makes it more critical than ever before for us to find solutions to help bring our guests closer together again after social distancing measures have been relaxed," said Ewelina Ochab, head of digital innovation design at IKEA Japan, adding: "This project aims to do just that." The event ran until Sunday but continues online so anyone can still visit. Ikea's activation came off the back its 2020 report into consumer trends, Future Ready Living 2030, which looked ahead to how life might look differently after we emerge from lockdown across Asia Pacific and Europe later this year. Among other things, the study found 46 percent of consumers agreed they don't want to return to pre-pandemic habits when restrictions lift because there will always be added value provided by AR products or services compared to previous experiences. Meanwhile, 36 percent believe going out won't feel quite normal without these kinds of technologies already available. This tallies roughly with research conducted among Asian consumers last month by Unit4 CEO Subodh Mhaisalkar, whose survey uncovered similar attitudes towards VRAR tech within his own market including China where 66 percent predicted live shows would eventually resume once public health concerns ease, alongside 67 percent expecting theatres to reopen partially sooner rather than later.

In Scandinavia, we predominantly use the same language, share a comparable cultural identity, and possess a similar historical background. Traveling through Norway, Sweden, and Denmark is virtually seamless. Our governance structures are largely alike, and we make similar political decisions both domestically and internationally. Historically, Scandinavia was a single nation, and today, we are essentially one country. The primary reasons why Scandinavia remains fragmented into distinct nations are two: 

1) Norway possesses an oil reserve that no other Scandinavian nation possesses, leading some Norwegians to believe they should remain separate. 
2) Denmark and Sweden are members of the European Union, whereas Norway is not, which may instill fear among Norwegian citizens that they might be coerced into joining the EU. 

On the positive side, Scandinavia has the potential to gain greater influence in global affairs and economic matters (such as the UN and NATO). Increased trade between the nations could lead to mutual prosperity. My proposed model is that Denmark, Norway, and Sweden should function as regions within a unified country, akin to the states in the United States. The location of the central authority is not important to me. Minor linguistic differences can be addressed over time if needed. I am Danish (and also Scandinavian; however, I welcome your perspective on this matter). An additional point to consider is that there could be administrative challenges. If the populace does not support me, there will need to be enhanced cooperation among the states. In fact, there already exists a functional council comprising all three nations known as the Nordic Council.

Eleven imams, sheikhs, and religious educators from nine nations gathered at the Nozyk Synagogue in Warsaw to visit a Holocaust survivor and Poles whose families faced execution to save Jews during the Nazis' reign. The group explored museums, including the newly opened Museum of the History of Polish Jews located at the site of the former Jewish Ghetto in Warsaw. They also toured the Auschwitz and Dachau concentration camps. Organized by Rabbi Jack Bemporad, leader of the U.S.-based Center for Interreligious Understanding, the trip aimed to persuade global Muslim leaders, especially in the Middle East, to recognize the truth of the Holocaust and educate those they oversee. Bemporad stood beneath the red-brick watchtower at Birkenau, the largest camp within the Auschwitz complex, where the Nazis erected four gas chambers and crematoria to accelerate the killing and burial of individuals, predominantly Jews, from across Europe. Auschwitz-Birkenau, established by the Nazis in occupied Poland, remains largely preserved and functions as a museum today. Historians estimate that approximately 1.1 million people were murdered there, with one million being Jews, though other groups such as Poles, Roma, Soviet prisoners of war, and others also perished. "I believe that when someone disputes the Holocaust or believes it is overstated—many of whom do and indeed follow such views—when they arrive here and witness the remnants of this place, their perspective changes completely," Bemporad stated. Near the ruins of one of the gas chambers, where the Nazis detonated them as they withdrew, the Muslim leaders paused for a moment of remembrance. "Reading books about the Holocaust is insufficient; seeing this site where people were burned is something entirely different," said Mohamed Magid, president of the Islamic Society of North America. "This is the building where people were destroyed."

Police fired tear gas to disperse protesters angered at their handling of Sunday's event, witnesses told the BBC. A doctor at a local hospital which received many of the dead told AFP news agency that he had seen no evidence of bullet wounds on the bodies. At the funeral of one of the victims in the town of Dankaka earlier, Tadese Biru, speaking to Reuters news agency, described his anger at his son's death. "The government is playing God's role.... Could this have happened if there were a so-called democratic system in place? "I saw bodies of people being loaded into trucks to be transported to the regions, just like aid wheat and maize. These are humans!" The town of Bishoftu, where the stampede took place, saw further unrest on Monday morning, according to an Ethiopian government official, quoted by the Associated Press news agency. Crowds took to the streets in Ambo, Guder, Bule Hora and other towns in the Oromia region in response to the deaths, witnesses told Reuters. In Ambo, 120km (75 miles) west of the capital, Addis Ababa, a local student said that everything was closed and gunshots could be heard, Reuters adds. Online, some Ethiopians have replaced their Facebook profile pictures with a black square, in solidarity with the victims. In a national address on state TV, Prime Minister Hailemariam Desalegn praised the security forces' "great efforts" to protect the public and blamed "evil forces" for the deaths on Sunday, vowing to bring to justice those responsible. Thousands had gathered for the religious festival in Bishoftu, 40km (25 miles) from Addis Ababa. The annual Irecha celebration is an important festival at which the Oromo people welcome spring. But the crowds were chanting, "We need freedom" and "We need justice," witnesses said. Police say they fired tear gas after anti-government protesters threw stones and bottles, but others said demonstrators were entirely peaceful. He said troops and a helicopter gunship had opened fire, driving people off a cliff and into a lake. The government-affiliated Fana Broadcasting Corporate (FBC) reported that people died falling from the cliff around the lake but it made no mention of a helicopter opening fire. There has been a series of deadly clashes in Ethiopia in recent months. People in Oromia and Amhara, two of Ethiopia's most populous regions, have complained about political and economic marginalisation. The US has expressed concern about what it termed the excessive use of force against protesters. The unrest was sparked last November by a plan to expand the capital into Oromia. This led to fears that farmers from the Oromo ethnic group, the largest in Ethiopia, would be displaced. The plan was later dropped but protests continued, highlighting issues such as marginalisation and human rights.

Water absorption happens when a material is exposed to high humidity or direct contact with water. Both the resin and reinforcement can absorb water, and water may penetrate through voids in the material and along the reinforcement via capillary action. Epoxy resins used in FR-4 materials have relatively low water absorption, typically around 0.15. Teflon exhibits extremely low water absorption, approximately 0.01. In contrast, polyimides and cyanate esters experience significant water absorption. Absorbed water can result in substantial deterioration of critical properties, including tracking resistance, breakdown voltage, and dielectric characteristics. The relative dielectric constant of water is about 73, compared to approximately 4 for typical circuit board materials. Additionally, absorbed moisture may evaporate upon heating, leading to cracking and delamination, similar to the "popcorning" damage observed in wet-packaged electronic components. Proper baking of the substrate may be necessary to mitigate these effects.

If you have absolutely no signal, you cannot make an emergency call. However, if your phone can connect to another provider’s tower (roaming), it can initiate an emergency call, and your phone might still display a usable signal. This typically works even when roaming is disabled on the phone.

When you make a commercially supported call, you’re tied to your provider’s infrastructure—such as Verizon’s equipment or those Verizon collaborates with. These are where the “bars” come from. When making an emergency call, you search for all available infrastructure that uses the same foundational technology as your phone (e.g., CDMA or GSM). This offers a few additional options. 

None of this guarantees you’ll be able to make a call. If you’re in a place with no cellular service and no phone can make a commercial call regardless of provider, you won’t succeed in an emergency call either.

Emergency frequencies are open across all networks and many countries require cellular providers to allow their use outside of normal operations. Phones are programmed to lock onto the nearest broadcasting tower and make the call. 

Signal strength depends on your carrier. Emergency calls prioritize the phrase “fuck the extra cost, this is an emergency,” using the best available tower. While you may be without service for your carrier, another provider may have service, and the emergency call will use that to transmit the message.

Touch screen phones use a technology called capacitive touch screens. The screen detects the electrical charge from our fingers. When our fingers are wet, the water on the surface of the skin can interfere with this electrical charge and affect the screen's ability to detect our fingers. Additionally, the water can create a conductive path across the screen, making it difficult for the touch screen to distinguish between different touches. This is why touch screen phones may not work well when our hands are wet. To avoid this issue, you can dry your hands first or use a stylus designed for capacitive touch screens.

We investigate the following problem: Given two embeddings G 1 and G 2 of the same abstract graph G on an orientable surface S, decide whether G 1 and G 2 are isomorphic. In contrast, there is no known algorithm with complexity better than O (n 4) for general embeddings.

Following a five-year review process, the modest Yakka Skink, a reclusive lizard known for hiding beneath rocks and within hollow logs, and the Ornamental Snake, which is considered one of Australia's most endangered species, halted a $12 billion (A$12 billion; $8 billion) mining, railway, and port initiative planned for the Galilee Basin in Queensland. These two creatures are among Australia's most vulnerable wildlife. The federal environment minister's prior approval of the mine was revoked by the Australian Federal Court due to failing to consider its potential impact on their habitats. While the mine might still proceed, this delay marks the latest episode in a prolonged history of Australian flora and fauna disrupting developer projects. 

In 1995, the last remaining population of the endangered Green and Gold Bell frog slowed down the construction of a large-scale residential development in Sydney's city center. Later, the frogs were observed playing in an abandoned brick pit, where authorities intended to construct a tennis court for the Sydney 2000 Olympics. The courts were built elsewhere, while the frogs received a special habitat. Now, they obstruct a significant major road project in Sydney. 

In the early 2000s, a novel species of flowering shrub was identified in the Lower Hunter Valley, near Sydney. Known as Persoonia pauciflora, botanists were thrilled to discover it thrives nowhere else on Earth. However, it was growing on the site of a proposed housing development. News spread quickly, leading to the removal of 300 of the final 500 of these rare plants. The responsible party was never identified. The discovery of a threatened or newly identified species can significantly disrupt developments, causing delays or even halting projects. 

What caused the reversal of the Queensland mine's approval? A small conservation group in Mackay, Queensland, contested the environment minister's decision to approve the mine, citing several legal grounds, including the presence of approved conservation advisories.

Emergency numbers differ significantly among nations. In the United Kingdom, the primary emergency number is '999'. In Australia, it is '000'. Many countries use distinct numbers for police, fire rescue, and ambulance services. Some nations have emergency numbers with just one or two digits. '112' is the most widely recognized international standard, though it is not universally adopted. Despite this, if you dial '112' on a GSM-enabled mobile phone, it will connect you to emergency services.

Flooding is a destructive and dangerous hazard and climate change appears to be increasing the frequency of catastrophic flooding events around the world. Physics-based flood models are costly to calibrate and are rarely generalizable across different river basins, as model outputs are sensitive to site-specific parameters and human-regulated infrastructure. In contrast, statistical models implicitly account for such factors through the data on which they are trained. Such models trained primarily from remotely-sensed Earth observation data could reduce the need for extensive in-situ measurements. In this work, we develop generalizable, multi-basin models of river flooding susceptibility using geographically-distributed data from the USGS stream gauge network. Machine learning models are trained in a supervised framework to predict two measures of flood susceptibility from a mix of river basin attributes, impervious surface cover information derived from satellite imagery, and historical records of rainfall and stream height. We report prediction performance of multiple models using precision-recall curves, and compare with performance of naive baselines. This work on multi-basin flood prediction represents a step in the direction of making flood prediction accessible to all at-risk communities.

If Black promotes to a queen, he has no legal moves, and the game ends in a stalemate (a draw). Typically, it's best to promote your pawn to a queen, though there are exceptions, such as the scenario depicted in the image. The reason for this exception is that a queen is harder to control due to its ability to attack more squares than a rook. Chess rules state that if a player has no legal moves and is not in check, the game is a draw. However, if a player has no legal moves and is in check, that results in an immediate loss. In the board configuration shown in the image, if White promotes his pawn to a queen, Black will have no legal moves and will not be in check, leading to a draw. If White promotes to a rook, the game is won, although this outcome isn't solely due to that move. There is a known endgame checkmate between a king and rook versus a king and queen. Therefore, even though promoting to a queen is usually the optimal choice, there are specific situations where another minor piece might be more advantageous.

Her dreams began, like many dreams began in those days, with hearing a song. Allison McLaughlin was on her way with her parents to the Tennessee Valley Fair when she heard "The Fight Song" by The Allman Brothers Band for the first time at the fairgrounds near Tuscaloosa, Alabama. That same year, Ms. McLaughlin made it to Woodstock and watched Bob Dylan perform there while listening to music as popular on FM radio stations as AAA Folk Club (now WXPN) or X100-FM in New York City. Her dream took another step forward that summer of 1969 - she got married. She met her husband, Mark, who would become one half of the pop duo The Crazy World of Arthur Brown after they broke up from Arthur Brown His Rhythm Kings. Her daughter Alyssa followed them into music later that decade. It is this musical genealogy that inspired Ms. McLaughlin's new album, "Old Soul." "I started writing to be able to tell my story," the singer said during an interview Wednesday offered via email. "My songs are built around themes: love lost, desire gone wrong, pain you feel inside but can't explain ... all these things which have happened to me over the years were what I wanted to say through music. That is why so much of my work has been about relationships... some good; others bad." Ms. McLaughin felt compelled to write several songs based upon stories told only to her family members because their loss resonated deeply within her, including stories involving her father and his own mother, both of whom had died before age 50. She wrote two more songs honoring other loved ones whose deaths affected Ms. McLaughlin personally: "Nobody Knows You When You're Down And Out," written specifically for her son, and "Hurt So Good," dedicated to her aunt Annabelle who passed away last December shortly after celebrating her 30th birthday. "These people impacted our lives greatly and changed us forever," says Ms. McLaughlin. "They taught us lessons we still live every day. These are the songs I want everyone else to hear because if anyone needs something to make them smile then maybe I'm the right person singing it!" A native of Jonesboro, Arkansas, Ms. McLaughlin grew up surrounded by musicians. Her dad Joe played guitar, bass and piano and sang in local bands until he moved to Indianapolis at age 15 where he ran a barber shop. In 1968, he joined the rhythm section of blues band Hampton Hawes, named for guitarist Hampton Hawes, who recently passed away. After six months together, Mr.Hawes' sister introduced him to Ms. McLaughlin, who learned to play guitar and soon became part of the group. They added John Lambert on drums and Chris Lewis on saxophone to complete the lineups, and the band released its self-titled debut LP in 1970. In 1971, the band recorded three albums under Atlantic Records, beginning with the hit "Sketchy," produced by David Foster. Two years later, they signed with Epic Records, releasing four top 10 singles between 1973 and 1975, including " (You Gotta Get a Hold On Me) " and "Life Is Like a Movie." But Epic went out of business two years later without having issued any new material and the label folded, leaving the surviving members struggling financially and unlikely ever to reunite again. After quitting the music industry altogether, Mr.Hawes reconnected with his former bandmates and toured Europe in 1988. The group continued playing gigs until 2005, recording small amounts of original music here and there throughout the process. One such moment occurred in 2001, when Ms. McLaughlinsaid she could not shake off the feeling that drummer John Lambert should rejoin the band despite never getting back together officially. So she picked up the phone and called him, finally convincing him to return home to Nashville. While always reluctant to sing in public outside of the studio setting behind closed doors, Lambert agreed to do just that on condition that Ms. McLaughlin record the song live instead of performing it on tape. Over the next few weeks, she worked diligently to perfect the track in a room without amplification or sound reinforcement. With no DJ spinning background tracks or kitchen noises coming from anywhere nearby, Ms. McLaughlin truly unleashed her vocal inflections and body language onto the microphone, letting go fully and allowing herself to forget everything except the words she needed to express. As she did so, she slowly discovered how emotional and raw her voice could get - the kind of emotion true Nashville legends like Merle Haggard knew well and used to great effect onstage. So now the rest of us will get to experience it too thanks to Ms. McLauglins' new release scheduled for March 22. For more information visit

Inflation is the rise in price levels, and disinflation refers to a decrease in this rate. For example, if prices rose by 3% last year but only 2% this year, disinflation has taken place. It's possible to state that the economy experienced a 1% decline in inflation, yet growth remained at 2%. This distinction differs from deflation, which involves falling prices. If inflation starts low or disinflation persists over an extended period, it might eventually result in deflation, though this isn't guaranteed. Disinflation commonly emerges during economic downturns. When disinflation is prolonged and leads to deflation, it poses challenges for the economy. Deflation occurs because the value of money increases, prompting individuals to save instead of spending, as a unit of currency will purchase more tomorrow than today. However, reduced consumer spending can exacerbate recessions. Japan faced such issues between 1990 and recent times.

Deflation (assuming this refers to deflation rather than disinflation, which is generally less problematic) is detrimental as it results in lower prices. When prices fall, consumers delay purchases to assess further declines, leading to continued price drops. If prices persistently decrease, money circulation diminishes, perpetuating the cycle. Japan encountered these challenges in the 1990s.

Cuttlefish are able to delay gratification. Scientists found that the cephalopods could wait a bit for preferred prey rather than settling for a less desirable prey. Other animals, such as apes and corvids, have also demonstrated the ability to delay gratification through future-oriented foraging. The Stanford marshmallow test was a study where 600 children between the ages of four and six were given a choice to eat a marshmallow immediately or wait 15 minutes for a second marshmallow. The study found a correlation between those who had demonstrated self-control and success later in life. Later studies found that the correlation was much less significant when factoring in aspects like family background and home environment.

Console pick a resolution and stick with it. If the target is 720p, the game will render at 1280x720 and upscale to 1920x1080 or downscale to 852x480. Games that have been scaled look like crap; PC gamers demand that games render at the native resolution of their monitor. Any game that doesn't is (properly) derided as crap. If there is only one resolution to render at, the designers can make a huge number of assumptions that greatly simplify development. Every user of a console game uses the same controller. The people that don't use that controller use a controller that emulates the normal controller. On the other hand, PC gamers not only demand that games work with whatever bizarre keyboard or speed pad or keypad or joystick they own, but they demand that the game allows buttons to be remapped to suit their similarly bizarre purposes. Ask 100 different WoW players what buttons do what and you'll get 150 different responses. Every console has the same CPU, the same video card, the same amount of RAM, the same storage medium, and none of them have any processes running in the background. If a game encounters a slowdown in a certain situation, the game will always slow down there on every single console owned by every single user every single time. You can then optimize that section or cut detail in that section. On the other hand, some PCs are CPU limited, some PCs are GPU limited, some PCs are memory bandwidth limited, some PCs are memory quantity limited, some PCs have more or less disk space or disk speed, some PCs have resident programs (malware, malware scanners, a browser that was left open with a flash animation running, crappy OEM software like picture organizers that are always running, the hideous monstrosity that is HP's printer suite) that sop up any given resource, and you typically can't predict the slow parts. You'll need to expose every detail setting to the user to enable them to configure it, and then you'll need to know when the user is a fucking moron and override some of their settings if you need to. Video cards from ATI and nVidia behave much differently. There are differences between each generation of video cards, sometimes drastic ones. You need a few different rendering paths, and need to pick the right one depending on what hardware is available. Consoles do not have this problem. Other devices can have similar problems (sound cards might perform certain functions slowly or at the use of a lot of CPU) and in all cases you need to be more tolerant of whacky inputs. PC gamers are, to varying degrees, tolerant of bugs at launch, console gamers are not. [ OT Realistic Answer ] The idea that we have silent genes is an old school misconception, like the notion that we only use 10 of our brains. Some genes are not constituitively expressed, and some do not code for protein, but they are transcribed and all play some function at some point (LNCRNA, miRNA, rRNA, etc). The only exception is transposons and viral DNA which is integrated into our genome, but even these detrimental genes can be turned on (apparently) randomly. There is no mysterious 5000. But lets say you do turn on genes that are silenced in certain cell types. Some of these would be globin genes, which would change the way your body absorbs oxygen, may be detrimental to your health. The expression of other genes would cause cells to change to different cell types, or most likely, would result in cell death. We are finely tuned machines, turning on any of these silenced factors would screw up your body's chemistry pretty badly, and might also result in cancer or other diseases. Source: IAMA biochemistry PhD candidate.

Minocycline has been shown to have potential neuroprotective effects by reducing neuroinflammation induced by diabetic metabolic disorder. Studies have suggested that minocycline might alleviate beta-amyloid protein and tau pathology, which are associated with Alzheimer's disease, by inhibiting the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines and reactive oxygen species. This, in turn, could help restrain neuroinflammation caused by diabetic metabolic disorders. However, more research is needed to fully understand the mechanisms through which minocycline interacts with these pathologies and to confirm its therapeutic potential in this context.

Buddhism began to spread throughout Japan during the Heian period, primarily through two major esoteric sects, Tendai and Shingon. Tendai originated in China and is based on the Lotus Sutra, one of the most important sutras of Mahayana Buddhism; Saicho was key to its transmission to Japan. Shingon is the Japanese transmission of the Chinese Chen Yen school. Shingon, brought to Japan by the monk Kukai, emphasizes Esoteric Buddhism. Both Kukai and Saicho aimed to connect state and religion and establish support from the aristocracy, leading to the notion of 'aristocratic Buddhism'. An important element of Tendai doctrine was the suggestion that enlightenment was accessible to "every creature." Saicho also sought independent ordination for Tendai monks. A close relationship developed between the Tendai monastery complex on Mount Hiei and the imperial court in its new capital at the foot of the mountain. As a result, Tendai emphasized great reverence for the emperor and the nation. Kammu himself was a notable patron of the otherworldly Tendai sect, which rose to great power over the ensuing centuries. Kukai greatly impressed the emperors who succeeded Emperor Kammu, and also generations of Japanese, not only with his holiness but also with his poetry, calligraphy, painting, and sculpture. Shingon, through its use of "rich symbols, rituals and mandalas" held a wide-ranging appeal.

Two police officers who a judge said gave inconsistent and unconvincing evidence to an inquest in to the death of an IRA man are to be reported to prosecutors. The two officers, who have not been named, are accused of giving false testimony during the inquest into the death of Seamus Ludlow in 1997. Ludlow, a 47-year-old father of three, was abducted and killed by a loyalist gang in 1976. His body was found in a ditch in Co Louth, close to the border with Northern Ireland. At the time, the RUC said they had no suspects and the case remained unsolved. However, in 1979, the Sunday World newspaper named four men it said were responsible for the killing. In 1996, the Irish government set up an independent inquiry into the murder, which heard that the RUC had failed to properly investigate the case and had failed to interview the four men named by the Sunday World. The inquiry also heard that the RUC had failed to tell the Ludlow family that one of the four men, James Fitzsimmons, had confessed to the killing while he was in prison in Northern Ireland. Fitzsimmons later retracted his confession, but the Ludlow family believe he was involved in the killing and that the RUC knew this but failed to act. In 2016, the High Court in Belfast ruled that there was enough evidence to justify holding an inquest into Ludlow's death. The inquest began in April 2018 and heard from a number of witnesses, including the two police officers. Judge Liam McCollum said in his ruling that the two officers had given "inconsistent and unconvincing" evidence and that there were "serious questions" about their credibility. He said there was enough evidence to warrant referring the officers to the Public Prosecution Service to consider whether they should be charged with perjury. The Ludlow family welcomed the judge's ruling and said they hoped the officers would now be prosecuted.

Good habits often require consistent practice over a prolonged period before they become rewarding. In contrast, bad habits provide immediate pleasure but may be harmful in some way. Many bad habits offer instant rewards; for instance, playing video games rather than studying brings immediate enjoyment. While studying might offer greater long-term benefits, it lacks the quick satisfaction of such activities. Furthermore, our biology sometimes favors unhealthy choices. The brain is wired to crave certain flavors due to historical survival advantages, where high-calorie, fatty foods were scarce and storing fat was beneficial during lean times. As a result, we have developed a tendency to seek these foods. However, today's abundance of such foods does not negate the influence of this biological wiring. Many individuals also underestimate how long it takes to develop a habit. I believe it typically takes around two months, yet many people think shorter periods are sufficient, leading them to abandon efforts before the habit is fully formed. They may focus intensely on one activity for three weeks, believing it is enough to establish the habit, only to later lose interest and forfeit progress.

Is it over? My heart was beating frantically. I closed my eyes and listened. The bombs have been dropped and the battle cries can no longer be heard. The wind blew gently, and nobody could ever tell that a war had just ended. It was too quiet. I peeked through the cracks of the wall that separated me from the rest of the world. The entire place was in shambles and not a single soul was in sight. Could it be? Is it even possible? I felt another contraction. It wasn't my first, but I knew my baby was coming soon. I panicked. I felt the cold sweat travel down my spine. I had to move! I had to get out! I pulled myself together and after much jittering, I finally made it through the tiny gap in the wall. This place was once a great city, but the rubble and the stench of death says otherwise. "I can't be the only one.... "I told myself, as I struggled to get past the ruins that blocked the road. For a moment, I wandered into the streets hoping to find another survivor like me, but I was getting frustrated. The sun was hot and my burden heavy. My legs were sore and I could barely walk. I stumbled as I felt another contraction. I can't give birth here, not in this place. I breathed deeply, but it didn't soothe the pain. I looked for a shade that could offer temporary relief but I was stunned when I saw a peculiar figure not too far from where I stand. I tried to ask for help but my mouth can not make out the words to say. Another contraction. No please don't. I tried to relax myself but the baby was already crowning. The pain was getting more intense and the figure from afar drew nearer with each breath. I kept pushing and with each push, the pain grew ten folds. It wasn't until I felt something snap that the baby came out. She was covered in water and blood but she was beautiful. "baby girl.... My baby girl." I muttered as tried to collect her into my arms. The baby squirmed and for a moment I felt joy like no other. By then the mysterious figure had already stood before me. I couldn't quite make out his face for the sun was bright and a deep shadow concealed it. "She is beautiful isn't she." He muttered. His voice made me tremble. My legs grew limb and I couldn't move. The earth shook before me or so it seemed. My hands were getting numb and my vision was slowly getting blurry. The world spinned and the silence made me feel deaf. For a moment the pain of birth escaped me and I knew what was coming next. He took the baby into his arms and wrapped her in fine cloth. He smiled to me and said: "I shall name her Eve."

So there is a way for programs to declare themselves to have "root" provileges and access, without the need of a human typing in the root password. On Windows, that sort of thing isn't called a rootkit, it's called a privilege-escalation exploit. On Windows, a rootkit is something specifically designed to hide malware files on your computer, by injecting itself into critical system processes and messing with their behavior. Specifically, they tend to inject themselves into the kernel or filesystem, so that when something requests a list of files in a given folder, it can intercept the request and give a response that hides the malware files. Police in Australia and Europe were aware of a paedophile site called the Love Zone hidden in the so-called dark web. It was protected by passwords, encryption and specialist software. Users were totally anonymous. The images and videos there were particularly disturbing - showing the abuse of babies and very young children. Members had to post increasingly graphic material to remain on the site. There were tens of thousands of accounts. Officers with Task Force Argos in Australia knew the creator of the site used an unusual greeting - the word "hiyas." After exhaustively trawling chatrooms and forums in the open internet, they found a Facebook page of a man who used the same greeting. Although the Facebook page was fake, they identified a picture of a vehicle and that led them to a man called Shannon McCoole - a childcare worker in Adelaide. When officers went through his door, he was actually online running the site. They took detailed photographs of McCoole's hands. This is where the freckle comes in - one on his finger matched exactly one seen in many of the images of abuse. In an unprecedented move, Task Force Argos assumed McCoole's identity and took over the running of the site. Last year he was given a 35-year prison sentence. One user who stood out was Huckle - given the number of children he had access to and his aggressive attitude. Using data gleaned from the site and information Huckle had posted on social media and other open internet sites, they identified who he was and where he lived. Realising he was coming back to the UK for the Christmas holidays in 2014, they tipped off Britain's National Crime Agency. As he landed at Gatwick airport he was met by officers from the NCA's Child Exploitation and Online Protection command. On his computer and encrypted drives they found tens of thousands of obscene images and videos.

Nestled amidst the shops at North Rockaway Park sits Kinu Matsuri, a sprawling establishment dedicated solely to sushi. This expansive eatery features two levels and serves over 50 original recipes handmade by chef Ryusuke Yamamoto. Also known as Tengu Sushi, Chef Yamamoto began his journey making sushi nearly 40 years ago at Tokyo's famous Sashimi Tsukiji Market. "The world has changed tremendously over these past four decades," he says. "Sushi received recognition from many quarters. In Japan, sushi restaurants proliferated greatly due to the popularity of popular shows featuring celebrity chef cooks preparing deluxe meals. People wanted to see celebrities prepare food instead of relying exclusively on ramen bars. Then the internet became readily accessible. Many young people wanted to share their cooking skills online - and sushi hit prime-time television screens nationwide through various videos hosted on YouTube channels. Fans could learn cuisine techniques easily via expert demonstrations posted onto video sites like Vine. Accordingly, sushi culture expanded rapidly across America over the last decade."

Google will keep its 200,000 full-time and contract employees working remotely until at least July 2021. Sundar Pichai, CEO of Alphabet, made the announcement last week following a meeting with the company's executive team. Google had initially planned to reopen its offices in phases starting in June, but Pichai said the company will instead extend its remote work policy due to the ongoing pandemic. He also noted that while some employees may be able to return to the office in a limited capacity, Google is still encouraging most of its staff to work from home. The decision has received mixed reactions from Google employees and commentators. Some have argued that the extended period of remote work could lead to a decrease in productivity, while others have welcomed the announcement as it provides more flexibility for workers. Regardless, Google's move shows how deeply the pandemic has impacted workplace culture. As more companies embrace remote work, it remains to be seen if this trend will continue beyond 2021.

The shortcomings of Aristotelian physics would not be fully corrected until the 17th century work of Galileo Galilei, who was influenced by the late Medieval idea that objects in forced motion could move faster than natural motion, thus imparting some of their motion to the surrounding air. The idea of the following of a natural motion came from the concept of inertia, which was studied as early as the 17th century by Galileo. The Earth was not the center of the universe. In the early 16th century, Nicolaus Copernicus proposed a heliocentric model of the Solar System in which the Sun was at the center, the planets revolved around it, and the Moon revolved around the Earth. Galileo was a strong proponent of this theory and worked to refine it. His most important contribution to astronomy was the discovery of the four largest satellites of Jupiter. Galileo thought that the Copernican model was the right one. When the Roman Inquisition judged that the Copernican model was contrary to the Bible, Galileo was forced to renounce his belief in it. He was given a lifetime ban on teaching or advocating the Copernican system. Galileo made several improvements in the telescope and invented a compound microscope. He was the first to use a telescope to observe the sky. He discovered that the Milky Way was made of stars, that Jupiter had moons, and that Venus showed phases. He discovered that sunspots were on the surface of the Sun, not on the background. He observed a large number of comets. Galileo's observations of the Milky Way and of Jupiter's satellites convinced him that the Copernican theory was correct. He also was the first to observe the phases of Venus, the first to use a telescope to view the sky, and the first to observe sunspots. He made a major contribution to the development of the telescope, and many sources credit him as the inventor of the telescope. His most famous telescopic observations were made on the surface of the Moon, the planet Jupiter, and Saturn's rings. Galileo also studied and taught the dynamics of bodies in motion. Galileo built many of his own instruments. Galileo's first telescope had a magnification of 3x, but he was able to increase the magnification by the end of 1609. Galileo used the telescope to observe Jupiter and discovered the four largest moons of Jupiter. Galileo also observed the phases of Venus, which were in opposition to the theory that the Earth was at the center of the universe. In 1612, Galileo was condemned by the Catholic Church for his defense of Copernicanism, and spent the rest of his life under house arrest. His books were banned, and he was forbidden to discuss his ideas. He spent the last years of his life blind, and it was said that during this period he wrote one of his finest works, Two New Sciences. Galileo died in 1642. His contributions to observational astronomy include the discovery of the four largest moons of Jupiter, which he named Medicean stars after his royal patron, Cosimo II de Medici. Galileo also observed a supernova in the Messier 39 nebula, and is also credited with the first detection of the satellites of the planet Neptune, which he noted in 1612 as tiny stars that disappeared within a few days. He discovered the Galilean moons, which are named after him. Galileo also observed the Moon's surface, a discovery which supported the view of Copernicus that the Moon was a sphere, not the "perfect" disk of Ptolemy. Kyra stared at the metallic container in her hands and felt a pang of disappointment. She fought to maintain a steady expression as she pulled herself out of the colorful, pink wrapping paper that had enclosed the box. The card contained no money. "Thank you, Uncle Rufus," she finally said, meeting his gaze. Kyra smoothed her expression into polite delight and smiled at the man sitting in the rocking chair by the window. Her mother did not approve of him, as he refused to take off his muddy boots when entering their home, and the tan shirt he wore smelled of pipe smoke and peat. His fingers were dirty, his hair was tousled by the wind, and his beard was messy, resembling a bird's nest. "I really like the gift," she said, placing her hand inside the box and gently poking the small, scaled creature within. It was smaller than a mouse, with tiny combs like a cockerel’s lining the back of its neck and extending down to its tail, no wider than a needle at its base. When she touched it, the dragon stirred and turned toward her hand. Its eyes were blue as sapphires, contrasting with the deep royal green of its scales. Two bumps on its back indicated the potential for wings. "They grow," Uncle Rufus assured her. "That's a Scotch dragon. One of the last. I found the mother myself, after she gave birth to six of them in a small cabin on my land. I almost burned myself getting it away from her! That was the smallest, though I thought it would be perfect for little Kyra here." The final part was addressed to Kyra's mother, who frowned. "I don't think it's entirely suitable for a child," she said. Her face hardened into a sharp line. Meanwhile, the dragon curled against the palm of Kyra's hand, closing its eyes and sniffing softly. She had intended to visit a pet hospital, but as the dragon's warmth pressed against her palm, she realized she wasn’t too adverse to it. "I like it, Mum," she said. "Can I keep it?" A moment of hesitation passed before she nodded.

American accents are most variable in terms of vowels, nasality, rhoticism (final R), intervocalic consonants (VCV), and final consonants. You will obviously find greater diversity in places like NYC. The dialect situation in America is very complicated. For example, one of the dialects of New Orleans is the 'yat' dialect, which can trace its ancestry directly to Brooklyn. In general, the Inland North is fairly 'standard.' It exhibits the Northern Cities Vowel Shift. The East and Northeast typically resists merging pinpen, cotcaught, marymerrymarry. As a result they have more vowel variation. Some NE dialects are non-rhotic and nasal. You will find larger differences between individual states here. The Midlands have some diversity, like in OhioIndiana.... I'm not familiar with them. The South has a good deal of diversity, but most dialects are characterized by the Southern Cities Vowel Shift. Some also have drawls, where an extra schwa vowel (uh) is added after glides. Some dialects have double negatives. Again, there is sometimes non-rhoticism. The North Central typically merges the vowels I mentioned resisted by the NE accents. This accent is on the UP of Michigan, and northern WIMN. They have strong rhotics and unreleased final consonants. "bagflagtag" are pronounced "beyg,fleyg,teyg." A new film is reviving the story of how the 1984-85 Miners Strike brought together two very diverse sections of society, which is getting its premiere in London's West End. The strike, which lasted a year, was a bitter conflict between the Thatcher government and the trade unions that involved hundreds of thousands of miners and their families. However, amidst the gloom and desperation, one heartwarming story emerged: the unlikely alliance formed between the miners and the gay community. The film, titled "United in Adversity," delves into the story of how a group of gay and lesbian activists came together to support miners through the strike, creating a bond that would transform perceptions of both communities. It tells of how the Lesbians and Gays Support the Miners (LGSM) group raised funds and offered spiritual and practical support to miners, in spite of initial suspicion and rejection from some of them. Over time, though, they formed friendships, solidarity and respect for each other's struggles. LGSM eventually raised more than 20,000 for the miners' cause, which became a lifesaver for struggling working-class communities, as government support dwindled. The film, directed by Tom Harper, stars Bill Nighy, Imelda Staunton and Andrew Scott. It premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival and was praised for its uplifting message of the power of community bonding over difference. The West End premiere is expected to draw large crowds and bring attention to the enduring need for grass-roots activism, solidarity and mutual support, as communities still grapple with socio-economic, and cultural divides. Hopefully, this movie will inspire a new generation to come together in the face of adversity and strive for a better and more connected world.

Libya's economy witnessed increasing privatization; although rejecting the socialist policies of nationalized industry advocated in The Green Book, government figures asserted that they were forging "people's socialism" rather than capitalism. Gaddafi welcomed these reforms, calling for wide-scale privatization in a March 2003 speech. In 2003, the oil industry was largely sold to private corporations, and by 2004, there was 40 billion of direct foreign investment in Libya, a sixfold rise over 2003. Sectors of Libya's population reacted against these reforms with public demonstrations, and in March 2006, revolutionary hard-liners took control of the GPC cabinet; although scaling back the pace of the changes, they did not halt them. In 2010, plans were announced that would have seen half the Libyan economy privatized over the following decade. While there was no accompanying political liberalization, with Gaddafi retaining predominant control, in March 2010, the government devolved further powers to the municipal councils. Rising numbers of reformist technocrats attained positions in the country's governance; best known was Gaddafi's son and heir apparent Saif al-Islam Gaddafi, who was openly critical of Libya's human rights record. He led a group who proposed the drafting of the new constitution, although it was never adopted, and in October 2009 was appointed to head the PSLC. Involved in encouraging tourism, Saif founded several privately run media channels in 2008, but after criticising the government they were nationalised in 2009. In October 2010, Gaddafi apologized to African leaders on behalf of Arab nations for their involvement in the African slave trade.

The U.S. dollar was established by the Constitution and outlined in the Coinage Act of 1792. It defined a "dollar" as being based on the Spanish milled dollar, with a weight of 371 grains and 4 sixteenths of a grain, or 416 grains (27.0 grams) of standard silver, and an "eagle" as 247 and 4 eighths of a grain or 270 grains (17 grams) of gold (depending on purity). The value of 371 grains was chosen because Alexander Hamilton decided to use the average weight of worn Spanish dollars as the basis for the new American unit. He had the Treasury measure a sample of Spanish dollars, and the average weight was found to be 371 grains. A new Spanish dollar typically weighed around 377 grains, making the new U.S. dollar slightly lighter than the Spanish dollar.

"None of the computers or machines worked except for the General Electric-powered machines like the MRIs [magnetic resonance imaging]," recalled Mykhailo Radutskyi, president of the Boris Clinic - Kiev's largest medical clinic. His radiologists decided to turn off the body scanners anyway as a precautionary measure after the building's IT system went down at two o'clock in the morning in late June. Doctors across the centre had to resort to taking records solely by paper and pen for the first time since the mid-1990s. "The main problem for us was that Ukrainian law requires us to keep all our patient info for 25 years, and we lost that medical documentation for the 24 hours when our systems were down," Mr Radutskyi divulged. "But thankfully we keep back-ups, so we didn't lose any information." All in all, Mr Radutskyi reckons his clinic's damage tally totalled 60,000 (PS46,000). Others have been unwilling to reveal how badly they were hit. Oschadbank - one of the country's biggest lenders - was among those that declined an interview with the BBC. Even now, almost a month after the so-called NotPetya strike, some companies inside and outside the nation are still facing disruption. Ukraine's top cyber-cop disclosed that some of the nation's largest companies were still too scared to share the full scale of the fallout with his investigators. And Sergiy Demedyuk - head of Ukraine's ministry of internal affairs' cybercrime division - added he has come to believe there are aftershocks still to come since the hackers appear to have compromised their targets for some time before they pounced, and might still be sitting on data they could yet exploit. NotPetya initially appeared to be a ransomware attack, but many now suspect its blackmail demands were a cover for something more ominous. Experts who have spoken to the BBC are seemingly sure of two things: first, Ukraine was the target, and second, it was not about money. Despite denials, suspicion has fallen on Ukraine's eastern neighbour, Russia. "Cyber-attacks are just one part of Russia's wider efforts to destabilise the country," Nato's former chief civil servant Anders Fogh Rasmussen told the BBC. "In my time as secretary general we agreed that a cyber-attack could trigger Nato's mutual defence clause. "The Alliance has been assisting Ukraine especially with monitoring and investigating security incidents. However.... more support is also needed for prevention." One cybersecurity veteran has been investigating how a local software developer's program, MeDoc, came to be hijacked to spread the malware. "It wasn't just [a case of] take over MeDoc's update server and push out NotPetya," explained Nicholas Weaver from University of California, Berkeley. "Instead, they had previously compromised MeDoc, made it into a remote-control Trojan, and then they were willing to burn this asset to launch this attack," he added, referring to the fact the servers have since been confiscated by the police. "That really is huge." MeDoc's tax filing services were used by more than 400,000 customers across Ukraine, representing about 90 of its domestic firms. Although it was not mandatory for local companies to use it, by virtue of its ubiquity, it's almost as if it were. "This was gold they had, basically a control point in almost every business that does business in Ukraine," said Mr Weaver. "And they burned this resource in order to launch this destructive attack." Mr Demedyuk said his police force had concrete evidence that MeDoc was hacked a long time ago and had been used to spy on economic activity within Ukraine. "The [developers] claimed on their website that it was certificated, that it had been examined with international audit and it's 100 safe. In fact, it wasn't true," he added. One ex-US Army cyber-expert said the hackers might have felt forced to carry out their attack through fear that MeDoc's computer servers were about to slip out of their control. "If you read [security firm] ESET's report, you see that they gained and lost access repeatedly as legitimate MeDocs updates were pushed," Jon Nichols said. "It is possible that the actors just wanted to cause as much damage as they could before they lost control again." This theory is backed up by another US expert. "It's not unheard of if you think you'll lose your position to launch prematurely," said Beau Woods deputy director of the Atlantic Council's Cyber Statecraft Initiative. He added that if the perpetrators had, indeed, gathered financial data about most of Ukraine's companies, they might still find ways to cause further damage. Mr Demedyuk said that although only four police officers had been assigned to his NotPetya investigation full-time, he had about 300 people across Ukraine supporting the inquiry. Furthermore, he has met with Interpol to discuss ways to share information with other international authorities. While they try to unravel how the attack was carried out, others are preparing for follow-up cyber-assaults. In particular, the chief executive of Ukraine's state-owned energy giant Ukrenergo is concerned it will be a target. "All our life as an independent country in the last 25 years, we've been connected to the Russian power grid and they've balanced us," Vsevolod Kovalchuk told the BBC. However, he explained, an agreement his firm has struck with European electricity transmission operators to modernise Ukraine's power grid might have put the firm in Moscow's cross-hairs. It might sound like paranoia, but Ukrenergo had already been hit by two cyber-attacks prior to NotPetya. One occurred just before Christmas. "That virus worked in our local network for over one year," Mr Kovalchuk said. "It collected information and after collecting the information, the hackers put another malware specific for our northern substation and switched it off for 15 minutes. It was only a test but they tried and it was successful." Before that Ukrenergo was caught up in the infamous Black Energy attack, in December 2015. It took down half a city's power for three hours in the dead of winter. The two incidents meant the firm was already battle-hardened when it was infected by NotPetya. "A dispatcher called me and said they couldn't do anything because all of their screens had turned black and were asking for money," recalled Mr Kovalchuk. "That was at 11:02 EET [Eastern European Time], and then several minutes later, other computers were in the same situation so I called to my chief IT officer and asked what is this, is this WannaCry or something similar?" he said referring to a ransomware attack that disrupted the NHS and others in May. "We disconnected our networks, switched off our computers, and then we used our protocols from the past, using paper standards, phones and continued to operate without any computers, without databases, without any systems." This time round, the electricity grid was unharmed and power flowed uninterrupted. But the company was left without secondary functions for 10 days. For Ukraine, the most important questions from here on seem to be: How bad does an attack have to be before serious international attention is paid to it? And: At what point does it become a war crime? "I think that every six months, we'll see attacks," predicted Prof Michael Schmitt, lead author of the Tallinn Manual - the definitive international legal guide to cyber-conflict. "Even though I'm not 100 sure that it's Russia, I don't understand which other country could attack Ukraine. It's the only logical answer." And Ukrainian cybersecurity experts like Alexey Yankovski believe every single business is at risk. "Ukraine is a playground for attacks, and a large part of the cyber-security community here believes that most of the companies have already been infected," he told the BBC. "Every company here should be prepared for the fact that it will be hacked sooner or later." This week BBC News is taking a close look at all aspects of cyber-security.
