... or to put it another way, I suppose it could be written that "People hold many opinions about the immoral nature of certain actions just because with no real logical reason for it." This is an opinion I've been trying to quantify for a while now, and my time on CMV has only seemed to reinforce this view. People posting everything from views about the morality of drugs, to homosexuality, etc... and so little of morality seems to make sense. There are taboos against drug use, against incest, against homosexuality, against open sexuality, against so many things. There's this kind of "moral disgust" for things which don't inherently do any harm. Most of the explanations I see for why these things are wrong are generic answers with little thought or reason to them: "It's unnatural," "It's an affront to god," "It just isn't, because it just isn't." As far as I believe morality should be concerned, we should be allowed to do whatever we want with our own bodies so long as nobody else is harmed. If you want to do drugs just because the high makes you happy, and you've been educated and warned about the potential damages to your own body... it is your body and your life, what is wrong? If you're gay and you choose to have consensual homosexual sex and that's what you both decide to do with your bodies, what is wrong? If you want to post nudes online and you feel empowered from it and the comments you get, what is wrong? The only explanation I could honestly come up with is the way others may react to you, but even that is just a biproduct of a culture which creates senseless taboos, and does things like shaming people for being "sluts" or for being gay without any real justification. What sense is there in these taboos, and the kind of bullying and shame that often comes with them? Where is the reasonable justification for deeming things that don't harm others immoral? CMV. The Premier League hosts huffed and puffed before Divock Origi stole behind the Leeds defence to sweep in Trent Alexander-Arnold's right-wing cross from close range. They secured a place in the last four when Wales Under-19 international Woodburn, aged 17 years and 45 days, fired in the second to beat Owen's record by 98 days. Liverpool hit a post through Georginio Wijnaldum shortly before the opener, but the scoreline was somewhat harsh on the Yorkshire side. Leeds winger Kemar Roofe curled against the inside of a post shortly after half-time. Hadi Sacko spurned a good opportunity for the visitors in the opening 10 minutes, and Kyle Bartley nodded a free header wide after the break. Liverpool will find out who they play in the semi-finals when the draw is made after Wednesday's matches. Liverpool boss Jurgen Klopp might have claimed his team has "unfinished business" in the EFL Cup, but this competition is clearly not the German's priority this season as the Reds chase the Premier League title and a Champions League return. And that has been clear by his team selections. Klopp, like he did in the earlier rounds, rotated his team by bringing in fringe players and a handful of youngsters, though that was forced in part by the absence of Philippe Coutinho, Roberto Firmino, Daniel Sturridge and Adam Lallana through injury. Without that attacking threat, the home side lacked fluency and potency in the final third until they clicked in the final 15 minutes to reach a record 17th League Cup semi-final. However, a laboured night was capped when Woodburn - on as a second-half substitute having made his debut on Saturday against Sunderland - beat Owen's record by 98 days. It was a special moment for the youngster in front of the Kop and former England striker Owen, who was watching from the main stand. Every one of Woodburn's outfield team-mates came to celebrate the historic moment as Anfield saluted their latest star. Matches between these two clubs may be rare in the modern era - but this is a fixture steeped in history. A rivalry born in the days of Bill Shankly and Don Revie, resurrected in the eras of Kenny Dalglish and Howard Wilkinson, consigned to longer memories post-Gerard Houllier and David O'Leary. And it attracted the imagination of both sets of fans, Leeds bringing almost 5,500 to a capacity crowd of 53,000. While this tie did not have the allure of a title-swinging league match or Wembley cup final of previous eras, it did provide an opportunity for Leeds to test themselves again at the highest level. Following a turbulent few seasons under Italian owner Massimo Cellino, there is a cautious optimism among Whites fans that their club may - finally - push for promotion back to the Premier League this season. Manager Garry Monk has provided a calm guidance rarely seen - or allowed - under Cellino's control, moving the club up to fifth in the Championship after four wins in their past five matches. The odds were stacked heavily in favour of the home side prior to kick-off, but the visitors created several decent opportunities against a casual Reds defence. Ultimately, they lost with a fight. But the reception given by the away fans to their players at the final whistle suggests they are optimistic a 13-year absence from the Premier League may be coming to an end in the near future. Leeds United manager Garry Monk: "I asked them to play in slightly different way to what we have been doing tactically, which we had to do against a very good side "We followed it to a tee. It just lacked us taking one of quite a few opportunities. We had the best chances of the game. "It needed a bit more composure, that's the only negative. Better decision-making in the final third and we would have had a couple of goals. Overall I was gutted for the players. "As a performance for a young, inexperienced team these type of nights set a marker for you. We're growing. We are disappointed but they will look back in time and think we have put on a good performance "I'm not going to criticise my team - they were excellent." Having a child is a complete gamble. The child can be potentially ugly, unintelligent, have bad social skills, be untalented, develop chronic pain or have some sort of medical condition, develop a mental illness, die tragically in a disasteraccident, or be murdered at random and that's only the beginning. When you bring a child into this world, you are literally guaranteeing that it must go to school (something all kids dread), worry about making friends, worry about performing well at school and in final exams so that it can finally go to college andor get a job as a wage slave. You are literally guaranteeing in the first world they will have to get a job and work their asses off to get by. Is that really all "worth it" for any tiny bits of pleasure they can experience here and there? And that's the first world. Don't even get me started on having kids in the third world. There is an inherent asymmetry between pain and pleasure. For example, would you take 1 hour of the most pure pleasure (some kind of heroin while eating KFC and having sex all at the same time) you have ever experienced if it were to be followed by 1 hour of the most intense pain you could ever experience (being burned alive, having limbs cut off etc)? Probably not. For any conscious being (whether human or non-human) it would have been better never to exist, since coming into being is always an overall harm, and thus worse than non-existence, for that being. Non-existence implies the absence of both pains and pleasures, but whereas the absence of the pains is something good, it is not the case that the absence of the pleasures is bad or something to be deplored. A potential person is not deprived of anything, claims Benatar, by not being brought into existence. Also, many parents willingly bring children into this world when they know life itself isn't even worth it in the long run. They perpetuate the suffering onto their children. When parents say "well, life isn't fair" they unknowingly reveal an important fact about the natalist attitude to life and to children. Life isn't fair, which means, prima facie, that perpetuating it is an injustice. In order to tolerate and extend the injustice of life, persons intent on reproduction must value life more than fairness. Are parents aware of this, and what do they mean when they say "well, life isn't fair"? Do they really stand by this statement, which seems so self-accusing? Lastly, children cannot consent to being brought into the world. They have no say in it, and I bet if they saw their lives before being born they would all choose to stay in a state of non-existence.

The cantons have a permanent constitutional status and, in comparison with the situation in other countries, a high degree of independence. However, there are considerable differences between the individual cantons, most particularly in terms of population and geographical area. Their populations vary between 15,000 (Appenzell Innerrhoden) and 1,253,500 (Zurich), and their area between 37 km2 (14 sq mi) (Basel-Stadt) and 7,105 km2 (2,743 sq mi) (Graubunden). The Cantons comprise a total of 2,485 municipalities. Within Switzerland there are two enclaves: Busingen belongs to Germany, Campione d'Italia belongs to Italy.

I was eight years old when I first noticed the horns. It wasn’t the horns themselves, of course—those had always been a recurring annoyance with any shirt I wore. They had been growing longer over time, which made me more accustomed to wearing flannel. I was eight when I first saw the stares. It’s strange how something so integral to me suddenly feels like an oddity. Of course, I’ve always had horns. My long hair usually conceals them, and even without it, I could still wear a hat. I decided to put one on—some might call it ignorance, but it’s just a matter of understanding the norm within my own perspective. For me, horns were normal, and that didn’t make me question why others didn’t have them. Until they started asking me questions. A younger boy asked me about the bumps and whether they were the same as my brother’s acne. I explained they were my horns, and he asked if he could try them on. When he couldn’t get them off, he ran to his mother with excitement. She ran away holding her cross necklace... but it was racist. I remember that was the day I asked my parents. Having horns is natural, isn’t it? I hadn’t noticed anyone else having them before… but then again, I never really paid much attention. Like a kid with a pushed-in sternum, they don’t notice that others don’t have them—they just assume their chest is a bit different, at least that’s what my friend Greg said. My mom looked at my dad, I remember. She knew it was coming. The Big Not-Sex Question. My dad sat down, rubbed my head, and gave me the usual gentle touch. He was kind to me, but firm. Maybe that’s why it stayed with me. Or perhaps some truths are things you can’t let go. The more true it is, the deeper it gets inside you. “It’s natural for you, son, and that’s all that matters,” I’ve only cared about since.

The extra "tenths" is a very old tradition that's never gone away. In 1935, a Reno Nevada newspaper wrote about "selling third grade gasoline at eight and nine-tenths cents a gallon." Around this time, federal and state excise taxes were also introduced in increments of tenths of a cent, so it made sense to keep the decimal value. Perpetuated for Profit? The tradition stuck. The U.S. Energy Information Administration, 'prime suppliers' of 'motor gasoline' reported sales of 372,833.5 thousand barrels sold in February 2007. These gas sales collected US 141 million in nine-tenths-of-a-cent increments. With gasoline prices in the US 2.00 to US 4.00 range, the 910 no longer serves a constructive purpose, and occasionally measures have been introduced to abolish it. Choose a resolution for your console and keep it consistent. If the target is 720p, the game will run at 1280x720 and upscale to 1920x1080 or downscale to 852x480. Games that are scaled appear poor; PC gamers prefer games to render at their monitor's native resolution. Any game that isn't rendered at the correct resolution is commonly criticized as low quality. If only one resolution is used, developers can make numerous simplifying assumptions. All console users use the same controller. Those who don’t use it employ an emulator for the standard controller. In contrast, PC gamers expect games to function with any odd keyboard, speedpad, keypad, or joystick they possess, and they also want the ability to remap buttons to suit their unique needs. Asking 100 World of Warcraft players what each button does yields 150 different answers. Every console shares the same CPU, video card, RAM, storage, and no processes are running in the background. If a game slows down in a specific scenario, it will do so consistently on every console and every user’s machine. You can then optimize that part or reduce its detail. Conversely, some PCs are CPU-bound, others GPU-bound, some are memory-bandwidth constrained, others are memory-limited, some have more or less disk space or speed, and some have persistent programs (like malware, malware scanners, a browser with a flash animation, or outdated OEM software) that consume resources. It's difficult to predict which parts will slow down. You must reveal all detail settings to the user so they can adjust them, and you’ll need to determine when a user is "fucking" something.

The Uniform Crime Reports (UCR) gather information from more than 17,000 law enforcement agencies nationwide. They offer comprehensive details on crime statistics, including arrests, case resolutions, and officer records. The UCR primarily collects data on violent crimes, hate crimes, and property crimes. Established in the 1920s, the UCR system is not as consistent as its name suggests. Instead they sat together, trying to understand each other better than anyone could hope to do alone. At least he hoped so. James looked around. They'd made their way down farther into the fissure until there was nothing above except more rock walling them in. Still, no sign of the end... nor a raft of drifting survivors. As far as James could tell there might still be thousands of people trapped deep below ground. If only Gennady hadn't lied! They continued walking slowly down toward the bottom while rock walls pinching forward became less frequent and finally disappeared altogether. There was barely room to walk two abreast, and soon they had to turn sideways because the tunnel widened again. Light streamed past them from above creating pools of soft light that danced across smooth stone walls, reflecting back dozens of colors. More of the ancient paintings remained intact here, revealing images in bright tones of blue, green, yellow, and red, covering every surface including sections of sheer white granite. Between images were faint splotches of darker color where centuries-old paint seemed to bleed from cracks and crevices into surrounding areas of fresher paint. But James saw only fragments: odd geometric shapes, animals, religious symbols. Nothing familiar. All he could distinguish were sweeping freehand strokes of red and orange, or dark brown and black swirls. Even the least interesting parts looked beautiful to him. To Ailith he was simply curious how old these pictures were, and whether any meaning was hidden beneath the murals' faded hues. Unbidden, thoughts came into mind so full of questions and curiosity, he forgot himself completely. He wished he could stop thinking so hard. His brain hurt with such great intensity that sleep began creeping closer and nearer. Although he fought against it, exhaustion claimed him fast, bringing on a fitful half dream filled with flames and fireballs. Soon he started dreaming dreamless sleep. Her face glowed with health, and her normally pale skin had taken on a rosy hue. Beyond her spread a view dominated by a vast crater. However it appeared smaller now compared to earlier, as though it had shrunk during its journey toward the center of Earth. A team of scientists launched a box containing four types of bacteria and fungus into the stratosphere to expose them to several hours of Mars-like conditions. The experiment found that yeast, fungi, viruses and other pathogens extracted from a single sample can affect or even destroy the cells they contain on Earth, in ways unseen before on any planet. The technique also allowed scientists to optimize the rate at which new microbes take over plants. According to NASA, each of the organisms within one million miles (1.2 billion kilometers) of earth's surface have enough enzymes to filter out microorganisms that are not needed for most food or medicine applications. However, the researchers believe that microbial production may be possible off-the-shelf by investing more energy into their experiments. Using tiny amounts of RNA used to make the enzyme, researchers discovered that the microbes' levels could be increased by up to 15 times. The same amount of RNA is needed to grow the microbes, but the researchers say they need only two one-tenths of this amount to produce the desired results. "This opens up an opportunity to understand how the efficient production and efficiency of microorganisms takes place," said lead author Rohit Uddhav, professor of biological biology at Rutgers University, who was not involved with the research, in a statement. "We will now begin our study."

In the later Imperial era, the burial and commemorative practises of Christian and non-Christians overlapped. Tombs were shared by Christian and non-Christian family members, and the traditional funeral rites and feast of novemdialis found a part-match in the Christian Constitutio Apostolica. The customary offers of wine and food to the dead continued; St Augustine (following St Ambrose) feared that this invited the "drunken" practices of Parentalia but commended funeral feasts as a Christian opportunity to give alms of food to the poor. Christians attended Parentalia and its accompanying Feralia and Caristia in sufficient numbers for the Council of Tours to forbid them in AD 567. Other funerary and commemorative practices were very different. Traditional Roman practice spurned the corpse as a ritual pollution; inscriptions noted the day of birth and duration of life. The Christian Church fostered the veneration of saintly relics, and inscriptions marked the day of death as a transition to "new life."

Cellular networks of massive MIMO base-stations employing TDDOFDM and relying on uplink training for both downlink and uplink transmission are viewed as an attractive candidate for 5G deployments, as they promise high area spectral and energy efficiencies with relatively simple low-latency operation. We investigate the use of non-orthogonal uplink pilot designs as a means for improving the area spectral efficiency in the downlink of such massive MIMO cellular networks. We develop a class of pilot designs that are locally orthogonal within each cell, while maintaining low inner-product properties between codes in different cells. Using channel estimates provided by observations on these codes, each cell independently serves its locally active users with MU-MIMO transmission that is also designed to mitigate interference to a subset of "strongly interfered" out-of-cell users. As our simulation-based analysis shows, such cellular operation based on the proposed codes yields user-rate CDF improvement with respect to conventional operation, which can be exploited to improve cell andor cell-throughput performance.

Multi-compartment modeling of diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging measurements is necessary for accurate brain connectivity analysis. Existing methods for estimating the number and orientations of fascicles in an imaging voxel either require access to a reference solution of a similar image or have a relatively high bias compared to true values. To resolve these issues, we present a novel method for the recovery of diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (DW-MRI) fascicle orientations in each voxel. Our approach estimates a multi-compartment model of the diffusion process in a voxel from the DW-MRI measurements. The multi-compartment model is then solved for each voxel to recover the number and orientations of the fascicles in that voxel. An image-based methodology is employed to reduce the number of unknowns and to efficiently estimate the orientations and locations of the internal nodes of the multi-compartment model. A numerical example illustrates the performance of the proposed method. F. Tsekouras, E. K. Galanis, P. B. Frey, J. E. Schreiner, J. A. Hess, and J. M. Haxby. MRI Fascicle Orientation Estimation. Neuroimage, 113 (2):717-730, July 2015.

The Facility for Rare Isotope Beams aims to create thousands of isotopes never before recorded on Earth. There are 285 isotopes of elements that exist on Earth, but there are thousands more out there in the universe. "A lot of the chemical processes that go on in the universe are still mysteries to us because we don't have the right materials," said Bill Foster, a professor at Fermilab. "When we get this new facility, we will have the materials. It will open the door to many new scientific discoveries." After a four-year wait, the project was given the green light last year. The laboratory has already begun construction. Once complete, FRIB will be the only place on Earth that can make more than 1,000 of the isotopes at the same time. It will produce 15,000 samples a month of isotopes that will go to researchers all over the world. "Isotopes are a bit like the alphabet," said Foster. "You can combine them in different ways and make different words, and the different words all have different properties. They may act differently chemically or even in terms of reacting with other elements." The facility will give scientists an understanding of the inner workings of stars, planets and even the origins of the universe. "What I really hope for is for people to not just use these isotopes to understand what's happening in the universe, but also use them to understand ourselves," said Anna Simons, a PhD student. "There are isotopes that are only found in meteorites, there are isotopes that are only found in the human body, and there are some isotopes that are only found in plants. So if you know the isotope of an element, you can use that to learn more about what it's doing." FRIB will open for business in 2017. Facility for Rare Isotope Beams, FRIB, Fermilab

We introduce a method for creating folds tailored for nested data types with dependent types. These folds are referred to as dependently typed folds and possess the following characteristics: (1) They are constructed via well-founded recursion and can be implemented in a total dependently typed language. (2) They do not rely on maps or map functions; instead, numerous terminating functions can be defined using these folds. (3) The induction rules applicable to nested data types emerge directly from the fold definitions and the programs generated by these folds. (4) Dependently typed folds are available for all nested data types and can be adapted to traditional higher-order folds. Through several examples, we demonstrate how to implement and analyze dependently typed folds. Additionally, we illustrate how to derive these folds generally and tailor them to their corresponding higher-order counterparts.

Automatic software plagiarism detection tools are widely used in educational settings to ensure that submitted work was not copied. These tools have grown in use together with the rise in popularity of online education and the increased use of computers in educational environments. Automatic software plagiarism detection tools are typically programmed to search for text that is identical or nearly identical to text found on other webpages, databases, or previous assignments. These tools can compare texts from different sources or between multiple documents, and then generate a report indicating the degree of similarity. This report can be used by instructors to determine if any part of a student's work has been plagiarized. In addition to accuracy and speed, these tools must also protect the privacy of both students and instructors. To ensure security, some software contains features such as data encryption, authentication, and authorization. Finally, automatic software plagiarism detection tools should also be user-friendly and easy to use. Many include tutorials and step-by-step instructions which guide users through each stage of the process. Additionally, many have customer support teams available to answer questions and provide assistance.

Terra preta (black earth), which is distributed over large areas in the Amazon forest, is now widely accepted as a product of indigenous soil management. The development of this fertile land was supported by rainforest vegetation that allowed it to be harvested and used for cattle feed without spreading fire across its surface during dry periods or clearing out thickets with herbicides before planting crops such as soybeans.[22] In contrast, the grasses found on the plateau are low-growing species whose seeds must compete among themselves for light from the sun, water, nutrients and moisture. They do not produce much biomass while they grow because their leaves absorb more power than they release; the extra energy costs them valuable time needed to germinate so these plants cannot reach sufficient size to sustain vegetative growth until the end of rainy seasons. Their small seedlings die off early during droughts, when rainfall drops below 60 cmyear,[2425] meaning they can never develop into trees, shrubs or other forms of habitat suitable for birds, mammals and insects. In addition, the shallow root systems make drainage difficult even though most soils there are at least moderately well drained compared to those at higher elevations[26]. Because of limited water availability many of the plant species thriving here have evolved specialized water requirements: shrub ferns, mosses, lichens, sedges, ginkgo biloba and quaking Aspen all thrive very well under drought conditions but form dense mats only if heavily shaded from sunlight [27]; conifers can retain enough heat through photosynthesis to survive year round despite being short lived plants wherever they occur due to their efficient root systems[28]. The soil found deep within the Andean mountains has been especially hardy for millennia. It contains high levels of calcium carbonate, an important element for the storage of organic matter produced by decomposing organic material like dead animals, roots, mushrooms, fungi, leaves, fruit skins, seeds and leavings - insect larvae pheromones, bird droppings and mold spores, broken bones and soft tissue. Calcium carbonates also help bind together clay minerals in the soil. This makes erosion unlikely and allows the formation stable humus layers around new plants growing after rains. Strong alkaline soils contain less calcium carbonate and react easily with neighboring acidic soil types, often causing the loss of individual cells along with the surrounding biotic community beneath them. These conditions further decrease the capacity of each layer's soil structure to recover from erosion events caused by windstorms and heavy storms.[29] Ecology A study conducted between 2009-2011 estimated the number of different species living on the Plateau de la Plata about half this total amount of life carried by Earth's largest ecosystem: 24,000 species were recorded in 1 hectare (2.5 acres) of the plateau area studied including both terrestrial and aquatic organisms. Some animal groups had larger numbers represented on the plateau than elsewhere in Ecuador:[30]the tapirs were responsible for 48 percent of the inhabitants in almost 40 of the areas covered by this group; 94 species made up 27 of the populations reported and 53 percent of their habitats; Avocet cormorants accounted for 15, or just 3 mortalities per square kilometer affected by avian colonies, compared to 7 fatalities for a typical colony of black-backed gulls in Patagonia.[31] Human impact The region has suffered extensive deforestation since the 1970s[32] owing to increased demand for livestock manure, timber, charcoal and wood for fuelwood. Deforestation rates fell somewhat after 2002 following forest fires set intentionally by farmers trying to clear pastureland for farming enterprises resulting from years of drought. In 2005, about 25 of the Andeans population live near already degraded forests and 90 receive some portion of drinking water from streams damaged by illegal logging operations.[33] Indigenous communities and local authorities say that environmental crimes linked to illegal logging continue to affect native wildlife on the plateau, although conservation efforts implemented in recent decades appear to have slowed the rate of deforestation and helped prevent steep declines in biodiversity seen throughout Latin America.[34] See also Notes

The 25th Amendment of the U.S. Constitution addresses this scenario. It states that when the Vice President and a majority of the principal officers of the executive branch, or any other body established by law, submit a written statement indicating that the President is unable to fulfill his duties, the Vice President assumes the role of Acting President. The [25th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution](URL0) outlines this process. If the President becomes incapacitated or cannot perform his duties, he may formally transfer power to the Vice President temporarily. If he later decides to reclaim these powers, he must do so through a formal declaration. If the President cannot make this decision, the Vice President, with the backing of a majority of the Cabinet, can issue a declaration taking over the President’s powers. The Vice President and Cabinet may challenge this action, which would then be decided by Congress.

The reliance of human-machine interaction on speech communication is growing, with machine learning models often used to process human speech commands. Nevertheless, these models can be vulnerable to adversarial examples—perturbations introduced deliberately to cause incorrect predictions without detection. Although significant efforts have been directed toward creating new methods for generating such perturbations, fewer studies have examined factors influencing how well humans detect these disturbances. This issue is critical because the efficacy of adversarial perturbation strategies hinges on their imperceptibility to humans. In this study, we examine whether the distortion metrics previously proposed for evaluating audio-based adversarial examples accurately reflect human perception of these disturbances. By employing an analytical model and conducting an experiment where 18 participants assess audio adversarial examples, we find that conventional metrics do not reliably capture the perceptual similarity of these examples in the audio domain.

Modern science is dominated by scientific productions from teams. Large teams have demonstrated a clear advantage over small teams in applying for funding, performing complicated research and producing works with high impact. A recent finding, however, shows that both large and small teams are essential in research, prompting us to analyze the extent to which a country's scientific work is carried out by bigsmall teams. Here, using over 26 million papers from Web of Science, we find that China's research output is more dominated by big teams than the rest of the world, followed by a sharp drop since 2000. As research teams in China shift from small to large size, the team diversity that is essential for innovative works does not increase as much as that in other countries. Using the national average as the baseline, we find that the National Natural Science Foundation of China (NSFC) supports fewer small team works than the National Science Foundation of U.S. (NSF) does, implying that big teams are more preferred by grant agencies in China. Our finding provides new insights into the concern of originality and innovation in China, which urges a need to balance small and big teams.

Unlike nonconvex optimization, where gradient descent is guaranteed to converge to a local optimizer, algorithms for nonconvex-nonconcave minimax optimization can have topologically different solution paths: sometimes converging to a solution, sometimes never converging and instead following a limit cycle, and sometimes diverging. In this paper, we study the limiting behaviors of three classic minimax algorithms: gradient decent ascent (GDA), alternating gradient decent ascent (AGDA), and the extragradient method (EGM). Numerically, we observe that all of these limiting behaviors can arise in Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN) training. To explain these different behaviors, we study the high-order resolution continuous-time dynamics that correspond to each algorithm, which results in the sufficient (and almost necessary) conditions for the local convergence by each method. Moreover, this ODE perspective allows us to characterize the phase transition between these different limiting behaviors caused by introducing regularization in the problem instance.

Cluster-based linear regression (CLR), which combines clustering and regression, aims to identify groups of entities so that the total sum of squared errors from regressions conducted on these clusters is minimized. Each cluster may exhibit varying levels of variance. We extend the CLR concept by enabling multiple observations per entity, introducing generalized CLR. Our methodology incorporates an exact mathematical programming approach grounded in column generation, a column generation-based heuristic algorithm that clusters predefined entity sets, a hybrid metaheuristic combining genetic algorithms with an adapted version of Lloyd's algorithm for K-means clustering, a two-step procedure, and a revised algorithm inspired by Spath for addressing generalized CLR. We evaluate the efficacy of these approaches on a stock-keeping unit (SKU) clustering task used in predicting halo and cannibalization effects during promotional activities, utilizing real-world retail data from a major supermarket chain. In this context, the retailer must group SKUs according to their seasonal responses to promotions. The seasonal impacts stem from regressions involving promotion strategies and seasonal indicators applied to clusters formed. We assess the performance of all developed algorithms against both real and simulated datasets for the SKU problem.

Various protective mechanisms help organisms resist infections, encompassing physical, chemical, and biological defenses. Mechanical barriers, such as the waxy cuticle on plant leaves, the exoskeleton of insects, the shells and membranes of external eggs, and human skin, serve as the initial line of defense. Despite this, since organisms can't fully isolate themselves from their surroundings, other systems function to safeguard bodily openings like the lungs, digestive tract, and reproductive system. In the lungs, coughing and sneezing physically remove pathogens and irritants from the airway. Tears and urine perform a cleansing action, removing pathogens, while mucus produced by these organs helps capture and bind microorganisms.

King Edward's Chair (or St Edward's Chair), the throne on which English and British sovereigns have been seated at the moment of coronation, is housed within the abbey and has been used at every coronation since 1308. From 1301 to 1996 (except for a short time in 1950 when it was temporarily stolen by Scottish nationalists), the chair also housed the Stone of Scone upon which the kings of Scots are crowned. Although the Stone is now kept in Scotland, in Edinburgh Castle, at future coronations it is intended that the Stone will be returned to St Edward's Chair for use during the coronation ceremony.[citation needed]

Critics had previously condemned officials for discontinuing MyTravelPass, a program offering a third discount on bus fares for 16-18-year-olds. However, the initiative will persist beyond April until a new plan, set for 2018, is implemented. The decision was praised by NUS Wales but criticized by the Welsh Conservatives, who viewed it as a "U-turn" highlighting past challenges in managing project initiatives. MyTravelPass was created under a budget agreement between the Welsh government and the Liberal Democrats during the previous assembly term. The government ended the scheme in January, prompting backlash from bus operators and Members of Parliament, such as Labour’s Lynne Neagle. CPT Cymru, representing the bus sector, noted that the scheme was poorly advertised and had low uptake at the time of its termination. The Welsh government stated at the time that the scheme was initially a pilot with funding up to March 2017 and that passholders rarely used their cards for travel outside their local areas. Economy Secretary Ken Skates later expressed support for a new youth travel pass, intending to introduce it in 2018. He proposed a consultation process and emphasized the need for a marketing campaign. NUS Wales’ deputy president Carmen Smith supported the decision but urged the new scheme to extend benefits to all learners aged 16-25. The Welsh Liberal Democrats also applauded the move, while Welsh Conservative skills spokesperson Mohammad Asghar called it an anticipated "U-turn," citing historical issues with project management in the economic department.

The invention of electronic computers in the 1940s, along with the development of mathematical information theory, led to a realization that brains can potentially be understood as information processing systems. This concept formed the basis of the field of cybernetics, and eventually gave rise to the field now known as computational neuroscience. The earliest attempts at cybernetics were somewhat crude in that they treated the brain as essentially a digital computer in disguise, as for example in John von Neumann's 1958 book, The Computer and the Brain. Over the years, though, accumulating information about the electrical responses of brain cells recorded from behaving animals has steadily moved theoretical concepts in the direction of increasing realism.

Human-machine interaction is increasingly dependent on speech communication. Machine Learning models are usually applied to interpret human speech commands. However, these models can be fooled by adversarial examples, which are inputs intentionally perturbed to produce a wrong prediction without being noticed. While much research has been focused on developing new techniques to generate adversarial perturbations, less attention has been given to aspects that determine whether and how the perturbations are noticed by humans. This question is relevant since high fooling rates of proposed adversarial perturbation strategies are only valuable if the perturbations are not detectable. In this paper we investigate to which extent the distortion metrics proposed in the literature for audio adversarial examples, and which are commonly applied to evaluate the effectiveness of methods for generating these attacks, are a reliable measure of the human perception of the perturbations. Using an analytical framework, and an experiment in which 18 subjects evaluate audio adversarial examples, we demonstrate that the metrics employed by convention are not a reliable measure of the perceptual similarity of adversarial examples in the audio domain.

Human survival relies on our instinct to perceive our own offspring as attractive, guided by specific "healthy baby" indicators such as small features, a rounded head, and large eyes. These traits evoke the label "cute," which demands care, attention, and affection. Young animals often experience this phase of cuteness, and some domesticated species have been selectively bred to maintain this appearance indefinitely. For instance, a chihuahua is engineered to resemble a baby due to its domed face and small features. My 14-year-old cat shares these characteristics and is exceptionally endearing. Disney animators excelled at capturing the essence of "cute," and studying classic Disney films reveals how these elements create a comforting, nurturing atmosphere that contributed to their popularity. I believe our attraction to animals stems from an innate inability to resist their charm, much like our reaction to a baby. While I find human infants unappealing, I appreciate the cuteness of animals. Although I recognize the emotional appeal of a human baby, it rarely influences my behavior. [URL1] (URL0) The evolutionary benefit of cuteness lies in encouraging adults to safeguard vulnerable children. We notice a baby's wide eyes, plump cheeks, and soft voice and respond with warmth, wanting to nurture and protect them. As the child matures, the allure diminishes, and by the time they can take care of themselves, they no longer evoke the same feelings. If we didn't find children cute, others would be less inclined to offer them food and care. Why do we find other animals endearing? It’s largely coincidental; they share similar physical attributes with human babies. Cute animals typically possess qualities like size, softness, innocence, sleepiness, and helplessness, along with expressive eyes and a tendency to be touched or held. Their resemblance to human babies activates the same caregiving response in us, and there's minimal evolutionary incentive for this trait to persist.

After its formation in 1871, Prussia emerged as the dominant state within the German Empire. However, the Treaty of Versailles following World War I transferred West Prussia to Poland and established East Prussia as an isolated territory within Weimar Germany (the new Polish Corridor dividing East Prussia from the rest of Germany). The Memel Territory was also separated and later annexed by Lithuania in 1923. After Nazi Germany's defeat in World War II in 1945, war-torn East Prussia was divided under Stalin's directive: the Soviet Union took control of the Kaliningrad Oblast in the Russian SFSR and the constituent counties of the Klaipeda Region in the Lithuanian SSR, while the People's Republic of Poland acquired the Warmian-Masurian Voivodeship. In 1946, the capital city of Konigsberg was renamed Kaliningrad. Many German residents were displaced during the war or expelled soon after, with approximately 300,000 people (about one-fifth of the population) dying due to wartime bombing or combat-related casualties. The perception that in some areas police had lost control of the streets was the most important reason disorder spread, they said. The Home Affairs Committee said insufficient numbers of officers were initially deployed and police training for public disorder was inadequate. The Metropolitan Police said it had outlined what it was doing to improve. The Policing Large Scale Disorder: Lessons from the disturbances of August 2011 report said flooding the streets with police was what ultimately quelled the disorder. "If numbers could have been increased more rapidly, it is possible that some of the disturbances could have been avoided," it said. "We regret this did not happen and, with the benefit of hindsight, we regard the operation to police the disorder in many towns and cities, and particularly in London as flawed." It said the mutual aid system, under which police officers are transferred to forces in need, could have operated more quickly; it may have left areas which had loaned officers to other forces "vulnerable." The report said anecdotal evidence from some of those convicted suggested the widespread disorder started when people saw police had "lost control" in Tottenham via television and social media. This echoes the findings of the independent Riots Communities and Victims Panel. "Clearly a feeling existed that desirable consumer goods could be made available by looting. There was a substantial element of opportunistic criminality and copycat behaviour," the report said. "The absence of a police presence or sight of police officers apparently standing by and allowing criminal behaviour to take place was distressing for those whose homes and businesses were being attacked," it added. Committee chairman Keith Vaz MP said: "Individual police officers acted with great bravery, and we commend them for their actions. However, in London and other areas, in contrast with the effectiveness of police responses in some towns and cities, there was a failure of police tactics. "This situation might have been avoided had police appreciated the magnitude of the task. "We urgently require a rapid improvement in police training to deal with public disorder. We urge the police to act more quickly in future and to review the arrangements for loaning officers from one force to another in this type of scenario." He said that, for those who lost their homes and businesses, "the state effectively ceased to exist - sometimes for hours at a time." Mr Vaz told BBC Radio 4's Today programme the committee felt that there should have been better communication between the police and the local business community to ensure that people knew what was happening and how best to protect their livelihoods. "Those areas where the chief constables had decided to take pre-emptive action and get police officers on the streets quickly were able to contain this violence much more effectively," he added. The MPs say had more officers been deployed different tactics could have been used. The Met Police is training more police to use baton rounds and is considering buying three water cannon. Mr Vaz said the committee did not feel water cannon would have helped police in the riots and may have caused "even greater disorders." Riots broke out in Tottenham, north London, on 6 August, two days after the fatal shooting by police of 29-year-old Mark Duggan. Unrest spread across London and to other cities, including Manchester, Birmingham and Bristol over the following days. But the committee's report said the specific causes behind the riots were still unknown. The report criticised the Met Police and the Independent Police Complaints Commission over failures in communication with Mr Duggan's family, which it said made a potentially tense situation worse. The committee also concluded it would be unhelpful to switch off social media during times of disorder, following claims rioters used it to organise themselves. "People who made an active decision to join in the disorder could equally well have heard about it on the television as on social media," the report said. The MPs say the government needs to urgently clarify whether the police authorities will be able to recover the PS89.827m it cost to police the riots. It says the riots were an exceptional series of events at a time the authorities were being asked to make savings. They also call on the government to speed up the process of reimbursing people under the Riot Damages Act. The Met Police said it had already recognised and publicised some of its findings on the issues identified and what it was doing to improve. A spokesman said: "This includes acknowledging that we didn't have enough officers available quickly enough to respond to the initial disorder or its subsequent unprecedented escalation. As a result we have changed our mobilisation plans." He added that the force was reviewing how it engaged with local communities and was working with Acpo and the IPCC to ensure communication was more effective in future investigations. The Association of Chief Police Officers said the report had identified issues it believed was critical to get right within current policing reforms. "This includes the capacity and ability to move sufficient numbers of police officers around the country when required to protect the public from national threats," a spokesman said. "We will continue to look at all the various reports into the disorder to examine how the police service can best respond in future to the kind of exceptional criminality seen in August."

This note outlines an algorithm for nonlinear fitting that integrates elements of linear least squares into a general minimum squared fit, along with a pure Python implementation. It combines the variable projection method (varpro) with a Newton optimization technique, employing a stabilized steepest descent approach. We tested the method using simulated data, and it is well-suited for fitting scenarios involving sums of exponentials, commonly encountered in Lattice Quantum Chromodynamics.

The Ottomans incorporated elements from the traditions, arts, and institutions of the cultures they subjugated, enriching them with new features. Many aspects from earlier empires—such as architecture, food, music, recreation, and governance—were adopted by the Ottoman Turks, who transformed them into novel expressions, giving rise to a unique and distinct Ottoman cultural identity. Although new combinations were introduced, the Ottoman dynasty, akin to its forebears in the Byzantine Empire and the Seljuks, remained deeply Persianized in terms of culture, language, behavior, and customs. As a result, the empire is often referred to as a Persianate state. Interethnic unions also contributed to shaping the defining characteristics of the Ottoman elite culture. Compared to Turkish rural traditions, it is evident that the impact of these foreign influences was significant in forging the cultural fabric of the Ottoman elite.

In 1997, mammals were thoroughly reclassified by Malcolm C. McKenna and Susan K. Bell, leading to the McKennaBell classification. Their 1997 publication, "Classification of Mammals above the Species Level," represents the most detailed study yet of the taxonomy, evolutionary relationships, and distribution of all mammalian groups, both extant and extinct, down to the genus level. Although recent molecular genetic findings question some of the higher-level classifications, the authors collaborated as paleontologists at the American Museum of Natural History in New York. McKenna took over the project from Simpson and, alongside Bell, developed a fully revised hierarchical system encompassing both present-day and ancient species, reflecting the evolutionary history of Mammalia.

The U.S. dollar was created by the Constitution and defined by the Coinage Act of 1792. It specified a "dollar" to be based in the Spanish milled dollar and of 371 grains and 4 sixteenths part of a grain of pure or 416 grains (27.0 g) of standard silver and an "eagle" to be 247 and 4 eighths of a grain or 270 grains (17 g) of gold (again depending on purity). The choice of the value 371 grains arose from Alexander Hamilton's decision to base the new American unit on the average weight of a selection of worn Spanish dollars. Hamilton got the treasury to weigh a sample of Spanish dollars and the average weight came out to be 371 grains. A new Spanish dollar was usually about 377 grains in weight, and so the new U.S. dollar was at a slight discount in relation to the Spanish dollar.

The Abbot of Monte Cassino, Desiderius, dispatched envoys to Constantinople around 1066 to recruit skilled Byzantine mosaics artists for the restoration of the rebuilt abbey church. As recorded by the chronicler Leo of Ostia, the Greek artisans adorned the apse, arch, and vestibule of the basilica. While their work was praised by contemporaries, it was entirely lost over time, with only two fragments—depicting greyhounds—remaining today at the Monte Cassino Museum. The chronicler notes that the abbot's decision to train many young monks in these artistic techniques played a significant role in reviving mosaic art in medieval Italy.

In recent years, the town of Wenatchee, Washington has become a hub for bitcoin mining. And now, local officials are grappling with how to deal with the influx of miners who are drawn to the area by its cheap hydropower. The problem began last year, when the city of Wenatchee's electric utility started receiving complaints from residents about high electricity bills. The utility investigated and found that some of its customers were using more than 10 times the amount of power than the average household. After some digging, the utility discovered that many of these homes were being used as bitcoin mines. Bitcoin mining is a process of verifying and adding transaction records to the public ledger, known as the blockchain. It's a computationally intensive process that requires a lot of energy. In Wenatchee, miners are attracted by the cheap hydropower that is generated by the Columbia River. But as more and more miners move into the area, local officials are concerned about the impact on the town's infrastructure and quality of life. The city council is currently considering an ordinance that would regulate bitcoin mining operations. Under the proposed ordinance, miners would be required to obtain a business license and pay a 500 fee. They would also be subject to inspections to ensure that their operations are safe and do not pose a nuisance to their neighbors. The ordinance has divided the community, with some people welcoming the regulation of bitcoin mining and others concerned that it will stifle innovation. The city council is expected to vote on the ordinance in the coming weeks. Whether or not the ordinance passes, it's clear that the town of Wenatchee is facing a challenges as it grapple with the influx of bitcoin miners.

A new color correction method is proposed for color biased images based on a linear image inversion approach. The proposed method is based on the principle that the spectral reflectance and the spectral sensitivity are inversely proportional. The spectral reflectance is first inverted into spectral sensitivity, and then the spectral sensitivity is used to invert the spectral reflectance into the true color by minimizing the least-squares method. In 2012, Abigail Fisher, an undergraduate student at Louisiana State University, and Rachel Multer Michalewicz, a law student at Southern Methodist University, filed a lawsuit to challenge the University of Texas admissions policy, asserting it had a "race-conscious policy" that "violated their civil and constitutional rights." The University of Texas employs the "Top Ten Percent Law," under which admission to any public college or university in Texas is guaranteed to high school students who graduate in the top ten percent of their high school class. Fisher has brought the admissions policy to court because she believes that she was denied acceptance to the University of Texas based on her race, and thus, her right to equal protection according to the 14th Amendment was violated. The Supreme Court heard oral arguments in Fisher on October 10, 2012, and rendered an ambiguous ruling in 2013 that sent the case back to the lower court, stipulating only that the University must demonstrate that it could not achieve diversity through other, non-race sensitive means. In July 2014, the US Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit concluded that U of T maintained a "holistic" approach in its application of affirmative action, and could continue the practice. On February 10, 2015, lawyers for Fisher filed a new case in the Supreme Court. It is a renewed complaint that the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit got the issue wrong - on the second try as well as on the first. The Supreme Court agreed in June 2015 to hear the case a second time. It will likely be decided by June 2016.

The 130th (St John) Field Ambulance has received recognition through the rededication of a plaque. The Archbishop of Wales and the Duke of Gloucester, who serves as the Grand Prior of St John, are among 200 invited attendees. The event takes place at 14:00 BST at St John the Baptist in Cardiff's central area. Dame Rosemary Butler, the presiding officer of the Welsh Assembly, also attended. The 130th unit consisted of St John Ambulance-trained personnel recruited from coal mining regions in southern Wales. These soldiers participated in significant battles during World War I, including the Battle of Mametz Wood on the Somme in July 1916 and the Pilckem Ridge during the Third Battle of Ypres in 1917. They earned 25 military medals for bravery, two Distinguished Conduct Medals, two Croix de Guerre, and three Military Crosses.
